0.title: Romans
0.overview:
Martin Luther called the letter to the Romans "the chief part of the New Testament and the very purest gospel." John Calvin wrote that "when anyone understands this Epistle, he has a passage opened to him to the understanding of the whole Scripture." Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached 366 sermons on it over some thirteen years and still felt he had not exhausted it. Romans is not one letter among many; it is the theological heart of the New Testament, the fullest and most systematic exposition of the gospel that God ever moved a human pen to write.

Paul wrote to a church he had never visited, in the capital of the empire, at the height of his apostolic ministry — probably from Corinth around AD 57. His purpose was not merely to introduce himself before a planned visit to Spain. It was to set before these believers, Jew and Gentile alike, the full panorama of the gospel: the universal guilt of humanity, the righteousness of God revealed in Christ, justification by faith alone, the transforming work of the Spirit, the sovereign purposes of God in election and in the mystery of Israel, and the shape of the redeemed life in the world. No letter covers more ground. No letter has changed more lives.

The structure follows the gospel's own logic. Chapters 1–3 establish the diagnosis: all humanity — pagan, moralist, and Jew — stands guilty before the righteous God, with no resources of its own to secure acquittal. Chapters 3–5 announce the remedy: the righteousness of God given freely through faith in Jesus Christ, who bore the wrath we deserved. Chapters 6–8 trace the fruit: union with Christ, death to sin, life in the Spirit, adoption as children, and the unshakeable security of those whom God has called. Chapters 9–11 address the mystery: if Israel is the covenant people, why has Israel largely rejected its Messiah? And chapters 12–16 show what the gospel-transformed life looks like in home, church, city, and empire.

Who were the Christians in Rome? No apostle founded the church. Luke lists visitors from Rome in the Pentecost crowd (Acts 2:10), and the gospel probably reached the capital through Jewish believers like them. Some years before this letter Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2), and for a time the congregations were largely Gentile. When Jewish believers returned after his death, they came back to churches whose leaders and habits had changed. That tension between Jewish and Gentile Christians lies behind much of the letter, especially chapters 9–11 and 14–15 (cf. 1:7).

And what of the New Perspective on Paul? Since the 1970s scholars such as E. P. Sanders, James Dunn and N. T. Wright have argued that first-century Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation; that works of the law means chiefly the marks that set Jews apart, such as circumcision, the food laws and the Sabbath; and that justification is mainly about who belongs to God’s people. They are right that the unity of Jew and Gentile is a real concern of Romans (3:29–30; 15:7), and that Judaism has sometimes been described unfairly. But the more likely reading is the Reformation one. Paul’s charge in 1:18–3:20 is not that Jews kept Gentiles out but that all have broken God’s law and stand guilty before him, so that every mouth may be stopped (3:19). Justification answers that guilt. It is God’s verdict of acquittal, given freely to the ungodly (4:5) on the ground of Christ’s blood (5:9). Belonging to God’s people follows from that verdict; it is not what the verdict means.

We will draw on the great Reformed interpreters of this letter: Calvin's magisterial commentary, Luther whose reading of 1:17 unlocked the Reformation, Lloyd-Jones whose fourteen volumes remain the richest English-language treatment, John Stott whose Message of Romans is a model of accessible depth, Timothy Keller's Romans for You, and scholars Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner. Come expecting to be undone and remade. Romans has that effect on everyone who takes it seriously.

1.title: The Gospel and the Wrath of God
1.overview:
Romans 1 opens with one of the most carefully crafted sentences in ancient literature — a single Greek sentence spanning seven verses, in which Paul introduces himself, his gospel, and his Lord with the precision of a theologian and the ardour of a man in love with what he believes. By the time the chapter ends, the same pen that wrote of the gospel as "the power of God for salvation" has traced the terrifying arc of divine wrath against human idolatry. These two things belong together: the good news is only truly good when the bad news is truly bad.

The movement of the chapter is deliberate. Paul establishes the gospel (vv. 1–17), then demonstrates the need for it (vv. 18–32). The power of God for salvation is proportionate to the depth of human lostness — and that depth, as Paul will show, is vertiginous. The world Paul describes in vv. 18–32 is not ancient history; it is every human culture that has suppressed the knowledge of the God it cannot stop knowing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Paul, the Gospel, and the Grace of Apostleship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's opening sentence is a controlled explosion of theology. In seven verses he identifies himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called as an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God — a gospel promised in the Old Testament Scriptures, concerning God's Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and declared to be the Son of God in power by the resurrection from the dead. Every phrase is a chapter of theology waiting to be unfolded. This is not a man warming up; this is a man who knows exactly what he believes and why it matters.

The word that unlocks everything is euangelion — gospel. It meant, in the first-century Roman world, the proclamation of good news, typically the accession of a new emperor or a great military victory. Paul seizes the word and repurposes it entirely. The great news is not that Caesar has triumphed; it is that Jesus Christ, Son of God, Lord, has been raised from the dead and now reigns over all things. This is a message with empire-shaking implications — which is precisely why Paul is eager to preach it in Rome itself.

The address of grace and peace — "to all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints" — is not a formality. It is a theological declaration. These people, in the capital of pagan power, are loved by God. They are called. They are saints — not by virtue of their moral achievement but by virtue of their union with Jesus Christ who is holy, and who has made them holy in him. Before Paul preaches a word of gospel to them, he speaks a word of gospel over them. This is the Pauline method: ground identity before applying imperatives.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Pauline Gospel

One of the most important features of Romans 1:1–4 is Paul's insistence that the gospel he preaches was "promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures." The gospel is not a Pauline invention or a Gentile innovation — it is the fulfilment of Israel's own scriptures. Jesus is the descendant of David (2 Samuel 7), declared Son of God by resurrection (Psalm 2). Calvin saw in this the unity of the two testaments: the Old Testament is the gospel in promise; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. Any reading of the Old Testament that does not find Christ there has missed its point.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's designation of himself as a doulos — slave — of Christ Jesus was shocking in a world where slavery was degradation. He inverts the social order: the highest dignity available to a human being is not freedom but bondage to Jesus Christ. Now: In an age that prizes autonomy above all things, the Christian claim that the best possible life is one of radical submission to Christ still provokes the same offence — and still offers the same liberation to those who discover that the lordship of Christ is the only yoke that is easy and the only burden that is light.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God,

Meaning first. Romans is Paul’s fullest explanation of the gospel. Written from Corinth around AD 57 to a church he had never visited, it lays out the whole plan of salvation: all are sinners under God’s wrath (1:18–3:20); God justifies the ungodly by faith in Christ alone (3:21–5:21); the justified are set free from sin’s power and given the Spirit (6–8); God’s purpose for Israel is not frustrated (9–11); and the gospel shapes a whole new way of life (12–16). Luther called it the clearest gospel of all. Augustine, Luther, Wesley and countless others were converted through it. Chapter 1 opens with Paul’s greeting and theme, and then begins the long argument: the wrath of God against a humanity that knew God and turned from him.

Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus. Key words. “Servant” translates the ordinary word for a slave, one wholly owned by a master (doulos). Paul’s first title is not apostle but slave. But in the Old Testament, “servant of the Lord” was also a title of honour for Moses, David and the prophets. Owned by Christ, and honoured by it.

Called to be an apostle. Not self-appointed (Galatians 1:1). An apostle: one sent with authority, an eyewitness of the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 9:1).

Set apart for the gospel of God. “Set apart” (aphōrismenos): separated, perhaps a play on “Pharisee,” the separated one. Once separated for the law; now separated for the gospel. “The gospel of God”: it comes from God, it is his good news.

In a sentence. Paul introduces himself as a slave of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle and set apart for the gospel of God.

On a Tuesday. Your first identity is Christ’s servant. Everything else comes after.
verseByVerse.note: “Servant” translates the ordinary word for a slave, one wholly owned by his master. Paul wrote Romans from Corinth, probably around AD 57, before taking the collection to Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: before you were born I consecrated you

verseByVerse.quote: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh
verseByVerse.commentary:
which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh

Which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures. Key words. The gospel is not new. It was promised in the Old Testament (Genesis 3:15; 12:3; Isaiah 53). The whole Bible is one story. “Holy Scriptures”: the first use of the phrase in the New Testament.

Concerning his Son. Key words. The gospel is about a person. Not first a system, a method, or a moral code, but God’s Son.

Who was descended from David according to the flesh. His human nature: a true man, born of David’s line, fulfilling the promise of an eternal son of David (2 Samuel 7:12–16). “According to the flesh” means according to his human descent.

In a sentence. God promised this gospel long ago through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, and it concerns his Son, who as a man was a descendant of David.

For worship. The gospel is about Jesus. Make him the centre of your faith.

parallels.desc: the promised son of David

verseByVerse.quote: and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection from the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,

And was declared to be the Son of God in power. Key words. “Declared” (horisthentos): appointed, marked out, installed. Not that he became God’s Son at the resurrection, since he is already called “his Son” in v. 3. But by the resurrection he was publicly installed as the Son of God “in power,” moving from weakness to power, from humiliation to exaltation (Philippians 2:6–11). Two stages: descended from David in weakness, declared Son in power.

According to the Spirit of holiness. Probably the Holy Spirit, by whose power he was raised (8:11). Or his own holy spirit. The contrast is between “according to the flesh” (v. 3) and “according to the Spirit”: two stages of his saving work.

By his resurrection from the dead. The proof (Acts 13:33; 17:31).

Jesus Christ our Lord. His full name and title.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jesus became the Son of God at the resurrection, as adoptionists taught. He is the eternal Son, who took flesh and was exalted.

In a sentence. By his resurrection from the dead, he was declared with power to be the Son of God by the Spirit of holiness: Jesus Christ our Lord.

On a Tuesday. The risen Jesus reigns in power. Serve him as your Lord.

parallels.desc: you are my Son

verseByVerse.quote: ...through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations, including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ... — Romans 1:5-6
verseByVerse.commentary:
through whom we have received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith for the sake of his name among all the nations, including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ,

Through whom we have received grace and apostleship. Grace first, then apostleship. Paul’s ministry rested on grace.

To bring about the obedience of faith. Key words. A key phrase, repeated at the end of the letter (16:26). Either the obedience that is faith (believing the gospel is obeying God), or the obedience that comes from faith. Both are true. Faith is a response of obedience to God’s call, and it produces obedience. Not faith versus obedience, but faith working through love (Galatians 5:6).

For the sake of his name among all the nations. The goal: Christ’s glory among every people.

Including you who are called to belong to Jesus Christ. “Called”: effectually called, summoned by God (8:28–30). They belong to Jesus.

In a sentence. Through Christ Paul received grace and apostleship to bring people from all nations to the obedience that comes from faith, for his name’s sake, including the Roman believers called to belong to Jesus Christ.

For worship. You are called to belong to Jesus Christ. There is no greater honour.

parallels.desc: the obedience of faith

verseByVerse.quote: To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. — Romans 1:7
verseByVerse.commentary:
To all those in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

To all those in Rome who are loved by God. Key words. Before they are anything else, they are loved.

And called to be saints. “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people: all believers, not a special class (Acts 9:13). Called saints: made holy by God’s call, not by their own achievement.

Grace to you and peace. Key words. Paul’s greeting combines the Greek greeting (charis, grace) and the Hebrew (shalom, peace). Grace is God’s undeserved favour; peace is its result: reconciliation with God and wholeness of life.

From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Jesus put alongside the Father as the source of grace and peace. Only God gives grace. A quiet but clear statement of Christ’s deity.

In a sentence. Paul writes to all in Rome loved by God and called to be saints: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. You are loved by God and called to be holy. Begin each day there.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers. The church at Rome was not founded by Paul; he had never been there.

parallels.desc: visitors from Rome at Pentecost

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — Paul's Longing and His Debt to All
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having established his gospel and his greeting, Paul opens his heart. He has prayed for the Roman Christians unceasingly. He has longed to visit them. He has been prevented — more than once. This passage is often passed over quickly on the way to the theological fireworks of vv. 16–17, but it deserves careful attention: it shows us what a gospel-shaped pastor looks like. Paul's longing is not merely strategic (Rome as a missionary base) but personal. He wants to see them, to be mutually encouraged, to share with them some spiritual gift.

The phrase "I am under obligation" (v. 14) — literally "I am a debtor" — is startling. Paul does not feel that preaching the gospel to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, is above and beyond the call of duty. He feels indebted to them. They have a claim on him. The grace that was lavished on him on the Damascus road was not for his private enrichment; it was for their benefit. He owes them what he received for free. This is the logic of all gospel ministry: grace received creates obligation discharged.

"I am not ashamed of the gospel" (v. 16) — the understatement implies the opposite: he is eagerly proud of it, itching to proclaim it in Rome's very centre. Rome was the most intimidating platform imaginable: the seat of empire, the crossroads of civilization, the city that had crucified the Lord of the gospel. And Paul cannot wait to get there.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pastoral and Missionary Logic of Paul

Romans 1:8–15 reveals that Paul's missionary strategy is inseparable from his pastoral affection. He does not view the Roman church as an audience for his theology or a resource for his mission; he views them as beloved brothers and sisters in whom he longs to rejoice. Reformed missiology has always insisted that mission and church are inseparable — the mission proceeds from the church, through the church, and for the establishment of the church. Paul's eagerness to visit Rome exemplifies this: he is not a lone-ranger evangelist but an apostle embedded in the body of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's sense of debt to all people — Greeks and barbarians, wise and foolish — erased every cultural and social hierarchy. The gospel belonged to no class or culture. Now: The contemporary church is perpetually tempted to preach a gospel shaped for those who are already culturally similar to us. Paul's "debtor" language is a rebuke: the gospel is owed to every person in our reach, regardless of whether they seem like likely converts or comfortable neighbours.

verseByVerse.quote: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I mention you
verseByVerse.commentary:
First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son, that without ceasing I mention you

First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you. Key words. Thanksgiving comes first. “My God”: personal. “Through Jesus Christ”: even thanks goes through the mediator.

Because your faith is proclaimed in all the world. A church in the capital of the empire: news of its faith travelled.

For God is my witness, whom I serve with my spirit in the gospel of his Son. “Serve” (latreuō): worship, priestly service. Preaching the gospel is an act of worship (15:16).

That without ceasing I mention you. Paul prayed constantly for a church he had never seen.

In a sentence. First Paul thanks his God through Jesus Christ for them all, because their faith was being reported throughout the world, and God, whom he serves wholeheartedly in the gospel of his Son, knows that he remembers them constantly...

For worship. Thank God for other believers, even those you don’t know. Pray for them by name.

verseByVerse.quote: always in my prayers, asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
always in my prayers, asking that somehow by God’s will I may now at last succeed in coming to you.

Always in my prayers. Constant intercession.

Asking that somehow by God’s will I may now at last succeed in coming to you. Key words. “Somehow”: Paul didn’t know how. “By God’s will”: submitted. He did come, in chains, after shipwreck (Acts 28). God answered, in his way.

In a sentence. In his prayers he always asks that now at last by God’s will he might succeed in coming to them.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your plans, by God’s will. He may answer in a way you don’t expect.

verseByVerse.quote: For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other's faith, both yours and mine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you — that is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both yours and mine.

For I long to see you, that I may impart to you some spiritual gift to strengthen you. Not one of the specific gifts of 1 Corinthians 12, but a spiritual blessing, strengthening.

That is, that we may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both yours and mine. Key words. The great apostle corrects himself humbly: not just me giving to you, but each of us strengthening the other. Fellowship is two-way. Even Paul needed encouragement (Acts 28:15).

In a sentence. Paul longs to see them to share some spiritual gift to strengthen them, or rather that they might encourage each other by their shared faith.

For worship. You need other believers, and they need you. Fellowship strengthens faith.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented), in order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles.

I do not want you to be unaware, brothers. The ESV notes that “brothers” can include sisters in the church. Brothers and sisters in God’s family.

I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented). By the work elsewhere (15:22). Even an apostle’s plans were often blocked (Acts 16:6–7).

In order that I may reap some harvest among you as well as among the rest of the Gentiles. “Harvest” (karpon): fruit. Conversions and growth.

In a sentence. Paul wants them to know that he had often planned to come, but had been prevented until now, so that he might have a harvest among them as among other Gentiles.

On a Tuesday. Hindrances don’t mean God has said no forever. Keep praying and planning.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “brothers” can include sisters in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. — Romans 1:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish. So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome.

I am under obligation both to Greeks and to barbarians. Key words. “Under obligation” (opheiletēs): a debtor. Paul owes the gospel to everyone. Not that they had given him something, but that Christ had entrusted him with good news for them. To withhold it would be theft. Greeks thought of all non-Greek speakers as “barbarians.” Paul owes the gospel to the cultured and the uncultured alike.

Both to the wise and to the foolish. Educated and uneducated.

So I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome. Even to believers: the gospel isn’t just for unbelievers. Christians need the gospel preached to them too.

In a sentence. Paul is under obligation to Greeks and non-Greeks, wise and foolish, so he is eager to preach the gospel to those in Rome too.

For worship. You are a debtor to everyone you know who doesn’t know Christ. Pay your debt.
verseByVerse.note: Greeks thought of all non-Greek speakers as “barbarians.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–17 — The Theme: The Righteousness of God by Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Two verses. The entire letter in miniature. Everything Paul will argue across sixteen chapters is compressed here with the density of a diamond. "I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written: 'The righteous shall live by faith.'" This is the thesis statement of Romans, and it is the sentence that changed the world.

Martin Luther, tormented by the phrase "the righteousness of God" — understanding it as the terrifying standard by which God condemns sinners — wrestled with it until the light broke. "At last," he wrote, "meditating day and night...I began to understand that the righteousness of God is that by which the righteous lives by a gift of God, namely by faith. And this is the meaning: the righteousness of God is revealed by the gospel, namely, the passive righteousness with which the merciful God justifies us by faith. Here I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates." The Reformation began in these two verses.

The gospel is power — not advice, not inspiration, not a moral framework, but the very power of God actively at work to save. It is power for salvation — not merely forgiveness of past sins, but the complete rescue of a human being from the dominion of sin and death and the wrath of God, and the restoration of that person to the full flourishing of life in God. And it is for everyone who believes — the one condition, the one instrument, the one hand that receives what God freely gives: faith.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Righteousness of God: Attribute or Gift?

Reformed exegesis has understood "the righteousness of God" in Romans 1:17 as a righteousness that originates with God and is given by God to the believing sinner — what the Reformers called iustitia aliena, an alien righteousness, a righteousness that is not our own. Luther's breakthrough was recognising that this righteousness is not the demanding standard that condemns but the gracious gift that saves. This is the doctrine of imputation: Christ's perfect righteousness is credited to the account of the believing sinner, so that God can be simultaneously just (the sin has been punished in Christ) and the justifier (the sinner is declared righteous). Calvin called this the "wonderful exchange" — Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Luther's discovery of Romans 1:17 broke the back of a system of salvation by merit and religious performance that had enslaved Western Christendom for centuries. The Reformation was, at its heart, a rediscovery of these two verses. Now: Every generation re-erects the system of merit that the gospel demolishes. Every human heart, left to itself, believes it must earn its standing with God. Romans 1:16–17 is the permanent, repeatable antidote: the gospel is not something you do; it is something done for you, received by faith, given by the merciful God who justifies the ungodly.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. — Romans 1:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.

For I am not ashamed of the gospel. Key words. Rome despised it. A crucified Jew as Saviour was foolishness to the Romans, a stumbling block to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). Paul could have been tempted to be ashamed, in the capital of power. He wasn’t.

For it is the power of God for salvation. Key words. The theme of the whole letter. The gospel is not just information about power; it is God’s power, at work. “Power” (dynamis): the Rome of the Caesars thought it had power. The gospel is greater. “Salvation”: rescue from sin, wrath and death, into eternal life.

To everyone who believes. The condition, and the only one. Not to everyone who obeys the law, but who believes. Open to all.

To the Jew first and also to the Greek. Israel first, in God’s order (Acts 13:46), but no less for Gentiles.

In a sentence. Paul is not ashamed of the gospel, because it is God’s power to save everyone who believes, first the Jew and then the Greek.

On a Tuesday. Don’t be ashamed of the gospel. It is the power of God, and it can save anyone you know.

verseByVerse.quote: For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, 'The righteous shall live by faith.' — Romans 1:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, “The righteous shall live by faith.”

For in it the righteousness of God is revealed. Key words. “The righteousness of God”: the phrase that changed Luther’s life. He had hated it, thinking it meant the justice by which God punishes sinners. Then he saw: it is the righteousness from God, which he gives to sinners as a gift (3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). God’s righteousness revealed in the gospel is both his own righteous character, shown in saving justly through the cross (3:25–26), and the righteous status he gives to all who believe. It is a gift, received.

From faith for faith. The ESV notes that “from faith for faith” can also be rendered “beginning and ending in faith.” Faith from start to finish. Not faith plus works.

As it is written, “The righteous shall live by faith.” Key words. From Habakkuk 2:4. The person who is righteous by faith will live: have life, eternal life. Faith alone, from the Old Testament.

Where Christians differ: what is the righteousness of God? Roman Catholic teaching sees it mainly as a righteousness God works into us over time, making us just. Some recent scholars (the New Perspective) see it as God’s covenant faithfulness. Verdict: it includes God’s faithfulness and his righteous character, but at its heart in Romans it is the gift of a righteous standing before God, credited to the believer on the basis of Christ’s work (3:21–26; 4:5–6; 5:17). We are justified by Christ’s righteousness imputed to us, not by our own righteousness imparted. This is the heart of the Reformation, and of the gospel.

In a sentence. In the gospel the righteousness from God is revealed, by faith from first to last, as Scripture says: the righteous will live by faith.

For worship. You are righteous before God by faith, clothed in Christ’s righteousness. Live by it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “from faith for faith” can also be rendered “beginning and ending in faith,” and the quotation “The one who by faith is righteous shall live.”

parallels.desc: the righteous shall live by his faith

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–32 — The Wrath of God and the Ruin of Idolatry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Having announced the gospel, Paul immediately establishes why it is necessary. The gospel is good news only against the backdrop of very bad news — and the bad news Paul now delivers is as stark and unsparing as anything in Scripture. God's wrath is being revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth in unrighteousness. The problem is not ignorance; it is suppression. Humanity knows God — knows him through creation, through conscience — and actively holds that knowledge down, refusing its implications, fleeing from its demands.

The structure of vv. 18–32 is a three-stage description of idolatry's logic and its consequences. First, the knowledge of God is suppressed (vv. 18–20). Then, God is exchanged for idols — images of creatures replacing the uncreated Creator (vv. 21–23). Then, God gives them up — three times that terrible phrase appears (vv. 24, 26, 28) — abandoning them to the sexual and moral dissolution that is both the consequence and the judgment of their idolatry. The wrath of God is not primarily a future event; it is a present reality, operating through the structure of a moral universe that reaps what it sows.

This passage is not a description of the worst of humanity — the serial killers and tyrants. It is a description of normal human culture operating without the restraining grace of God. The Rome to which Paul wrote would have recognised itself in these verses. So would every culture in every age. So would every human heart that is honest enough to look clearly at itself.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Wrath of God

Reformed theology has insisted, against every attempt to soften or allegorize it, that the wrath of God is real, personal, and active. It is not merely the impersonal outworking of a moral law (as C.H. Dodd argued), nor a primitive metaphor for natural consequences. It is the holy, settled, righteous opposition of the living God to everything that contradicts his character. Leon Morris showed definitively that in both Testaments, divine wrath is personal and purposeful — God's moral revulsion at sin, expressed in active judgment. The gospel is only fully good news when this wrath is fully real: Christ bore the wrath we deserved (3:25), and those who are in Christ are saved from the wrath to come (5:9).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's description of idol worship in vv. 22–23 — exchanging the glory of the immortal God for images of mortal creatures — described the Roman religious world exactly. The pantheon of Rome was populated by humanised gods and deified emperors, all of them creatures rather than Creator. Now: The idols have changed shape but not substance. We exchange the glory of God for the image of the successful career, the perfect family, the autonomous self, the entertained mind. Every idol is a creature thing promoted to Creator status — and Paul's analysis of the consequences (futile thinking, darkened hearts, moral dissolution) maps precisely onto what happens when any created thing is made to bear the weight only God can carry.

verseByVerse.quote: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth.

For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven. Key words. Before Paul explains the good news fully, he shows why we need it. The wrath of God is not uncontrolled rage, but his holy, settled opposition to evil. It is “revealed” now, in the present, as God gives people over to their sins (vv. 24, 26, 28), and will be revealed fully at the judgment (2:5).

Against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. “Ungodliness”: sin against God; “unrighteousness”: sin against people. Both.

Who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth. Key words. “Suppress” (katechontōn): hold down, as one holds something under water. The truth about God is known, but held down. Unbelief is not innocent ignorance, but active suppression.

Where Christians differ: is God’s wrath real? Some say a loving God cannot be wrathful, or that wrath is just the natural consequence of sin. Verdict: God’s wrath is personal and real, the reaction of his holiness to evil. Love and wrath are not opposites; a God who did not oppose evil would not be good. And the gospel is God’s answer: Christ bore that wrath (3:25; 5:9).

In a sentence. God’s wrath is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of people who suppress the truth by their wickedness.

On a Tuesday. God’s wrath is real. That is why the gospel is such good news.

verseByVerse.quote: For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse.

For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. Key words. General revelation: God shows himself to everyone through creation (Psalm 19:1–4; Acts 14:17).

His invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived. Two things are clear from creation: God’s power (he must be powerful to make all this), and his divine nature (he is God, not part of the world). Not the gospel, but enough.

So they are without excuse. Key words. Enough to condemn, not enough to save. Everyone knows there is a God, and is responsible for not honouring him. No one can say at the judgment, “I didn’t know.”

In a sentence. What may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain: since the creation of the world his invisible qualities, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen in what he has made, so they have no excuse.

For worship. Creation shouts that God exists. Look at the stars tonight and worship him.

parallels.desc: the heavens declare the glory of God

verseByVerse.quote: For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools,

For although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him. Key words. The root sin: not honouring God as God, and ingratitude. Not atheism first, but refusal to give God his due. Every sin begins here.

But they became futile in their thinking. “Futile” (emataiōthēsan): empty, vain. Rejecting God empties the mind.

And their foolish hearts were darkened. The heart, the centre of the person, darkened.

Claiming to be wise, they became fools. Key words. Human wisdom without God becomes folly (1 Corinthians 1:20–21; Psalm 14:1). The great irony of proud intellect.

In a sentence. Although they knew God, they neither glorified him as God nor thanked him, but their thinking became futile and their foolish hearts were darkened, and claiming to be wise, they became fools.

On a Tuesday. Give thanks to God today. Ingratitude is the first step away from him.

parallels.desc: they went after worthlessness

verseByVerse.quote: and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things.

And exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images. Key words. “Exchanged”: the key word of this section (vv. 23, 25, 26). A terrible trade. The glory of God for an image. Idolatry is replacing God with something less. An echo of Israel’s golden calf (Psalm 106:20).

Resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things. Downward: man, birds, beasts, reptiles. Each step lower. Greek statues of gods in human form, Egyptian gods with animal heads. And today’s idols too: money, pleasure, power, self. Whatever takes God’s place.

In a sentence. They exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images made to look like mortal humans, birds, animals and reptiles.

For worship. What have you exchanged for God’s glory? Turn back to him.

parallels.desc: they exchanged the glory of God for the image of an ox

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.

Therefore God gave them up. Key words. “Gave them up” means God handed them over to what they chose. Three times (vv. 24, 26, 28). This is the present revelation of God’s wrath: not always fire from heaven, but letting people have what they want, and its consequences. The worst judgment is to be left to yourself.

In the lusts of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves. Rejecting God leads to the degrading of the body.

Because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie. The lie: that something other than God is God.

And worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator. The essence of idolatry.

Who is blessed forever! Amen. Paul can’t speak of the Creator without praising him.

In a sentence. So God gave them over in their hearts’ desires to impurity, degrading their bodies with one another, because they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshipped and served created things rather than the Creator, who is praised for ever, Amen.

On a Tuesday. Being left to your own desires is a judgment, not freedom. Ask God not to leave you to yourself.
verseByVerse.note: “Gave them up” means God handed them over to what they chose — his judgment working through their own desires.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature; and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another, men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature; and the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another, men committing shameless acts with men and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.

For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. The second giving up.

For their women exchanged natural relations for those that are contrary to nature. Key words. “Exchanged” again. The exchange of God for idols is mirrored in exchanging the natural for the unnatural. “Contrary to nature” (para physin): against the created order of male and female (Genesis 1:27; 2:24). The only place in Scripture explicitly mentioning women in same-sex relations.

And the men likewise gave up natural relations with women and were consumed with passion for one another. Paul describes homosexual practice as a vivid example of humanity’s rebellion against the Creator’s design.

And receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error. The consequences of the sin itself.

Where Christians differ: same-sex relationships. Some today argue that Paul was only condemning exploitative relationships, pederasty, or excessive lust, not committed same-sex unions. Verdict: Paul grounds his teaching in creation (“nature,” “the Creator”), not in the culture of his time; he includes women, which rules out the pederasty reading; and the rest of Scripture consistently teaches that sex belongs within the marriage of a man and a woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6; 1 Corinthians 6:9–11). This is the historic Christian view. It must be held with compassion: same-sex attraction is a real and often painful struggle, and those who experience it are to be loved and welcomed. This sin is listed among many (vv. 29–31); every one of us is a sinner in need of grace. And the gospel offers washing, sanctification and justification to all (1 Corinthians 6:11).

In a sentence. Because of this, God gave them over to shameful lusts: women exchanged natural sexual relations for unnatural ones, and men likewise abandoned natural relations with women and burned with lust for one another, committing shameful acts with other men and receiving in themselves the penalty they deserved.

For worship. God’s design for sexuality is good. And his grace is for every sinner, including you. Hold both truths with love.

verseByVerse.quote: And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God gave them up to a debased mind to do what ought not to be done.

And since they did not see fit to acknowledge God. Key words. A wordplay: because they did not “see fit” (edokimasan) to acknowledge God, he gave them a mind that is “unfit” (adokimon), failing the test. They rejected God as unworthy; he gave them minds that are unworthy.

God gave them up to a debased mind. The third giving up. A mind that can no longer think straight about right and wrong.

To do what ought not to be done. What is improper, unfitting.

In a sentence. And since they did not think it worthwhile to keep God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what ought not to be done.

On a Tuesday. Keep God in your thinking. A mind without him becomes twisted.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: because they did not “see fit” (edokimasan) to acknowledge God, he gave them up to a “debased” (adokimon, literally “unfit”) mind.

verseByVerse.quote: They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. They are gossips,

They were filled with all manner of unrighteousness, evil, covetousness, malice. Key words. A catalogue of sins, twenty-one in all. Notice how ordinary many are. Not only the shocking sins, but covetousness, envy, strife, gossip. Every reader is included.

Full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, maliciousness. Envy and murder side by side (Matthew 5:21–22).

They are gossips. “Gossips” (psithyristas): whisperers. Listed with murder.

In a sentence. They are filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, greed and depravity, full of envy, murder, strife, deceit and malice, and they are gossips...

For worship. Examine yourself against this list. We all need the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.

Slanderers, haters of God. “Haters of God”: the root of it all.

Insolent, haughty, boastful. Pride in its many forms.

Inventors of evil. Creative in sin.

Disobedient to parents. Key words. Listed among the serious sins. Breakdown in the family is a sign of a society turned from God (2 Timothy 3:2).

Foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless. Four Greek words starting with “a-”: without understanding, without faithfulness, without natural affection, without mercy.

In a sentence. ...slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant and boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, senseless, faithless, heartless and ruthless.

On a Tuesday. Sin destroys love: in families, friendships, societies. Christ restores it.

verseByVerse.quote: Though they know God's righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die, they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though they know God’s righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die, they not only do them but give approval to those who practice them.

Though they know God’s righteous decree that those who practice such things deserve to die. Key words. The conscience knows (2:14–15). People know deep down that these things deserve judgment. “Deserve to die”: the wages of sin is death (6:23).

They not only do them but give approval to those who practice them. Key words. The final step: not just sinning, but celebrating sin, calling evil good (Isaiah 5:20). A society that approves of sin has gone furthest from God.

In a sentence. Although they know God’s righteous decree that those who do such things deserve death, they not only keep doing them but approve of those who practise them.

For worship. Don’t celebrate what God condemns. But remember: the same God offers forgiveness to all who turn to him.
