2.title: God's Impartial Judgment
2.overview:
Chapter 1 ended with a catalogue of Gentile vice that a first-century Jewish reader would have heard with satisfaction, nodding along at the depravity of the pagan world. Chapter 2 turns without warning on that same reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges." The trap is sprung. The person who condemns the sins of others while practising the same things is not morally superior to the Gentile; he is, Paul argues, in an even more culpable position — because he knows better.

Paul's target in chapter 2 is not the pagan but the moralist — specifically, the Jewish moralist who believes that covenant membership and religious privilege provide a buffer against divine judgment. They do not. God's judgment is impartial: He renders to each according to his works, to Jew and Gentile alike. The Gentile who has only the law of conscience will be judged by that; the Jew who has the law of Moses will be judged by that. In either case, the verdict will be the same: all fall short.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — God's Righteous and Impartial Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The rhetorical brilliance of Romans 2:1 is breathtaking. Paul has spent fifteen verses describing the moral ruin of the Gentile world — and now he wheels on the approving reader: "Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things." The knife Paul had been pointing at the Gentile he now turns on anyone who imagines that moral judgment of others places them above judgment themselves.

The principle Paul establishes is foundational: God's judgment is according to truth (v. 2), according to works (v. 6), without partiality (v. 11). These three principles together demolish every form of religious self-satisfaction. "According to truth" means God sees through performance to reality. "According to works" means the whole life is the evidence, not merely the religious moments. "Without partiality" means no ethnic or covenant privilege exempts anyone from accountability before the Judge of all the earth.

Verses 14–15 introduce the remarkable teaching about the conscience as a moral witness — Gentiles who do not have the Torah nonetheless "show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness." This is Paul's doctrine of moral general revelation: human beings are not morally blank. The conscience, however distorted by sin, retains something of the moral law written at creation. This is why all human beings, without exception, will have no excuse on the day of judgment.

Two things in this section deserve naming here, because they are easily lost between the principles. The first is verse 4, the warmest sentence in the passage and the most often misread: the riches of God’s kindness and forbearance and patience are not evidence that he does not mind. They are “meant to lead you to repentance”. Every day on which judgment does not fall is not indifference; it is an invitation still being held open — and Paul’s charge is that we presume on it, reading the delay as a verdict already returned in our favour. The second is verse 16, which tells us when this happens and who conducts it: “on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus”. The Judge is not a principle but a person with a face, and the material to be weighed is not the record other people can see but the secrets. Which is the most frightening sentence in the chapter, or the most freeing — since for those who are his, the one who will weigh what nobody else knows about them is the one who died for it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Judgment According to Works

Romans 2:6–11 appears to teach salvation by works — "to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life." Reformed exegesis has understood this as describing the principle of judgment (God will judge the whole life) rather than the means of salvation (which is faith alone). The person who truly seeks God from the heart will be given — by grace — the faith that produces the works that evidence genuine conversion. Works are the evidence of salvation, never its ground. Paul is not contradicting 1:16–17; he is establishing the standard of divine judgment that makes grace necessary for everyone.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in covenant privilege — circumcision, Torah, temple — as a buffer against divine judgment was a live pastoral issue in Paul's day. Many Jews believed that while Gentiles might face judgment, the covenant people were secure by virtue of their membership. Paul demolishes this with surgical precision. Now: The equivalent today is the nominal Christian who trusts in baptism, church membership, or moral respectability as a substitute for genuine faith and repentance. Paul's word is the same: God is not impressed by religious credentials. He is looking for the transformed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things.

Meaning first. Romans 2 turns from the openly wicked pagan world of chapter 1 to the moral, religious person who judges others, and especially to the Jew who has God’s law. Paul shows that they too are guilty. God judges by truth, not by privilege; he judges everyone by their deeds, Jew and Gentile alike, and knows the secrets of the heart. Having the law, being circumcised, knowing God’s will: none of these saves, if you break the law. True Jewishness, true circumcision, is of the heart, by the Spirit. The point: all are under sin, and no one can be justified by their own record.

Therefore you have no excuse, O man, every one of you who judges. Key words. Paul turns to someone nodding along to chapter 1. The moralist who condemns pagan sins. “No excuse”: the same word as 1:20.

For in passing judgment on another you condemn yourself, because you, the judge, practice the very same things. Key words. By judging, you show you know right from wrong, and so you condemn yourself, since you do the same things, at least in heart (Matthew 7:1–5). Envy, deceit, gossip, pride: the list of 1:29–31 includes respectable sins.

We know that the judgment of God rightly falls on those who practice such things. “Rightly” (kata alētheian): according to truth. God’s judgment is based on reality, not appearances.

In a sentence. So you who judge others have no excuse, for in judging them you condemn yourself, since you do the same things, and we know God’s judgment on those who do such things is based on truth.

On a Tuesday. Before you condemn someone else’s sin, look at your own heart.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you suppose, O man — you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself — that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you suppose, O man — you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself — that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?

Do you suppose... that you will escape the judgment of God? The religious person often thinks he is safe.

Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience. Key words. “Presume” (kataphroneis): despise, look down on, take for granted. Because God hasn’t punished you yet, you think he won’t. Three words for God’s goodness: kindness, forbearance (holding back judgment), patience.

Not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? Key words. The purpose of God’s patience: not to let you off, but to give you time to repent (2 Peter 3:9). His goodness should melt you, not make you comfortable.

In a sentence. Do you think, you who judge others while doing the same, that you will escape God’s judgment, or do you show contempt for the riches of his kindness, forbearance and patience, not realising that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?

For worship. God’s patience with you is an invitation to repent. Accept it today.

parallels.desc: slow to anger

verseByVerse.quote: But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God's righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works:
verseByVerse.commentary:
But because of your hard and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed. He will render to each one according to his works:

But because of your hard and impenitent heart. “Hard” (sklērotēta): the word gives us “sclerosis,” hardening. A heart that won’t repent.

You are storing up wrath for yourself. Key words. Like saving money in a bank, but wrath. Every day of unrepentance adds to it. A terrible image.

On the day of wrath when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed. The day of judgment, at Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 1:7–10).

He will render to each one according to his works. Key words. From Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12. Everyone will be judged by their deeds (Matthew 16:27; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Revelation 20:12). Does this contradict justification by faith? See v. 13.

In a sentence. Because of your stubborn, unrepentant heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself for the day of wrath, when God’s righteous judgment will be revealed and he will repay each person according to what they have done.

On a Tuesday. Every day without repentance adds to the store. Repent today, and the account is cleared in Christ.

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

verseByVerse.quote: to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life; but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life; but for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury.

To those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality, he will give eternal life. Key words. Patient, persistent good works, seeking God’s glory. Who are these? Not people who earn eternal life by works, since Paul will show that no one does that (3:9–20). They are those whose lives show that God has worked in them: believers, whose faith produces persevering good works (Ephesians 2:10; Philippians 2:12–13).

But for those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury. “Self-seeking” (eritheias): selfish ambition. Their deeds show their hearts.

In a sentence. To those who persist in doing good, seeking glory, honour and immortality, God will give eternal life, but for the self-seeking who reject the truth and follow evil, there will be wrath and anger.

For worship. Seek glory, honour and immortality from God, by patient well-doing. Your works show where your heart is.

verseByVerse.quote: There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek, but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek, but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.

There will be tribulation and distress for every human being who does evil. “Every human being”: no exceptions.

The Jew first and also the Greek. Key words. The same phrase as 1:16. First in privilege, first in responsibility. Greater light means greater accountability (Luke 12:48; Amos 3:2).

But glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good. Again, Jew first.

In a sentence. There will be trouble and distress for everyone who does evil, Jew first and then Greek, but glory, honour and peace for everyone who does good, Jew first and then Greek.

On a Tuesday. The more you know of God, the more you are responsible for. Live up to your light.

verseByVerse.quote: For God shows no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God shows no partiality.

For God shows no partiality. Key words. The principle behind it all (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34). God doesn’t favour Jews because they are Jews, or the religious because they are religious. He judges everyone by the same standard. This truth humbles the proud and gives hope to the outsider.

In a sentence. For God does not show favouritism.

For worship. God shows no favouritism. Neither should you.

verseByVerse.quote: For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. — Romans 2:12–13
verseByVerse.commentary:
For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.

For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law. Gentiles, who didn’t have the law of Moses, will not be judged by it, but they will still perish for their sins against what they knew (1:20; 2:15).

And all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. Jews will be judged by the law they had.

For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified. Key words. Having the law, hearing it read in synagogue, is not enough. You must do it. In principle, a perfect law-keeper would be justified. But no one keeps it perfectly (3:10, 20, 23). So this verse shuts every mouth. The only way to be a “doer” is through Christ, who kept the law perfectly for us, and by the Spirit who writes it on our hearts (8:4).

Where Christians differ: does Paul teach salvation by works here? Some read vv. 6–13 as teaching that final justification depends on good works. Verdict: Paul is establishing the standard: God judges by deeds, and only perfect doers could be justified by the law. He then shows no one meets it (3:9–20), so justification must be by faith apart from works (3:21–28). The good works of believers are the evidence of true faith, not its ground. We are justified by faith alone, and judged according to works that show whether that faith was real (James 2:14–26).

In a sentence. Everyone who sins without the law will perish without the law, and everyone who sins under the law will be judged by the law, for it is not those who hear the law who are righteous before God, but those who obey it who will be declared righteous.

For worship. No one keeps the law perfectly except Christ. Thank God he kept it for you.

verseByVerse.quote: For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them

For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature do what the law requires. Key words. Pagans who don’t have Moses’ law still often do what it requires: honour parents, avoid murder, keep promises. Common grace.

They are a law to themselves. Not that they make up their own rules, but that their own nature carries God’s law within.

They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts. The moral law is built into human nature (natural law). Every culture knows that some things are wrong.

While their conscience also bears witness. Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that God has given every person. A witness inside us, testifying for or against us.

And their conflicting thoughts accuse or even excuse them. An inner courtroom. Mostly accusing.

Where Christians differ: who are these Gentiles? Some say Paul means Gentile Christians, in whom the new covenant writes the law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Others say he means unbelieving Gentiles who show moral awareness. Verdict: the context (v. 12, “perish without the law”; v. 15, “accuse”) points to unbelieving Gentiles. Paul’s point is that they are not without moral knowledge, so they too are accountable. This is not saving obedience, but evidence of guilt.

In a sentence. When Gentiles, who don’t have the law, naturally do what it requires, they show that its requirements are written on their hearts, as their consciences also testify, with their thoughts sometimes accusing them and sometimes defending them.

On a Tuesday. Listen to your conscience. It is God’s witness inside you. And bring its accusations to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Conscience is the inner sense of right and wrong that God has given to every person.

parallels.desc: I will write it on their hearts

verseByVerse.quote: on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
on that day when, according to my gospel, God judges the secrets of men by Christ Jesus.

On that day when... God judges the secrets of men. Key words. God judges the secrets: not only what we do in public, but our hidden thoughts and motives (1 Corinthians 4:5; Hebrews 4:13). Nothing escapes.

According to my gospel. Judgment is part of the gospel. The good news is not that there is no judgment, but that there is a way to be safe in it.

By Christ Jesus. Key words. Jesus is the judge (Acts 17:31; John 5:22). The one who died for sinners will judge them. For those in him, the judge is their Saviour.

In a sentence. This will happen on the day when God judges people’s secrets through Christ Jesus, as Paul’s gospel declares.

For worship. God will judge your secrets. Bring them to Christ now, and they will be covered by his blood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — The Failure of Israel: Circumcision of the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now addresses the Jewish interlocutor directly, and the charge he levels is devastating. The Jew who possesses the Torah, who teaches it to others, who relies on it for his identity — does he keep it himself? "You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery?" The indictment is not that the Torah is worthless but that it cannot save those who merely possess and teach it without obeying it from the heart.

The climax of the argument comes in the citation from Isaiah and Ezekiel: "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you." This is the ultimate indictment. Israel, entrusted with the oracles of God, called to be a light to the nations, had become in its hypocrisy a reason for the nations to despise the God of Israel. The covenant privilege had become a covenant disgrace. Nothing has changed in principle: every generation of the church must face the same charge — does our life commend the God we profess?

The solution Paul gestures toward is one of the most important concepts in the entire letter: "circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter" (v. 29). This is the Old Testament's own vision — Deuteronomy 10:16, Deuteronomy 30:6, Jeremiah 31:33, Ezekiel 36:26 — now being fulfilled in the new covenant. The mark of true belonging to God is not an outward physical sign but the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. This will be Paul's great theme in chapters 6–8.

One move in the middle of the section should not be passed over, because it is the sharpest thing in it. At verse 27 Paul does not merely say that circumcision without obedience is worthless. He says that the physically uncircumcised man who keeps the law will judge the man who has the letter, the circumcision, and a record of breaking it. The outsider is called as the prosecution witness. It is the same reversal our Lord made when he said of a Roman soldier that he had not found such faith in all Israel (Matthew 8:10), and it is designed to be intolerable to anyone whose security rests in the marking rather than in the obedience the marking was given to signify.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Purpose and Limits of the Law

Romans 2:17–29 is the first extended treatment of the law's purpose and limits in the letter. Calvin identified three uses of the law: to reveal sin, to restrain wickedness in society, and to guide the redeemed life. Paul is here invoking the first use: the law reveals sin. The Jew who possesses the Torah has a clearer mirror than the Gentile — and therefore a clearer sight of his own failure to meet its demands. The law cannot save; it can only expose the need for a Saviour. This is precisely why chapters 3–4 follow: the righteousness the law demands but cannot provide is given freely in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish confidence in circumcision as the defining covenant mark was absolute in Paul's day. To question its saving significance was to question the entire structure of Second Temple Jewish identity. Paul does not question circumcision's historical significance; he relativises it entirely: the physical sign points to a spiritual reality, and when the sign is present without the reality, it is worse than useless. Now: The equivalent is any Christian community that trusts in the outward marks of religion — baptism, church attendance, doctrinal orthodoxy, moral reputation — as substitutes for the inward transformation of the heart by the Spirit. Paul's word stands: God looks at the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God and know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law;

But if you call yourself a Jew. Key words. Now Paul names his hearer directly. The Jew who has every privilege.

And rely on the law. “Rely” (epanapauē): rest on, lean on. Trusting in having the law, rather than in God.

And boast in God. Boasting in God can be good (5:11), but here it is the pride of privilege.

And know his will and approve what is excellent, because you are instructed from the law. Real privileges (9:4–5). The problem is not the privileges, but trusting in them.

In a sentence. If you call yourself a Jew, relying on the law and boasting in God, knowing his will and approving what is best because you are taught by the law...

On a Tuesday. Religious privileges, church membership, Bible knowledge, are gifts. But they can’t save you. Trust Christ, not your privileges.

verseByVerse.quote: and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
verseByVerse.commentary:
and if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—

And if you are sure that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those who are in darkness. Key words. Israel had been called to be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). A real calling. But they thought of themselves as superior, as teachers of the ignorant Gentiles. Jesus called the Pharisees blind guides (Matthew 15:14; 23:16).

An instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children. Teachers of Gentile converts.

Having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth. The law really did embody truth. But having it is not obeying it.

In a sentence. ...and if you are convinced that you are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness, an instructor of the foolish and a teacher of little children, because you have in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth...

For worship. If you teach others, be taught yourself. Humility is the teacher’s first lesson.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been called to be a light to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
verseByVerse.commentary:
you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? While you preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?

You then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? Key words. The great hypocrisy question. Every teacher, every preacher, every parent must ask it.

While you preach against stealing, do you steal? Not every Jew stole. But the point is: the law you teach condemns you too. And Jesus showed that the law reaches the heart: lust is adultery, hatred is murder (Matthew 5:21–28).

You who abhor idols, do you rob temples? Jews hated idols. But some may have dealt in goods stolen from pagan temples (Acts 19:37). Or it may mean robbing God himself, as in Malachi 3:8. Pharisees condemned idolatry while their hearts served money (Luke 16:14).

In a sentence. You who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say not to commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who hate idols, do you rob temples?

On a Tuesday. Preach to yourself before you preach to others. Practise what you teach.

verseByVerse.quote: You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law.

You who boast in the law dishonor God by breaking the law. Key words. The worst result of hypocrisy: it dishonours God. Boasting in God’s law while breaking it makes God look bad. The church’s hypocrisy still does this today.

In a sentence. You who boast in the law dishonour God by breaking it.

For worship. Your life either honours or dishonours God’s name. Ask him to make it honour him.

verseByVerse.quote: For, as it is written, "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For, as it is written, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you. Key words. From Isaiah 52:5 and Ezekiel 36:20–23. The exile itself, caused by Israel’s sin, made the nations mock Israel’s God. The behaviour of God’s people affects how outsiders see God. Christians who live badly cause the name of Christ to be blasphemed (1 Timothy 6:1; Titus 2:5).

In a sentence. As Scripture says, God’s name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.

On a Tuesday. People judge Christ by Christians. Live so that his name is honoured, not mocked.

parallels.desc: my name is continually despised

verseByVerse.quote: For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision?

For circumcision indeed is of value if you obey the law. Key words. Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham (Genesis 17). A sign of belonging to God’s covenant people. Valuable, but only with obedience. Many Jews thought circumcision guaranteed a place in the age to come.

But if you break the law, your circumcision becomes uncircumcision. The sign without the reality is worthless. A circumcised law-breaker is no better than a pagan.

So, if a man who is uncircumcised keeps the precepts of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision? The reality without the sign is what counts. Paul is preparing for the point that Gentile believers, by the Spirit, fulfil what the law requires (8:4).

A lesson for sacraments. The same applies to baptism and the Lord’s Supper. They are valuable signs, but they don’t save without faith. A baptised unbeliever is no better than an unbaptised one.

In a sentence. Circumcision has value if you keep the law, but if you break it, you are as if uncircumcised, and if an uncircumcised person keeps the law’s requirements, won’t he be regarded as circumcised?

For worship. Don’t trust outward signs. Trust Christ, and let the signs point you to him.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.

Then he who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you. Key words. A startling reversal. The Gentile will judge the Jew. As Jesus said: the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment and condemn this generation (Matthew 12:41).

You who have the written code and circumcision but break the law. “Written code” (grammatos): the letter. The outward, written law, without the Spirit.

In a sentence. The one who is not physically circumcised but obeys the law will condemn you who, though you have the written code and circumcision, break the law.

On a Tuesday. On the last day, some outsiders will shame insiders. Don’t rest on being an insider.

verseByVerse.quote: For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God. — Romans 2:28–29
verseByVerse.commentary:
For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. His praise is not from man but from God.

For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision outward and physical. Key words. Being a true member of God’s people is not a matter of race or ritual.

But a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart. Key words. The Old Testament already said it: circumcise your hearts (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4). God always wanted the inward reality. True Israel is defined by the heart.

By the Spirit, not by the letter. Key words. The Spirit does what the written law cannot: changes the heart (2 Corinthians 3:6; Ezekiel 36:26–27). This is the new covenant. Gentile believers, circumcised in heart by the Spirit, are true Jews in this sense (Philippians 3:3; Colossians 2:11).

His praise is not from man but from God. A wordplay: “Jew” comes from Judah, which means “praise” (Genesis 29:35). The true Jew seeks praise from God, not from people.

In a sentence. A person is not a Jew who is one only outwardly, nor is circumcision merely outward and physical, but a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code, and such a person’s praise comes from God, not from people.

For worship. Seek God’s praise, not people’s. And ask the Spirit to circumcise your heart.

parallels.desc: the LORD will circumcise your heart

3.title: No One Righteous — But Now, Righteousness
3.overview:
Romans 3 is one of the most concentrated pieces of theological argument in the entire Bible. It moves through three distinct but connected moments: the faithfulness of God despite human faithlessness (vv. 1–8), the universal verdict of guilt on the entire human race from the Old Testament's own testimony (vv. 9–20), and then — with the two most beautiful words in the letter — "But now" (v. 21): the announcement of a righteousness from God that is apart from the law, given through faith in Jesus Christ to all who believe.

The emotional architecture of the chapter is deliberate. Paul has spent two chapters building the case for universal human guilt — the Gentile guilty through creation and conscience, the Jew guilty despite law and covenant. Now he delivers the verdict that springs from the evidence: no one righteous, not even one. And then, from within the deepest valley of human hopelessness, he sounds the trumpet of the gospel: the righteousness of God has been manifested. The darkness is real. The light is realer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — God's Faithfulness and Human Faithlessness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
If Jewish identity and covenant privilege provide no buffer against divine judgment (chapter 2), an obvious question arises: what advantage has the Jew? Was the entire covenant history of Israel pointless? Paul will not allow this conclusion. The advantage is real and great: "they were entrusted with the oracles of God." The Torah, the prophets, the promises — these are not nothing. They are the priceless repository of God's self-revelation and covenant purposes. The problem is not the oracles; the problem is the people who received them.

But what about God's faithfulness? If Israel has been faithless to the covenant, does that mean God's covenant promises have failed? Never, Paul declares — and the energy of his negation (mē genoito — "by no means!", "God forbid!", the strongest possible denial in Greek) is palpable. God's faithfulness is not contingent on human faithfulness. He remains true even when every human being is a liar. The covenant will not fail because the Covenant God cannot fail.

This brief passage anticipates the great argument of chapters 9–11: the apparent failure of Israel to embrace her Messiah does not represent a failure of God's word. His purposes stand. His faithfulness endures. The mystery of Israel's unbelief is not the defeat of God's plan but a part of it — and Paul will unfold that mystery with breathtaking scope later in the letter.

The second half of the section (vv. 5–8) turns to a pair of objections that Paul was evidently hearing in real life, and both are attempts to turn grace into a licence. If our unrighteousness only serves to display God’s righteousness more brightly, is God not unjust to punish it? And if my lie makes his truth more evident, why am I still condemned — why not simply “do evil that good may come”? Paul reports that last slander as something people were actually saying he taught, which tells us how radical his gospel of free grace sounded to its first hearers; no one ever accused the Pharisees of encouraging sin. He does not argue the point here — he refuses it, notes that God could judge nothing at all if the objection held, and reserves the full answer for chapter 6. But the objection itself is a compliment in disguise. A gospel that cannot be misheard as permission is probably not the gospel Paul preached.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divine Faithfulness and Human Failure

The question of whether human sin can thwart God's covenant purposes is one of the deepest in all theology. Romans 3:3–4 gives the Reformed answer: it cannot. God's faithfulness is not a function of human response; it is grounded in his own immutable character. Calvin wrote that God's truth stands firm even against the unfaithfulness of the whole world. This has practical implications for Christian assurance: our standing in the covenant does not rest on our faithfulness but on God's. He who called us is faithful; he will do it (1 Thessalonians 5:24).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jewish readers would have been relieved by Paul's affirmation of Israel's covenant privileges, but troubled by his insistence that these privileges provide no exemption from judgment. The tension — covenant advantage, yet equal accountability — was genuinely new, though rooted in the Old Testament prophets. Now: Christians face the same tension. The advantages of covenant community — Scripture, sacrament, preaching, prayer — are real and great. They are also not saving substitutes for personal faith and repentance. Privilege and accountability always travel together.

verseByVerse.quote: Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.

Meaning first. Romans 3 is the hinge of the letter. First Paul answers objections: if Jews are no better off, what was the point of being God’s people? (vv. 1–8). Then he closes the case: all, Jews and Gentiles, are under sin; no one is righteous; every mouth is stopped (vv. 9–20). Then come the greatest verses in the Bible on how God saves: “But now” the righteousness of God has been revealed apart from the law, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. All have sinned; all who believe are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption in Christ, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, so that God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (vv. 21–26). Boasting is excluded; we are justified by faith apart from works (vv. 27–31).

Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision? After chapter 2, a natural objection.

Much in every way. Real privileges (9:4–5).

To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God. Key words. “The oracles of God” are the Scriptures. God’s very words, entrusted to Israel to keep and pass on. The greatest privilege of all. Through them, the whole world received the Bible.

In a sentence. What advantage is there in being a Jew, or in circumcision? A great deal, above all that the Jews were entrusted with the very words of God.

On a Tuesday. You have been entrusted with God’s word too. It is your greatest treasure. Open it.
verseByVerse.note: “The oracles of God” are the Scriptures.

verseByVerse.quote: What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, "That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.”

What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? Key words. If Israel failed, does God fail? Has he broken his promises?

By no means! “By no means” (mē genoito): God forbid! Paul’s strongest denial, used ten times in Romans.

Let God be true though every one were a liar. Key words. God’s faithfulness doesn’t depend on ours (2 Timothy 2:13). Even if every human failed, God would remain true.

That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged. From Psalm 51:4, David’s confession after his adultery with Bathsheba. David admitted that God was right to judge him. Human sin shows God’s righteousness in judging it.

In a sentence. If some were unfaithful, does their unfaithfulness cancel God’s faithfulness? Not at all! Let God be true and every human a liar, as Scripture says: so that you may be proved right in your words and win when you are judged.

For worship. God is faithful even when you are not. Rest in his faithfulness.

parallels.desc: so that you may be justified in your words
all mankind are liars

verseByVerse.quote: But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) By no means! For then how could God judge the world?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) By no means! For then how could God judge the world?

But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? A twisted objection: if my sin makes God look good, why does he punish me?

That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.) Paul is embarrassed even to say it.

By no means! For then how could God judge the world? Key words. If sin couldn’t be punished because it shows God’s goodness, no sin could ever be judged. But God must judge the world (Genesis 18:25). The objection destroys itself.

In a sentence. If our unrighteousness highlights God’s righteousness, is God unjust to punish us? Paul speaks in human terms. Certainly not! Otherwise how could God judge the world?

On a Tuesday. Never excuse your sin by thinking God can use it. He will, but you are still responsible.

parallels.desc: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?

verseByVerse.quote: But if through my lie God's truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? And why not do evil that good may come? — as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if through my lie God’s truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? And why not do evil that good may come? — as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.

But if through my lie God’s truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner? The same objection, stated personally.

And why not do evil that good may come? Key words. The logical end of the objection. Some accused Paul of teaching this: if grace covers sin, sin more (6:1). His gospel of free grace was so radical that people thought it encouraged sin.

As some people slanderously charge us with saying. If your gospel is never accused of encouraging sin, you may not be preaching grace as Paul did.

Their condemnation is just. Those who reason this way deserve judgment. Paul will answer fully in chapter 6.

In a sentence. If my lie makes God’s truth shine more brightly for his glory, why am I still condemned as a sinner? Why not do evil that good may result, as some slanderously claim we say? Their condemnation is deserved.

For worship. Grace never gives permission to sin. It gives power not to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — No One Is Righteous: The Verdict of Scripture
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul has argued the guilt of the Gentile from creation and conscience. He has argued the guilt of the moralist and the Jew from their own failure to live by the law they possess. Now he seals the case with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures. The catena of Old Testament citations in vv. 10–18 — drawn from Psalms 14, 5, 140, 10, 36, and Isaiah 59 — forms a comprehensive indictment: no one is righteous, no one understands, no one seeks God; their throats are open graves, their mouths full of cursing and bitterness, their feet swift to shed blood, and there is no fear of God before their eyes.

The theological move is masterful. Paul is not importing foreign charges against Israel; he is using Israel's own sacred texts to establish Israel's own guilt. The Torah was given to the Jew; and the Torah says that no one is righteous. Therefore the Jew who trusts in the Torah as a source of righteousness has not read the Torah carefully enough. The law's purpose is not to provide righteousness but to reveal the absence of it: "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (v. 20).

"No one" — the universality is relentless. Not most people. Not unreformed people. Not people without religion. No one. The scope of the verdict prepares for the scope of the remedy: the gospel is for everyone because everyone needs it equally. There are no moral high achievers who need it slightly less. There are no spiritual derelicts for whom it is too late. The ground is completely level: all have sinned, all fall short (v. 23), all are justified freely by grace (v. 24).

And the section closes with a courtroom image worth naming, because it is the most vivid thing in it. The purpose of the whole indictment, Paul says, is “so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God” (v. 19). A stopped mouth is what happens at the end of a trial that has gone badly: the defendant who arrived with explanations has run out of them, and the silence in the dock is the verdict arriving before the judge speaks it. That silence is not the aim of the passage but its precondition — because a man still talking is a man still defending himself, and nobody has ever been justified by grace while he was still presenting a case.
verseByVerse.theology:
Total Depravity

Romans 3:9–20 is the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of total depravity. The doctrine does not mean that every human being is as bad as possible, but that sin has corrupted every dimension of human nature — the mind ("no one understands"), the will ("no one seeks for God"), the affections, the speech, the conduct, the very orientation of the soul. No part of the human person is untouched by the fall. This means that the human contribution to salvation is precisely zero: we do not contribute our goodwill, our moral achievement, our religious sensitivity. Salvation is entirely of God from beginning to end. This is why Paul can say in v. 24 that justification is "freely" given — there is nothing in us to which it could be a response.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The catena of psalms and prophets Paul deploys was drawn from Israel's own worship book. These were texts sung in the temple, prayed in the synagogue, memorised by devout Jews. Their application to Israel's own guilt was deeply confrontational — like a church being indicted by its own hymns. Now: The contemporary church sometimes prefers a more optimistic anthropology — emphasising human potential and the image of God while minimising the ravages of the fall. Romans 3:9–20 is the permanent corrective. The doctrine of human depravity is not pessimism; it is realism. And realism about the disease is the precondition for gratitude for the cure.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: "None is righteous, no, not one;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin, as it is written: “None is righteous, no, not one;

Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. Privileges, yes; but not better before God’s judgment.

For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin. Key words. “Under sin”: under its power and its guilt, like slaves under a master (7:14; Galatians 3:22). Paul’s conclusion from 1:18–2:29.

As it is written: “None is righteous, no, not one.” Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah to prove it from Scripture (Psalm 14:1–3; 53:1–3; 5:9; 140:3; 10:7; Isaiah 59:7–8; Psalm 36:1). A chain of Old Testament verses, the way rabbis argued. This first one: not one person is righteous before God. Not one.

In a sentence. Are we Jews any better? Not at all, for Paul has already charged that Jews and Gentiles alike are all under the power of sin, as Scripture says: no one is righteous, not even one.

On a Tuesday. Not one is righteous. Including you. That is the bad news that makes the gospel good.
verseByVerse.note: Paul strings together quotations from the Psalms and Isaiah to show that all are under sin.

parallels.desc: not a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins

verseByVerse.quote: no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one."
verseByVerse.commentary:
no one understands; no one seeks for God. All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one.”

No one understands; no one seeks for God. Key words. Fallen people don’t seek the true God. They may seek religion, or meaning, or help, but not God himself, on his terms. Anyone who truly seeks God does so because God first sought them (John 6:44; Luke 19:10).

All have turned aside. Turned off the road.

Together they have become worthless. “Worthless” (ēchreiōthēsan): useless, gone sour, like spoiled milk.

No one does good, not even one. Not that no one does anything kind, but that no one does what is truly good before God, from a heart that loves him and for his glory.

Where Christians differ: how bad is human nature? Some believe people are basically good, or that fallen humans retain the ability to seek God on their own. Verdict: Scripture teaches total depravity: not that people are as bad as they could be, but that every part of human nature is affected by sin, and no one can, by their own power, seek God or do spiritual good (8:7–8; Ephesians 2:1–3). This is why salvation must be entirely by grace.

In a sentence. No one understands, no one seeks God; all have turned away and become worthless together; no one does good, not even one.

For worship. If you seek God today, it is because he sought you first. Thank him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive." "The venom of asps is under their lips." "Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive.” “The venom of asps is under their lips.” “Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness.”

Their throat is an open grave. Key words. From Psalm 5:9. Speech that smells of death, corrupt. Sin shows itself first in words.

They use their tongues to deceive. Lies.

The venom of asps is under their lips. From Psalm 140:3. Poisonous words.

Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness. From Psalm 10:7.

The tongue. Four of the quotations are about speech: throat, tongue, lips, mouth. The tongue reveals the heart (Matthew 12:34; James 3:6–8).

In a sentence. Their throats are open graves, their tongues practise deceit, the poison of vipers is on their lips, and their mouths are full of cursing and bitterness.

On a Tuesday. Watch your words today. They show what is in your heart.

parallels.desc: their throat is an open grave
the venom of asps
his mouth is filled with cursing

verseByVerse.quote: "Their feet are swift to shed blood;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Their feet are swift to shed blood;

Their feet are swift to shed blood. Key words. From Isaiah 59:7. From words to deeds. Violence comes quickly. Human history is a story of bloodshed, from Cain onwards.

In a sentence. Their feet are quick to shed blood.

For worship. Pray for peace in a violent world. And be quick to forgive, not to harm.

parallels.desc: their feet run to evil

verseByVerse.quote: "in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
in their paths are ruin and misery, and the way of peace they have not known.”

In their paths are ruin and misery. From Isaiah 59:7–8. Sin leaves destruction behind.

And the way of peace they have not known. Key words. Fallen humanity cannot find peace: with God, with others, within. Christ alone is the way of peace (5:1; Ephesians 2:14).

In a sentence. Ruin and misery mark their ways, and they do not know the way of peace.

On a Tuesday. True peace is found only in Christ. Point people to him.

parallels.desc: the way of peace they do not know

verseByVerse.quote: "There is no fear of God before their eyes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

There is no fear of God before their eyes. Key words. From Psalm 36:1. The root of it all. No reverence for God, no sense of accountability to him. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (Proverbs 9:10); its absence is the beginning of folly and sin.

In a sentence. There is no fear of God before their eyes.

For worship. Ask God to put his fear before your eyes. It is the start of wisdom.

parallels.desc: there is no fear of God before his eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin. — Romans 3:19-20
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may be held accountable to God. For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.

Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law. The quotations come from the Jewish Scriptures, so they apply especially to Jews.

So that every mouth may be stopped. Key words. Silenced, like a defendant with no defence. No excuses, no protests. Total guilt.

And the whole world may be held accountable to God. The whole world, guilty before God’s court.

For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight. Key words. The conclusion of 1:18–3:20. No one is declared righteous before God by keeping the law. Not one. From Psalm 143:2.

Since through the law comes knowledge of sin. Key words. The law’s purpose is not to save, but to show sin (7:7). It is a mirror, not a washbasin.

Where Christians differ: what are works of the law? The New Perspective on Paul argues that “works of the law” means mainly Jewish identity markers like circumcision, food laws and Sabbath, so that Paul is opposing ethnic pride rather than earning salvation. Verdict: the identity markers are included, but Paul’s argument is wider: the law shows sin (v. 20), and no one keeps it (vv. 10–18; 2:21–23). Works of the law are any obedience to God’s commands offered as a basis for acceptance. Paul’s point is that no human obedience can justify, because all have sinned (v. 23; 4:4–5).

In a sentence. We know that what the law says applies to those under it, so that every mouth is silenced and the whole world is accountable to God, for no one will be declared righteous in his sight by works of the law; rather, through the law we become conscious of sin.

For worship. Stop defending yourself before God. Let your mouth be stopped, and then open it to call on Christ.

parallels.desc: no one living is righteous before you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–31 — But Now: The Righteousness of God Through Faith
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"But now" — nuni de. Two words in Greek that change everything. After three chapters of unrelenting diagnosis — the Gentile without excuse, the moralist self-condemned, the Jew convicted by his own scriptures, the entire world accountable to God — these two words open a door out of a sealed room. The righteousness of God has been manifested. Apart from the law. Through faith in Jesus Christ. For all who believe. Freely. By grace. Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.

This is the centre of Romans. This is the centre of Paul's gospel. This is the theological core of the Reformation. Every word of vv. 21–26 has been weighed and debated and celebrated for two millennia — and still it burns with the same fire. God put Christ forward as a propitiation — a mercy seat, a place of atonement — by his blood, to be received by faith. In this act, God demonstrated his own righteousness: He passed over former sins (under the patient forbearance of the old covenant) and he condemned the sin that deserved condemnation — in his own Son, at Calvary. The God who justifies the ungodly (4:5) is not a God who winks at sin. He is a God who bore its full weight in the person of his Son.

Boasting is excluded (v. 27). The person who is justified by faith through Christ has nothing to boast of but Christ. The Jew cannot boast in the Torah; the Greek cannot boast in philosophy; the moralist cannot boast in her record; the religious cannot boast in his devotion. The ground is level. There is one God, and he justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. The gospel is the great leveller — and the great glorifier, because it redirects all glory from the creature to the Creator.

Two things at the edges of the section should not be lost. The first is the sentence on which the whole offer rests, and it is the shortest in the passage: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (v. 23). It is not an insult dropped into a paragraph about grace; it is the reason there is a paragraph about grace, and everything from 1:18 onward has been written to make that sentence land as a plain description rather than an accusation. The second is the question Paul asks last, which is the one his critics had been asking loudly: do we then overthrow the law by this faith (v. 31)? He has just said righteousness comes apart from the law, and the obvious inference is that the law has been discarded — the very charge of 3:8. His answer is the strongest denial in his vocabulary, and then four words that will take him the whole of chapter 4 to prove: we uphold the law. Justification by faith does not abolish the Old Testament. It is what the Old Testament was about.
verseByVerse.theology:
Propitiation: The Heart of the Atonement

Romans 3:25 introduces one of the most important words in the New Testament: hilastērion — propitiation. This word carries the specific meaning of an offering that averts divine wrath by satisfying it. Leon Morris demonstrated exhaustively that this is the correct reading against C.H. Dodd's attempted substitution of "expiation" (which only removes sin, without reference to wrath). Christ's death on the cross was not merely a moral demonstration or a removal of guilt; it was the bearing of the holy wrath of God against sin, so that God could be both just (the sin was punished) and the justifier (the sinner is acquitted). The Reformed tradition has always insisted on this: without propitiation, justification has no foundation. If the wrath was not truly satisfied, the forgiveness is not truly free.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of vv. 24–25 deliberately echoes the Day of Atonement ritual of Leviticus 16: the mercy seat (hilastērion) where blood was sprinkled to cover the sins of the people. Paul is saying: what the Day of Atonement pointed to, Christ has accomplished — once for all, for all who believe. The entire sacrificial system of the old covenant found its fulfilment and its terminus in the cross. Now: Every human religion has some mechanism for dealing with the problem of guilt — sacrifice, ritual, moral achievement, reincarnation, denial. Romans 3:21–31 announces that the only mechanism that actually works is the one God provided: the substitutionary death of his own Son, received by faith. There is no other name, no other blood, no other righteousness that avails.

verseByVerse.quote: But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it—the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it — the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:

But now. Key words. Two of the greatest words in the Bible. After the long, dark account of sin, “but now.” God has acted (Ephesians 2:13).

The righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law. The righteous standing that God gives (1:17), revealed in Christ, apart from law-keeping.

Although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it. The Old Testament itself pointed to it (Genesis 15:6; Habakkuk 2:4). Chapter 4 will prove it.

The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. Key words. Received through faith in Christ. Not earned, but received. “For all who believe”: open to all, with one condition, faith.

Where Christians differ: faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ? The Greek (pisteōs Iēsou Christou) can mean faith in Jesus Christ or the faithfulness of Jesus Christ. Some scholars prefer the second, emphasising Christ’s obedience. Verdict: Christ’s faithful obedience is indeed the ground of our justification (5:19), but here the phrase most naturally means faith in Christ, since Paul immediately adds “for all who believe.” We are justified by faith in Christ, whose faithful obedience is credited to us. Both truths stand.

For there is no distinction. Jew and Gentile alike.

Justification. To be “justified” is to be declared righteous by God as judge: a legal verdict, not a process of being made righteous. God, the judge, declares the believing sinner righteous on the basis of Christ’s work.

In a sentence. But now God’s righteousness has been revealed apart from the law, as the Law and the Prophets testify: a righteousness from God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe, without distinction.

On a Tuesday. But now. Whatever your past, these words mean God has acted for you. Believe.
verseByVerse.note: To be “justified” is to be declared righteous by God as judge.

verseByVerse.quote: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,

For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. Key words. The universal problem. “Have sinned”: a completed fact. “Fall short”: present tense, keep falling short. “The glory of God”: what we were made to reflect, his image (Genesis 1:27), and what we were meant to share. We miss the mark, like an archer.

And are justified by his grace as a gift. Key words. The universal remedy. “Justified”: declared righteous. “By his grace”: undeserved favour. “As a gift” (dōrean): freely, for nothing, without cost. The same word as “without a cause” in John 15:25. Grace is free for us, though infinitely costly for God.

Through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Key words. “Redemption” was the word for buying a slave’s freedom. Christ paid the price to free us from sin (Mark 10:45; 1 Peter 1:18–19). Free for us, because he paid.

In a sentence. For all have sinned and fall short of God’s glory, and all are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.

For worship. All have sinned. All who believe are justified freely. You are both. Rejoice.
verseByVerse.note: “Redemption” was the word for buying a slave’s freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: ...whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. — Romans 3:25-26
verseByVerse.commentary:
whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.

Whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood. Key words. A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The word (hilastērion) is used in the Greek Old Testament for the mercy seat, the lid of the ark of the covenant, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15; Hebrews 9:5). Christ is the true mercy seat, where God’s wrath against sin is satisfied and his mercy given. “God put forward”: God himself provided the sacrifice. It is not a reluctant God being persuaded by a loving Son; it is the loving God providing the means to satisfy his own justice.

To be received by faith. The means of receiving it.

This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. Key words. Before Christ, God forgave sinners like David and Abraham without fully punishing their sins. Was God unjust? The cross shows he wasn’t: he punished those sins in Christ.

So that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. Key words. The heart of the gospel. How can God declare the guilty righteous without being unjust? Because he punished sin in his Son. God is just: sin is punished. God is the justifier: the sinner who believes is declared righteous. Justice and mercy meet at the cross.

Where Christians differ: propitiation or expiation? Some translate hilastērion as “expiation,” the removing of sin, and deny that God’s wrath needed to be satisfied. Verdict: the context is God’s wrath (1:18; 2:5) and his justice (vv. 25–26). Christ’s death removes sin, yes, but by bearing the wrath it deserved. This is penal substitution: Christ suffered the penalty of our sins in our place (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13). It is the centre of the gospel.

In a sentence. God presented Christ as a sacrifice of atonement, a propitiation through his blood, received by faith, to demonstrate his righteousness, since in his patience he had left earlier sins unpunished, and to show his justice now, so that he would be both just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus.

On a Tuesday. At the cross, God’s justice and mercy kissed. Your sins were punished there, so you will never face that wrath.
verseByVerse.note: A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s wrath. The same word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the “mercy seat,” the lid of the ark where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

parallels.desc: blood on the mercy seat

verseByVerse.quote: Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.

Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. Key words. Shut out, slammed out the door. If salvation is God’s gift, received by faith, no one can boast (Ephesians 2:8–9; 1 Corinthians 1:29–31). The proud Jew of 2:17, boasting in the law, and the proud moralist: all silenced.

By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith. “Law” here means principle. A system of works would allow boasting; the principle of faith excludes it. Faith is empty hands, receiving.

For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Key words. The thesis of the Reformation. Luther translated it “by faith alone,” and was attacked for adding a word. But “apart from works” means exactly “by faith alone.” Faith isn’t a work that earns; it is the hand that receives Christ.

Where Christians differ: faith alone? The Council of Trent (1547) condemned the teaching that we are justified by faith alone. Verdict: “apart from works of the law” leaves faith alone as the instrument. Not faith plus baptism, faith plus penance, or faith plus good works. Good works are the necessary fruit of justifying faith (Ephesians 2:10; James 2), but they are not part of its ground. This is sola fide, the article on which the church stands or falls.

In a sentence. Where then is boasting? It is excluded, not by a principle of works but by the principle of faith, for we maintain that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law.

For worship. You have nothing to boast of before God except Christ. Boast in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one—who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also, since God is one — who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.

Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? If salvation were by the law, only Jews could have it.

Since God is one. Key words. “God is one” echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession (Deuteronomy 6:4). If there is one God, he is God of all, and he saves all the same way.

Who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. Same God, same way, for all.

In a sentence. Is God the God of Jews only, and not of Gentiles too? Yes, of Gentiles too, since there is only one God, who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through the same faith.

On a Tuesday. There is one God and one way of salvation for every person on earth. Tell them.
verseByVerse.note: “God is one” echoes the Shema, Israel’s daily confession.

parallels.desc: the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.

Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? The obvious objection. If salvation is by faith, is the law pointless?

By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law. Key words. Faith establishes the law. How? Faith takes the law’s verdict seriously: we are guilty, we need a substitute. Christ fulfilled the law’s demands and bore its penalty (8:3–4). The law itself testified to justification by faith (chapter 4). And those justified by faith are given the Spirit, who enables them to fulfil the law’s righteous requirement (8:4; 13:8–10).

The law in the Christian life. Reformed theology speaks of three uses of the law: to restrain sin in society, to show us our sin and drive us to Christ, and to guide believers in grateful obedience. The law cannot save, but it shows the shape of the love that salvation produces.

In a sentence. Do we then nullify the law by this faith? Not at all! Rather, we uphold the law.

For worship. The law shows you your need of Christ, and then shows you how to love him. Thank God for it.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then what advantage has the Jew? Or what is the value of circumcision?<sup>2</sup>Much in every way. To begin with, the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.<sup>3</sup>What if some were unfaithful? Does their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?<sup>4</sup>By no means! Let God be true though every one were a liar, as it is written, “That you may be justified in your words, and prevail when you are judged.”<sup>5</sup>But if our unrighteousness serves to show the righteousness of God, what shall we say? That God is unrighteous to inflict wrath on us? (I speak in a human way.)<sup>6</sup>By no means! For then how could God judge the world?<sup>7</sup>But if through my lie God’s truth abounds to his glory, why am I still being condemned as a sinner?<sup>8</sup>And why not do evil that good may come?—as some people slanderously charge us with saying. Their condemnation is just.<sup>9</sup>What then? Are we Jews any better off? No, not at all. For we have already charged that all, both Jews and Greeks, are under sin,<sup>10</sup>as it is written: “None is righteous, no, not one;<sup>11</sup>no one understands; no one seeks for God.<sup>12</sup>All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; no one does good, not even one.”<sup>13</sup>“Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues to deceive.” “The venom of asps is under their lips.”<sup>14</sup>“Their mouth is full of curses and bitterness.”<sup>15</sup>“Their feet are swift to shed blood;<sup>16</sup>in their paths are ruin and misery,<sup>17</sup>and the way of peace they have not known.”<sup>18</sup>“There is no fear of God before their eyes.”<sup>19</sup>Now we know that whatever the law says it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be held accountable to God.<sup>20</sup>For by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.<sup>21</sup>But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it—<sup>22</sup>the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction:<sup>23</sup>for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,<sup>24</sup>and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,<sup>25</sup>whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God’s righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins.<sup>26</sup>It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.<sup>27</sup>Then what becomes of our boasting? It is excluded. By what kind of law? By a law of works? No, but by the law of faith.<sup>28</sup>For we hold that one is justified by faith apart from works of the law.<sup>29</sup>Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also,<sup>30</sup>since God is one—who will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith.<sup>31</sup>Do we then overthrow the law by this faith? By no means! On the contrary, we uphold the law.

4.title: Abraham: The Father of All Who Believe
4.overview:
If justification is by faith and not by works of the law, Paul faces an immediate objection from Jewish readers: what about Abraham? Abraham is the father of the Jewish nation, the recipient of the covenant, the model of obedience. If he was justified by his works, then surely righteousness is earned, not given. Romans 4 is Paul's extended answer — and it is devastating in its exegetical precision and its theological reach.

The answer is simple and irrefutable: Abraham was justified by faith before he was circumcised (Genesis 15:6 precedes Genesis 17), and before the law was given (by four centuries). The very man whom Judaism claimed as the exemplar of covenant faithfulness is in fact the exemplar of justifying faith — and therefore the father not only of circumcised Jewish believers but of all Gentile believers as well. The gospel does not contradict the covenant with Abraham; it fulfils it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Abraham Justified by Faith, Not Works or Circumcision
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's argument from Abraham is both simple and lethal to the works-righteousness position. He goes directly to Genesis 15:6: "Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness." The verb "counted" (Greek: logizomai; Hebrew: chashab) is an accounting term — to reckon to someone's account. God reckoned Abraham righteous — not because Abraham had earned it but because Abraham believed. The righteousness was credited; it was not achieved.

Paul then deploys a second argument from David. Psalm 32:1–2 speaks of the blessedness of the man whose sins are not counted against him. David was not speaking of a man who earned God's favour; he was speaking of a man who received forgiveness he did not deserve. Blessed is the man whose iniquity is forgiven — not whose record is clean. The whole Old Testament agrees: righteousness before God is received, not achieved.

The third and clinching argument concerns the timing of Abraham's circumcision. The justification of Genesis 15:6 precedes the circumcision of Genesis 17 by perhaps fourteen to twenty-four years. Abraham was declared righteous while still uncircumcised — which means circumcision was a sign and seal of a righteousness already received by faith, not the means by which that righteousness was obtained. This means Abraham is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not: his pattern is faith, not ethnicity.

And at the centre of it stands a phrase so shocking that Paul can only have chosen it deliberately: God “justifies the ungodly” (v. 5). Not the sincere, not the searching, not the imperfect but well-intentioned. The ungodly — the very people the God of the Old Testament had sworn he would not acquit, since his own law had called the justifying of the wicked an abomination. Paul is not softening the difficulty; he is naming it in the strongest available terms, because the cross has already answered it (3:25–26). This is the sentence the whole chapter is arranged around, and every reader who has ever wondered whether he is too far gone should notice which category is being justified here.
verseByVerse.theology:
Imputation: The Reckoning of Righteousness

The word logizomai (count, reckon, credit, impute) appears eleven times in Romans 4. This is deliberate. The doctrine of imputation — that God credits Christ's righteousness to the believing sinner's account — is the hinge of the doctrine of justification. Luther's language of the "wonderful exchange" captures it: Christ takes our sin; we receive his righteousness. Not infused into us (as Rome taught), but credited to us — declared righteous in Christ, clothed in a righteousness that is not ours by achievement but ours by gift. Luther called this the "alien righteousness" (iustitia aliena) — foreign to us by nature, ours by grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's appeal to Abraham was the ultimate trump card in Jewish theological discussion. If Abraham himself was justified by faith and not by works, the works-righteousness position has lost its founding father. Paul turns the Jewish trump card against itself. Now: Every form of religious merit-earning — "I'm basically a good person," "I attend church," "I pray every day," "I've never done anything really terrible" — collapses before Romans 4. Abraham, the father of the faithful, stood before God with nothing but faith in the promise. So must we.
