But that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law. Key words. Israel ran hard after righteousness through the law, and failed to reach it. The irony: the ones who tried hardest missed, because they ran on the wrong track.

What it does not mean. It does not mean effort is bad, or that the law was a bad goal. The law itself pointed to Christ (10:4). The problem was the way they pursued it.

In a sentence. What then shall we conclude? That Gentiles, who were not seeking righteousness, have received it, the righteousness that comes by faith; but Israel, who chased a law that would bring righteousness, did not attain it.

On a Tuesday. Religious effort cannot win God’s approval. Stop running on the wrong track. Receive Christ’s righteousness as a gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written, “Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.”

Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. Key words. The reason. Israel treated the law as a ladder of works to climb up to God, rather than receiving his promise by faith. “As if”: works were never the true way. Even in the Old Testament, people were justified by faith (4:1–8).

They have stumbled over the stumbling stone. Key words. The stumbling stone is Christ. A crucified Messiah offended them (1 Corinthians 1:23). He tells them their works cannot save; that is the offence.

As it is written. Key words. Paul combines Isaiah 28:16 (a tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion) with Isaiah 8:14 (a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling). The same stone is a foundation for those who trust it and a stumbling block for those who do not. Peter uses the same combination (1 Peter 2:6–8).

And whoever believes in him will not be put to shame. Key words. Believing in him is the way. Not put to shame: never disappointed or disgraced at the judgement. “Whoever” opens the door to anyone, Jew or Gentile. This leads into chapter 10, where everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved.

Where Christians differ: sovereignty and responsibility. Some think that if God elects, human responsibility vanishes; others think that if humans are responsible, God cannot be fully sovereign. Verdict: Paul holds both in the same chapter without apology. Israel’s unbelief is truly their fault (vv. 30–33; 10:21), and salvation is truly God’s sovereign mercy (vv. 6–24). We cannot fully reconcile them in our minds, but Scripture teaches both, and we must too (Westminster 3.1; Acts 2:23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Christ is a trap. He is offered as a foundation to all. Only those who refuse him stumble over him.

In a sentence. Why? Because they sought it by works, not by faith. They tripped over the stumbling stone, as Scripture says: “Look, I am placing in Zion a stone that makes people stumble and a rock that makes them fall, and the one who believes in him will never be put to shame.”

For worship. Build on Christ the cornerstone. Whoever trusts him will never be put to shame.

parallels.desc: a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone
a stone of offence

Amen.<sup>6</sup>But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel,<sup>7</sup>and not all are children of Abraham because they are his offspring, but “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>8</sup>This means that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.<sup>9</sup>For this is what the promise said: “About this time next year I will return, and Sarah shall have a son.”<sup>10</sup>And not only so, but also when Rebekah had conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac,<sup>11</sup>though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls—<sup>12</sup>she was told, “The older will serve the younger.”<sup>13</sup>As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”<sup>14</sup>What shall we say then? For who can resist his will?”<sup>20</sup>But who are you, O man, to answer back to God? 10.title: Faith Comes by Hearing
10.overview:
Romans 10 moves from the theology of election (chapter 9) to the human experience of faith and the missionary imperative of proclamation. Paul's pastoral heart is again on display: his heart's desire and prayer for Israel is their salvation. Their problem is not a lack of religious commitment but a misdirection of it — a zeal for God that is not according to knowledge, a pursuit of their own righteousness that refuses to submit to the righteousness of God.

The great passage of vv. 9–15 moves from confession and faith to calling on the name of the Lord to preachers sent with good news — a chain that runs from individual conversion back to the sovereign act of apostolic commissioning. The gospel does not reach people automatically; it reaches them through preachers who are sent, who go, who speak. The chapter ends with the sobering testimony of Israel's own scriptures: they have heard, they have understood, and they have not believed. The tragedy of unbelief is complete.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Righteousness for All Who Call: The Nearness of the Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul's pastoral longing for Israel's salvation (v. 1) is the emotional key to the chapter. He is not writing as a detached analyst of Israel's religious failure; he is writing as a broken-hearted brother who knows exactly what his people are missing and cannot stop praying for them. The diagnosis is precise: "a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge." Zeal without knowledge is not a small problem; it is perhaps the most dangerous religious condition possible, because it generates confident misdirection.

The contrast between the righteousness of the law and the righteousness of faith (vv. 5–8) draws on Deuteronomy 30, where Moses speaks of God's word as near to the people — not beyond the sea, not in the heights of heaven, but in their mouths and in their hearts. Paul identifies this nearness with the gospel: "the word of faith that we proclaim." The righteousness of God is not a distant achievement to be scaled by heroic effort; it is a near word to be received by confession and faith.

Two verses stand between the diagnosis and that contrast, and they should not be passed over. They are the hinge of the chapter. Israel, Paul says, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, did not submit to God’s righteousness (v. 3).

Watch the sequence, because it is a clinical description of how a religious life goes wrong. First not knowing what God was offering; then setting about producing a version of it themselves; and finally — the word that makes it a moral matter rather than a misunderstanding — refusing to submit.

That verb is the surprise. One does not expect righteousness to be something a person submits to. But a righteousness that arrives as a gift has to be received on the giver’s terms, and receiving is precisely what a competent, disciplined, self-respecting person finds hardest. The offence of the gospel is not that it asks too much. It is that it will not let you contribute.

Then v. 4, which the chapter cannot do without: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. The word is telos, and it carries both senses at once — the terminus and the goal, where a road stops and what it was built to reach.

Both are true here and neither should be dropped. As a route to righteousness the law has come to its end, because the destination has arrived. And it was always heading there; Christ is not an alternative to the law but the thing it was pointing at, which is why Paul can say elsewhere that he does not overthrow the law but upholds it (3:31).

Note also the last clause, because it is the one that opens the door: to everyone who believes. The universal that will ring three times in vv. 11-13 has already sounded here, before the famous verses begin.

Verses 9–13 are among the most frequently memorised in Paul's letters — "If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved." The simplicity is staggering. Two things: confession of lordship, belief in resurrection. Both are the expression of the same faith. And the word "all" rings three times: everyone who believes (v. 11), everyone who calls (v. 13), for he is Lord of all and bestows riches on all who call (v. 12). The gospel has no ethnic or social exclusion clause.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Confession of Lordship

Romans 10:9 makes the confession "Jesus is Lord" (Kyrios Iēsous) the central act of Christian profession. In the first-century Roman world, "Kyrios" was the title of Caesar — the one to whom ultimate allegiance was owed. To confess "Jesus is Lord" was therefore not merely a theological statement but a political one: Jesus, not Caesar, holds ultimate authority over my life. The early church was often persecuted for refusing to say "Caesar is Lord" — because they had already given that title to another. Every true Christian confession has this political dimension: it declares a transfer of ultimate allegiance.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses's vision of the nearness of God's word (Deuteronomy 30) had originally been given to Israel on the plains of Moab, just before they entered the land — as a word of covenant accessibility. God was not hiding himself; he had given his word and it was near. Paul's application to the gospel makes the same point: the righteousness of God is not a distant achievement but a near word, proclaimed by apostles, received by faith. Now: The simplicity of Romans 10:9 is the permanent rebuke to every complicated scheme of salvation. Salvation does not require a theology degree, a track record of spiritual achievement, or a passage through elaborate ritual. It requires the honest confession of a changed allegiance and the genuine belief in a historical resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.

Meaning first. Romans 10 continues the explanation of Israel’s unbelief that began in 9:30, now from the human side. Chapter 9 showed God’s sovereign choice; chapter 10 shows Israel’s responsibility. Israel was zealous, but sought to establish its own righteousness instead of submitting to God’s righteousness, which comes in Christ, the end of the law (vv. 1–4). The righteousness of faith is not a hard climb to heaven or a deep dive into the grave: Christ has already come down and risen up. It is near, in the gospel word: confess that Jesus is Lord and believe that God raised him, and you will be saved, whether Jew or Greek, for everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (vv. 5–13). But calling requires believing, believing requires hearing, and hearing requires preachers who are sent (vv. 14–17). Israel has heard, and has understood enough to be guilty, while Gentiles who were not looking have found God, who still stretches out his hands all day long to his stubborn people (vv. 18–21). Election never makes preaching unnecessary; it makes it hopeful.

Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved. Key words. “Heart’s desire” is eudokia, good pleasure, longing. Right after the strongest teaching on election in the Bible, Paul prays for the salvation of unbelieving Jews. Election does not make prayer pointless. God ordains the means as well as the end, and prayer is one of his means.

For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God. Key words. Paul speaks from experience. He had been zealous himself, so zealous that he persecuted the church (Acts 22:3–4; Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:6).

But not according to knowledge. Key words. Knowledge here is epignōsis, true, full understanding. Sincerity is not enough. Zeal without truth can drive people hard in the wrong direction.

What it does not mean. It does not mean zeal is wrong, or that sincere people are saved because they are sincere. Paul’s point is that sincere, zealous people can be lost if they reject God’s way of righteousness.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, Paul’s deepest longing and prayer to God for the Jews is that they be saved, for he can testify that they are zealous for God, but their zeal is not based on true knowledge.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the salvation of those you know, even when you believe God is sovereign. Especially then: he is able to answer.

verseByVerse.quote: For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God. Key words. Not ignorant that God is righteous, but of the righteousness that God gives, the gift of right standing revealed in the gospel (1:17; 3:21–22). They did not understand that God himself provides the righteousness he demands.

And seeking to establish their own. Key words. “Establish” (histēmi) means set up, make stand, like building a monument. Their own righteousness: a record of law-keeping that they hoped would stand before God (Philippians 3:9).

They did not submit to God’s righteousness. Key words. Receiving a gift requires humility. To accept God’s righteousness, you must admit you have none of your own. Pride refuses.

For Christ is the end of the law. Key words. “End” is telos, which can mean the termination, or the goal and fulfilment. The ESV note mentions that it can mean the goal.

For righteousness to everyone who believes. Key words. The law as a way of earning righteousness ends at Christ. Everyone who believes receives righteousness in him.

Where Christians differ: end or goal. Some take telos to mean that the law is entirely finished for Christians, with no ongoing role. Others take it to mean only that the law pointed to Christ. Verdict: Both senses are present, and they belong together. Christ is the goal the law aimed at: its sacrifices, promises and demands all pointed to him (3:21; Galatians 3:24). And so he is the end of the law as a way to gain righteousness: for everyone who believes, the attempt to be justified by law-keeping is over. But the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, remains the rule of life for the believer, fulfilled by those who walk by the Spirit (8:4; 13:8–10; Westminster 19.5–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians may live lawlessly (6:15). The law no longer condemns believers, but it still shows them how to love.

In a sentence. Because they did not know the righteousness that comes from God and tried to set up their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the culmination of the law, so that there is righteousness for everyone who believes.

For worship. Give up building your own monument. Christ is your righteousness. Rest in him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 4 can also be read “Christ is the end of the law, that everyone who believes may be justified.” “End” can mean goal as well as termination.

verseByVerse.quote: For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" (that is, to bring Christ down)
verseByVerse.commentary:
For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them. But the righteousness based on faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)

For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law. Key words. Paul contrasts two ways of righteousness, both described by Moses.

That the person who does the commandments shall live by them. Key words. From Leviticus 18:5. Paul quotes it also in Galatians 3:12. The principle of law: do, and live. If you kept the law perfectly, you would live. But no sinner can (3:20; Galatians 3:10). So as a way to life, the law brings only death to sinners.

But the righteousness based on faith says. Key words. Paul personifies the righteousness of faith, letting it speak. It speaks words from Deuteronomy 30:11–14, where Moses told Israel that God’s word was not far off or too hard: it was near, in their mouth and heart.

“Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down). Key words. “Do not say in your heart” echoes Deuteronomy 9:4, where Moses warned Israel not to think God gave them the land because of their righteousness. No one needs to climb to heaven to fetch Christ. He has already come down, in the incarnation. You do not have to make salvation happen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Moses contradicted himself, or that the law was a mistake. Leviticus 18:5 states what the law demands; Deuteronomy 30 speaks of the grace that would circumcise hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6). Both were in Moses, and both point to Christ.

In a sentence. Moses describes the righteousness of the law this way: the one who does these things will live by them. But the righteousness of faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will go up into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down).

On a Tuesday. You cannot climb up to God. Christ has come down to you.

parallels.desc: by doing them a person shall live
who will ascend to heaven for us?

verseByVerse.quote: "or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
verseByVerse.commentary:
“or ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);

“Or ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). Key words. In Deuteronomy, the image was crossing the sea; Paul uses the abyss (abyssos, the deep, the realm of the dead), a related Old Testament idea (Psalm 107:26; Jonah 2). No one needs to go down to the grave to bring Christ up. He has already risen. The great work is done.

But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” Key words. From Deuteronomy 30:14. Salvation is not far away. It is as close as the word you hear and speak.

(That is, the word of faith that we proclaim). Key words. Paul explains: the near word is the gospel message, the word that calls for faith. Paul applies Moses’ words about the nearness of God’s word to the gospel, because the gospel is what the law always pointed to.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation requires no response. The near word must be believed and confessed, as Paul says next.

In a sentence. “Or ‘Who will go down into the deep?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead). But what does it say? “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart,” that is, the message about faith that we preach.

For worship. The word of salvation is not far away. It is in your mouth and heart. Speak it and believe it today.
verseByVerse.note: Paul applies Moses’ words about the nearness of God’s word to the message about Christ.

parallels.desc: the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart

verseByVerse.quote: Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. — Romans 10:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved.

Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord. Key words. “Confess” (homologeō) means agree, declare openly. “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession (1 Corinthians 12:3; Philippians 2:11). “Lord” (kyrios) is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for God’s name, the LORD. To confess Jesus as Lord is to confess him as God and to bow to his rule. In Rome, where people were expected to say Caesar is Lord, it was costly.

And believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead. Key words. Believing the resurrection is not just accepting a historical fact. It is trusting in the living Christ whom God vindicated (4:24–25). The heart in the Bible is the centre of the person: mind, will and affections.

You will be saved. Key words. A promise, firm and simple.

For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved. Key words. Paul reverses the order: heart first, then mouth. Faith in the heart is what receives righteousness; confession with the mouth is its outward expression. They are not two separate conditions but one response, inside and outside. True faith does not stay silent.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that saying the words is a magic formula, or that someone who cannot speak cannot be saved. It does not mean faith is a work that earns salvation. Faith receives; Christ saves.

In a sentence. If you declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For it is with your heart that you believe and are justified, and with your mouth that you profess your faith and are saved.

On a Tuesday. Say it out loud, at work, at home, among friends: Jesus is Lord. Believe it in your heart, and live as one who belongs to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was the earliest Christian confession. “Lord” is the title the Greek Old Testament used for God’s name.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Scripture says, "Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame." For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.

For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.” Key words. Isaiah 28:16 again (9:33), now with “everyone” added to stress its universal reach. The Greek Old Testament says “whoever believes,” which implies everyone.

For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. Key words. In 3:22–23 there was no distinction in sin; here there is no distinction in salvation. Same need, same remedy.

For the same Lord is Lord of all. Key words. One Lord, Jesus, over Jews and Gentiles alike (3:29–30; Acts 10:36).

Bestowing his riches on all who call on him. Key words. “Riches”: the riches of his grace and glory (2:4; 9:23; 11:33). To call on him is to pray to him for salvation, trusting him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that everyone will in fact be saved. The riches are for all who call on him.

In a sentence. As Scripture says, “Anyone who believes in him will never be put to shame.” For there is no difference between Jew and Gentile: the same Lord is Lord of all and richly blesses all who call on him.

For worship. The Lord is rich, and generous to all who call. Call on him today, with confidence.

parallels.desc: whoever believes will not be in haste

verseByVerse.quote: For "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.” Key words. Paul quotes Joel 2:32, which Peter also quoted at Pentecost (Acts 2:21). In Joel, the Lord is the LORD, Yahweh. Paul applies it to Jesus, whom he has just called Lord (v. 9). This is a strong testimony that Jesus is God: to call on Jesus is to call on Yahweh.

To call on the name of the Lord. To pray to him, appeal to him, trust in him, worship him (Genesis 4:26; 12:8; 1 Corinthians 1:2). It is faith speaking.

Everyone. The door is open to all without exception. No sinner who calls will be turned away. This free offer of the gospel is real, and it fits with God’s sovereign election: the elect are those who are brought to call, and none who call are turned away (John 6:37).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that people can call on him without believing, as Paul says next.

In a sentence. For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

On a Tuesday. Tell people plainly: anyone who calls on the Lord Jesus will be saved. Then call on him yourself.

parallels.desc: everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–21 — The Sent Preacher and Israel's Unbelief
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The logic of the gospel creates a missionary chain that runs backwards from salvation to sending: how can anyone call on one in whom they have not believed? How can they believe in one they have not heard? How can they hear without someone preaching? How can anyone preach unless they are sent? Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7 — "How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!" — and the beauty he celebrates is not aesthetic but teleological: the feet that carry the gospel are beautiful because of what they carry and what their arrival means for those who hear.

The rhetorical questions tighten the logic inexorably: sending → preaching → hearing → believing → calling → saved. Remove any link and the chain breaks. This is Paul's theological argument for the absolute necessity of gospel proclamation. The sovereignty of God in election does not make preaching unnecessary; it makes preaching the instrument through which God calls his elect. "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" (v. 17). The word is the means; the Spirit works through the means; the elect hear and believe. Preach.

The chain does not then run smoothly to its conclusion, and v. 16 is where Paul says so: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. Every link held. They were sent, they preached, Israel heard — and it was not believed. Paul reaches for Isaiah again, and the line he takes is the first verse of Isaiah 53, in the middle of the fourth Servant Song: Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? (Isaiah 53:1). It stands immediately before the description of the man despised and rejected, pierced for our transgressions. So the unbelief being grieved here is not a late development. It was written into the prophecy of the cross itself: the servant was foretold as one who would not be believed.

The chapter ends with the testimony of Israel's own scriptures against Israel's unbelief. Have they not heard? Yes — all the earth has heard (v. 18). Did they not understand? Yes — Moses had already anticipated a day when Israel would be provoked to jealousy by a foolish nation (v. 19; Deuteronomy 32:21).

And then Isaiah, whom Paul says is so bold as to put it like this: I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me (v. 20; Isaiah 65:1). That is the hardest sentence in the chapter for anyone who assumes that finding God is the reward for looking for him. God turns up among people who were not enquiring, while the people who held the oracles do not come. Israel's rejection is not ignorance; it is disobedience (v. 21) — the stretching out of God's hands to a disobedient and contrary people. The love of God remains; the response of Israel does not.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Necessity of Preaching

Romans 10:14–17 is the most important New Testament text on the theology of preaching. Preaching is not one option among many for communicating the gospel; it is the divinely appointed means by which faith comes. The Spirit of God works through the proclaimed word — the word heard, the word believed — to create the faith that saves. This is why the Reformed tradition has always given preaching the central place in worship: not as a performance or an educational exercise but as the means of grace through which God speaks and through which his people hear. "Faith comes from hearing" — and hearing requires a preacher, and a preacher requires a sending. The missionary imperative is embedded in the very logic of salvation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The "beautiful feet" of Isaiah 52:7 originally referred to the herald who would bring to Jerusalem the news that the exile was over — Babylon had fallen, and God's people were coming home. Paul applies this image to the heralds of the new exodus: those who proclaim that sin, death, and the wrath of God have been overcome in Christ. The gospel is the announcement that the exile from God is over; the journey home has begun. Now: In an age that has substituted social media presence, personal authenticity, and lifestyle witness for the proclamation of the gospel, Romans 10:14–17 is a direct challenge: people are not saved by our online presence or our admirable lives. They are saved by hearing the word of Christ. We must preach — in whatever form that takes in our cultural moment — because faith comes by hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!' — Romans 10:14–15
verseByVerse.commentary:
How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!”

How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? Key words. A chain of questions, working backwards. Calling requires believing.

And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? Key words. Believing requires hearing. Some read it “him whom they have never heard”: in the preaching, Christ himself speaks (Ephesians 2:17).

And how are they to hear without someone preaching? Key words. Hearing requires a preacher (kēryssō, to herald, announce publicly).

And how are they to preach unless they are sent? Key words. Preaching requires sending (apostellō, the root of apostle). God sends preachers, and the church sends missionaries (Acts 13:2–3).

As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!” Key words. From Isaiah 52:7, describing the messengers who ran across the mountains with news of Israel’s return from exile. Their feet, dusty and tired, were beautiful because of the news they carried. The gospel is the greater good news of deliverance from sin.

Where Christians differ: those who never hear. Some say people who never hear the gospel can be saved by following their conscience or other religions; this is called inclusivism. Verdict: Paul’s chain says otherwise: calling requires believing, and believing requires hearing of Christ. There is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). This is why missions matter so much. God may use many means to bring the word, but salvation is through conscious faith in Christ (Westminster 10.4). Infants dying in infancy, and those incapable of being outwardly called, are in God’s hands and saved by Christ through the Spirit as he pleases (Westminster 10.3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean only ordained preachers can share the gospel. Every Christian can speak of Christ. But God appoints preaching as the main means of salvation (1 Corinthians 1:21).

In a sentence. How can people call on someone they have not believed in? How can they believe in someone they have not heard of? How can they hear without someone preaching? And how can anyone preach unless they are sent? As Scripture says, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”

For worship. Pray for preachers and missionaries. Give to send them. And open your own mouth: your feet can be beautiful too.

parallels.desc: how beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news

verseByVerse.quote: But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, 'Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?' — Romans 10:16
verseByVerse.commentary:
But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?”

But they have not all obeyed the gospel. Key words. The problem is not that Israel lacked preachers. They heard, but did not obey. The gospel is a command as well as an offer: repent and believe (1:5; Acts 17:30). “Obeyed” (hypakouō) is related to “hear” (akouō): to hear under, hearing that submits.

For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?” Key words. Isaiah 53:1, opening the great passage on the suffering servant. Even the prophet lamented that few believed his message about the servant who would be wounded for our transgressions. John quotes it too, of the Jews who saw Jesus’ signs and did not believe (John 12:38).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the gospel has failed when people reject it. Isaiah foresaw it.

In a sentence. But not all the Israelites accepted the good news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our message?”

On a Tuesday. Hearing is not enough. Respond to the gospel with obedient faith.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. — Romans 10:17
verseByVerse.commentary:
So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.

So faith comes from hearing. Key words. The summary. Faith (pistis) is born when the message is heard. “Hearing” (akoē) can mean the act of hearing or the message heard. God creates faith through his word.

And hearing through the word of Christ. Key words. The word (rhēma) of Christ is the message about Christ, and also Christ’s own word, for he speaks through his messengers. Some manuscripts read “word of God,” as the ESV note says, but “word of Christ” is the better reading.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith is our own achievement after hearing. The Spirit uses the word to give new birth and faith (James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:23). It does not mean reading is excluded. Reading the Scriptures is also a way the word reaches us.

In a sentence. So faith comes from hearing the message, and the message is heard through the word about Christ.

For worship. If you want more faith, go to the word. Sit under preaching, read Scripture, listen. God grows faith by his word.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the word of God.”

verseByVerse.quote: But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for "Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world." But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, "I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry.”

But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have. Key words. Israel cannot excuse itself by saying it never heard.

For “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” Key words. From Psalm 19:4, about the heavens declaring God’s glory. Paul borrows the words to describe how widely the gospel had spread: through synagogues across the Roman world, the message had reached Jews everywhere (Colossians 1:6, 23). As creation’s witness goes everywhere, so has the gospel to Israel.

But I ask, did Israel not understand? Key words. Maybe they did not grasp it? But Scripture itself had told them that God would turn to the Gentiles.

First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation.” Key words. From Deuteronomy 32:21, in the Song of Moses. Israel made God jealous with idols, no-gods; so God would make them jealous with a no-people, the Gentiles. This theme of jealousy returns in 11:11–14: the salvation of Gentiles is meant to provoke Israel to seek Christ.

With a foolish nation I will make you angry. Key words. A nation without understanding, without the law. That Gentiles like this should be welcomed would anger proud Israel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every single Israelite had personally heard the gospel. Paul is speaking broadly: the message had reached the nation.

In a sentence. But have they not heard? Of course they have: their message has gone out into all the earth, to the ends of the world. Did Israel not understand? Moses was the first to say, “I will make you envious by those who are not a nation; I will make you angry by a nation that has no understanding.”

On a Tuesday. Let your life as a Christian be so full of joy in God that it makes others jealous for what you have.

parallels.desc: their voice goes out through all the earth
I will make them jealous with those who are no people

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, "I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me." But of Israel he says, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, “I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.” But of Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”

Then Isaiah is so bold as to say. Key words. Isaiah dared to say something shocking. Paul quotes Isaiah 65:1–2.

“I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.” Key words. The Gentiles. They were not seeking God, but God sought them. This is grace: God takes the initiative. Compare 9:30.

But of Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.” Key words. A moving picture: God, like a parent, standing with hands stretched out all day, pleading with his children to come home. “Disobedient” (apeitheō, refusing to be persuaded) and “contrary” (antilegō, speaking against). Israel’s unbelief is not because God did not care. He held out his hands, and they refused.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God has given up on Israel. The very next chapter begins: has God rejected his people? By no means. His hands are still held out.

Where Christians differ: the sincerity of the offer. Some argue that if God has elected only some, his offer of salvation to the non-elect cannot be sincere. Verdict: God’s outstretched hands are real. He truly calls all who hear the gospel to come, and he is grieved by their refusal (Ezekiel 33:11; Matthew 23:37). His secret purpose in election and his revealed will in the gospel do not cancel each other. We do not fully understand how they fit together, but Scripture teaches both, and we must preach freely to all (Canons of Dort 2.5; 3/4.8).

In a sentence. And Isaiah boldly says, “I was found by those who did not seek me; I revealed myself to those who did not ask for me.” But concerning Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and stubborn people.”

For worship. God sought you when you were not looking for him. And he still holds out his hands to the stubborn. If you have been resisting him, come home.

parallels.desc: I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me
I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people

10.text: <sup>1</sup>Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.<sup>2</sup>For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.<sup>3</sup>For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness.<sup>4</sup>For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.<sup>5</sup>For Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does the commandments shall live by them.<sup>6</sup>But the righteousness based on faith says, “Do not say in your heart, ’Who will ascend into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)<sup>7</sup>“or ’Who will descend into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).<sup>8</sup>But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);<sup>9</sup>because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.<sup>10</sup>For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved.<sup>11</sup>For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”<sup>12</sup>For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; for the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him.<sup>13</sup>For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”<sup>14</sup>How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching?<sup>15</sup>And how are they to preach unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!”<sup>16</sup>But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?”<sup>17</sup>So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.<sup>18</sup>But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have, for “Their voice has gone out to all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”<sup>19</sup>But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, “I will make you jealous of those who are not a nation; with a foolish nation I will make you angry.”<sup>20</sup>Then Isaiah is so bold as to say, “I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me.”<sup>21</sup>But of Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”

11.title: The Mystery of Israel and the Doxology of Grace
11.overview:
Romans 11 completes the great argument about Israel that began in chapter 9. Paul has shown that God's word has not failed (chapter 9) and that Israel has heard and not believed (chapter 10). Now he asks: has God rejected his people? The answer is again the most emphatic negative in the letter: By no means! God has not cast away the people he foreknew. The evidence: Paul himself is a Jew, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin — and he has believed. The remnant is real.

But the chapter moves beyond the remnant to the mystery: Israel's hardening has served the purpose of Gentile inclusion, and Gentile inclusion is the means by which Israel will eventually be provoked to jealousy and saved. The olive tree image (vv. 17–24) holds the whole argument together: natural branches were broken off; wild branches were grafted in; the natural branches can and will be grafted back in. The God of the olive tree is the God of Israel's future. And that future ends not in permanent rejection but in the breathtaking statement: "all Israel will be saved" (v. 26).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Remnant: God Has Not Rejected His People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Has God rejected his people? By no means!" The vehemence of Paul's denial is significant — the same mē genoito he has used throughout the letter for the most outrageous misunderstandings of the gospel. The question of Israel's rejection is in the same category as the question of whether God is unjust (9:14) or whether we should sin that grace may abound (6:1). The answer is the same: unthinkable.

Paul's primary evidence is himself. He is a Jew. He has believed in Jesus as Messiah. Therefore God has not totally rejected Israel, because here is at least one Israelite who has been saved — and not the most promising one, either. The former persecutor of the church, the man who breathed threats and murder against the disciples of Jesus, stands as Exhibit A for the continued saving purposes of God toward Israel.

The parallel with Elijah (vv. 2–4) is instructive: when Elijah was convinced he was the only faithful Israelite left, God corrected him — seven thousand had not bowed to Baal. The prophet's perception of total abandonment was wrong. Paul draws the application: there is a remnant chosen by grace. Not by works, not by ancestry — by grace. And where grace operates, it is no longer works; the two principles are mutually exclusive. The remnant is real, small though it appears.

Then comes the harder half of the section, and it is not an appendix to the remnant — it is the same breath. What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened (v. 7). Three parties in one line: Israel as a whole, the elect within it, and the rest. Paul has just insisted that God has not rejected his people; he now says that most of them are hardened. The chapter is written by a man who saw no contradiction between those two sentences, and it cannot be read by anyone who holds only one of them.

The hardening is given scriptural warrant from two places welded together (v. 8) — God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, Isaiah 29:10 joined to Deuteronomy 29:4. The Deuteronomy setting repays knowing. Moses stands at the end of the wilderness years reciting what the people have watched with their own eyes: the plagues, the sea, forty years of bread out of the sky. His verdict on all of it is that to this day the LORD has not given you a heart to understand. Evidence was never the missing ingredient.

Then David (vv. 9–10), and the psalm is not chosen at random. Psalm 69 is the psalm of the righteous sufferer, the one the evangelists reach for to describe the cross — zeal for your house has consumed me; for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink. Paul turns its imprecation on those who rejected the very sufferer it was describing. And notice what is asked to become a snare: their table. Not their enemies, not their circumstances. Their provision. The privileges listed back in 9:4–5 are the things they trip over.

None of which is the section’s last word, and it would misrepresent Paul to stop here. His very next sentence asks whether they stumbled in order that they might fall, and answers it with the same violent negative this section opened with.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remnant Principle in Scripture

The remnant theology of Romans 11:1–10 runs through the entire Old Testament: Isaiah's "remnant of Israel" (Isaiah 10:20–22), Micah's "remnant of Jacob," the faithful seven thousand in Elijah's day. God has never saved the entire nation of Israel simply by virtue of their physical membership in the covenant people; he has always worked through a called, believing remnant within the larger community. This remnant is not self-selecting; it is chosen by grace. Paul's point is that this has always been God's method — the new covenant does not represent a change in approach but a clarification and fulfilment of the approach God has always taken.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal were invisible to Elijah — unknown to him, underground, silent. The remnant of God is often invisible to human perception. The prophet who declares the cause lost may be wrong; God's remnant is not necessarily visible or audible. Now: In seasons when the church appears to be in irreversible decline — when the statistics are grim and the cultural momentum runs entirely against Christian faith — the Elijah phenomenon is a perpetual danger: "I alone am left." The church is always smaller than it should be and larger than it appears. God preserves what he has promised to preserve.

verseByVerse.quote: I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has not rejected his people, and Paul, a Jew who believes, is himself the proof.

By no means! Paul’s strongest denial.

Benjamin. The tribe of Israel’s first king, also named Saul. Paul’s credentials are not in doubt (Philippians 3:5).

Whom he foreknew. As in 8:29, foreknowledge is God’s loving choice beforehand. He does not discard those he set his love on.

On a Tuesday. God does not abandon those he has chosen, however things look.

parallels.desc: the LORD will not forsake his people

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel? "Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life." But what is God's reply to him? "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As in Elijah’s day, when the prophet thought he stood alone, God had kept a faithful remnant for himself.

1 Kings 19. Elijah, exhausted and afraid, judged by what he could see.

I have kept for myself. The remnant is God’s doing, not their own heroism.

On a Tuesday. When you feel alone in faithfulness, remember there are more than you can see.

parallels.desc: I, even I only, am left
seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal

verseByVerse.quote: So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace. — Romans 11:5–6
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is still a remnant chosen by grace, and if it is by grace, it is not by works.

Chosen by grace. Election itself is an act of grace, not a reward for foreseen merit.

Grace would no longer be grace. Mix in works, even a little, and grace stops being grace.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add a mirror clause: “But if it is by works, it is no longer grace.” The earliest manuscripts lack it, and it is probably a later expansion.

For worship. Thank God that your place among his people rests on his grace, not your record.

verseByVerse.quote: What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened, as it is written, "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel as a whole failed to obtain what it sought, the elect obtained it, and the rest were hardened.

Two outcomes. Paul names God’s election and hardening plainly, as in 9:18.

Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10. A spirit of stupor: judicial blindness, God giving people over to the blindness they chose (1:24).

What it does not mean. The hardened are not innocent victims; they were seeking righteousness by works (9:32).

On a Tuesday. Do not trifle with light. Refused truth can become truth you can no longer see.

parallels.desc: the LORD has not given you eyes to see
a spirit of deep sleep

verseByVerse.quote: And David says, "Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David’s words in Psalm 69 describe the hardening of those who refused God’s anointed.

Their table. What should have nourished them, their privileges and Scriptures, became a trap.

Psalm 69. A psalm the New Testament reads of Christ’s sufferings (John 2:17; 15:25).

What it does not mean. Paul is not cursing the Jewish people. The very next verse says they have not fallen beyond recovery.

parallels.desc: let their own table before them become a snare

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The Olive Tree: Gentiles Grafted In, Israel Recoverable
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The section does not begin at the tree. It begins with a question about the difference between two ways of going down: did they stumble in order that they might fall? (v. 11). The distinction is the whole argument. A stumble is what happens on the way somewhere — you go down, and you get up. A fall, in the sense Paul is denying, is terminal. His answer is the same violent negative that opened the chapter.

What follows is the mechanism, and it is stranger than a consolation. Their trespass has meant salvation for the Gentiles, and that Gentile salvation is aimed back at Israel — so as to make Israel jealous, which is Moses’ own word from Deuteronomy 32:21, quoted a chapter earlier (10:19). Then the arithmetic of v. 12: if their failure has meant riches for the world, how much more their full inclusion. Paul is reasoning from the lesser to the greater, and the reasoning only works if there is a fullness still to come.

Verses 13–14 are more startling than they look, and they are addressed to Gentiles explicitly. Paul says he makes much of his Gentile ministry precisely in order to provoke his own people and save some of them. The apostle to the Gentiles is running a strategy whose second target is Israel; the two ministries are not in competition, and the Gentile church is, without knowing it, part of how God intends to reach the synagogue.

Then two images before the tree. If their rejection meant reconciliation for the world, their acceptance will mean life from the dead (v. 15) — a phrase Paul does not explain, and which readers have taken either as the general resurrection at the end or as a quickening of such magnitude that no smaller word would do. And v. 16: if the firstfruits of the dough are holy, so is the whole lump; if the root is holy, so are the branches. That is the offering of Numbers 15:20–21, where a consecrated portion makes the batch consecrated — a part standing for a whole, which is exactly what a remnant is and exactly what the tree is about to illustrate.

The olive tree is one of the most evocative images in the letter. The cultivated olive tree is Israel — the covenant people, rooted in the patriarchs, sustained by the promises of God. Natural branches (unbelieving Jews) have been broken off — not because God has given up on the tree, but because of unbelief. Wild branches (believing Gentiles) have been grafted in — not because of their natural superiority but purely by grace, "grafted in contrary to nature" (v. 24). The tree itself, its root and its sap, remains unchanged; what changes is which branches are bearing fruit on it.

Paul's warning to the Gentile believers is sharp and pointed: "Do not be arrogant toward the branches" (v. 18). The Gentile who imagines that the Jewish people have been permanently and finally replaced, that God has transferred his covenant purposes entirely and irreversibly to the Gentile church, has not been paying attention to chapters 9–11. God is able to graft the natural branches back in (v. 23). Indeed, he has said he will. The mercy shown to Gentiles is not a reversal of God's purposes for Israel; it is part of the very mechanism by which those purposes will ultimately be fulfilled.

The warning against Gentile pride is not merely a pastoral nicety; it is a theological corrective to supersessionism — the view that God has permanently replaced Israel with the church, that the covenant promises to Abraham and his physical descendants are entirely and exhaustively fulfilled in the Gentile church. Romans 11 will not allow this. The natural branches can be grafted back in; the God of the olive tree has not changed his mind about the tree.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Olive Tree and the Question of Supersessionism

Romans 11:17–24 is the central text in the debate between supersessionism (the church has entirely replaced Israel as the covenant people) and its alternatives. The text resists the supersessionist reading: unbelieving Jews are broken off branches — not dead stumps — and can be grafted back in. The root and richness of the olive tree (the Abrahamic covenant and its promises) remain; what changes is which branches are currently bearing fruit. The Reformed tradition has generally held to a form of "fulfilment theology" — the church is the continuation and fulfilment of Israel — while resisting the conclusion that God's purposes for ethnic Israel are entirely exhausted. Romans 11:25–29 will make this explicit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gentile believers in Rome were apparently in danger of looking down on Jewish unbelief with a degree of spiritual smugness. Paul's corrective is immediate: you stand only by faith; the one who broke off natural branches can break off wild ones too. The Gentile's security in the olive tree rests on the same grace that brought him in — and that grace is not a possession he holds, but a gift he receives. Now: Two thousand years of church history have produced exactly the Gentile arrogance Paul warned against — anti-Semitism often wrapped in theological language, the assumption that God has finished with the Jewish people. Romans 11 stands against this permanently. God has not and will not abandon the people he foreknew.

verseByVerse.quote: So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous. Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s stumbling is not final: through it salvation came to the Gentiles to provoke Israel to jealousy, and their full inclusion will mean far greater blessing.

Stumble, not fall. A trip, not a fatal fall.

God’s strategy. Israel’s rejection opened the door to the nations (Acts 13:46); the nations’ blessing is meant to draw Israel back.

Jealous. Not spite, but a holy envy: seeing Gentiles enjoy Israel’s Messiah and longing for him too (Deuteronomy 32:21).

How much more. If their failure enriched the world, their full inclusion will enrich it beyond measure.

For worship. Praise the God who turns even unbelief into the spread of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, apostle to the Gentiles, makes much of his ministry in the hope of making his fellow Jews jealous and saving some.

Magnify my ministry. His Gentile mission serves his love for Israel; the two are not rivals.

Save some. Paul speaks of himself as an instrument: God saves, through human messengers (1 Corinthians 9:22).

On a Tuesday. Live so that the joy of Christ in you makes others want what you have.

verseByVerse.quote: For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead? If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel’s rejection brought reconciliation to the world, their acceptance will be like life from the dead; and the holy root and firstfruits mean the branches are holy too.

Life from the dead. Either a spiritual awakening that brings new life to the world, or the final resurrection. Either way, something glorious.

Firstfruits and root. The patriarchs, with God’s promises to them (Numbers 15:20–21). God’s commitment to Abraham still sets Israel apart.

What it does not mean. “Holy” here means set apart by covenant, not personally saved. Unbelieving branches can still be broken off (v. 17).
verseByVerse.note: The first portion of dough was offered to God, and it made the whole batch holy. The “root” is the patriarchs.

parallels.desc: a loaf from the first of your dough

verseByVerse.quote: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree, do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you. — Romans 11:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentile believers, grafted in as wild branches, share the nourishment of Israel’s root, and must not boast over the natural branches.

One olive tree. Not two peoples of God, but one tree, with Gentiles grafted into Israel’s root.

The root supports you. The church does not replace Israel’s story; it is brought into it.

What it does not mean. There is no room here for Christian contempt of Jewish people. The church’s sad history of such contempt is a defiance of this verse.

On a Tuesday. Read the Old Testament as your family history.
verseByVerse.note: Israel is often pictured as God’s olive tree.

parallels.desc: a green olive tree

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will say, "Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in." That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Branches were broken off for unbelief, and Gentiles stand only by faith, so they must not be proud but fear.

That is true. Paul concedes the fact, not the boast.

By faith. Faith is the opposite of boasting (3:27).

Fear. Not anxious terror, but reverent humility that keeps a believer leaning on God.

parallels.desc: let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you. Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God's kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider God’s kindness and severity: severity to those who fell, kindness to you if you continue in his kindness, otherwise you too will be cut off.

Kindness and severity. Both are true of God. A gospel without severity is not Paul’s, nor one without kindness.

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be cut off? Arminians read this as warning that genuine believers may fall away and be lost. Verdict: Paul is speaking to Gentile Christians as a group, and the warning is one of the means by which God keeps his own (8:30, 38–39; Philippians 2:12–13). Those who persevere are the true believers; those who fall away show they never truly belonged (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and so is the promise.

Provided you continue. Perseverance is not automatic; it is God working through our continued faith.

On a Tuesday. Keep near to God’s kindness today. That is where safety lies.

verseByVerse.quote: And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again. For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If Israel does not persist in unbelief, God is able to graft them back in, and it would be far more natural than grafting in Gentiles.

Not continue in unbelief. The door is not shut on any Jewish person.

God has the power. The issue is not whether Israel is capable but whether God is able.

Contrary to nature. Gardeners graft cultivated branches onto wild stock. God’s grafting of Gentiles was the unexpected one.

For worship. Praise God that grace can restore what unbelief broke off.
verseByVerse.note: Growers normally grafted a cultivated branch onto wild stock; grafting a wild branch into a cultivated tree is, as Paul says, “contrary to nature.”

parallels.desc: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–36 — The Mystery, the Promise, and the Doxology
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reveals a mystery so that the Gentile believers will not become proud: a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved, as the prophets foretold of a Deliverer from Zion who will remove ungodliness from Jacob. As regards the gospel, Israel is at present opposed to it for the Gentiles’ sake; as regards God’s choice, they are loved because of the patriarchs, for God does not take back his gifts and call. Just as Gentiles once disobeyed and now have received mercy, so Israel has disobeyed so that they too may receive mercy; God has shut everyone up in disobedience in order to have mercy on all. Paul ends in wonder at the depth of God’s riches, wisdom and knowledge, whose ways no one can trace or advise: all things are from him, through him and to him, and to him be glory for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Irrevocability of God's Covenant Purposes

Romans 11:29 — "the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" — is the theological capstone of chapters 9–11 and one of the most important statements about God's faithfulness in Scripture. The word translated "irrevocable" (ametamelēta) means without repentance — God does not change his mind about what he has given and whom he has called. Applied to Israel: whatever the full meaning of "all Israel will be saved" (v. 26), it means at minimum that God has not and will not permanently and finally abandon the people he chose. Applied to the individual Christian: the calling and justification God has effected in her life will not be revoked. The golden chain of 8:29–30 and the irrevocability of 11:29 are two sides of the same coin.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The doxology of vv. 33–36 was Paul's own response to the argument he had just made. Having argued through three chapters about divine sovereignty, human responsibility, the mystery of Israel, and the purposes of God — he does not end with a systematic summary. He ends with worship. This is the correct response to the depth of God: not the mastery of a doctrine but the surrender of a doxology. Now: In an age that demands that every theological mystery be resolved into a satisfying rational system, the doxology of Romans 11:33–36 is the necessary reminder: we are not God. The depths of his wisdom and knowledge exceed our categories. The only posture that is finally appropriate before the mystery of divine election and human salvation is the posture Paul strikes: "From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever."

verseByVerse.quote: Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, "The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob"; — Romans 11:25–26
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reveals a mystery to humble the Gentiles: Israel’s partial hardening lasts until the full number of Gentiles has come in, and in this way all Israel will be saved.

Mystery. Something once hidden, now revealed by God.

Partial and until. The hardening is in part, and it has an end written into it.

The fullness of the Gentiles. The full number of Gentiles God intends to save, gathered in through the gospel. The Deliverer from Zion (Isaiah 59:20): Christ, who turns ungodliness away from Jacob by forgiving and renewing, not by force.

Where Christians differ: who is “all Israel”? Some take it as the whole church of Jews and Gentiles (Galatians 6:16; 9:6). Some take it as the elect Jews down through history (the remnant of vv. 1–10). Others take it as a great future turning of the Jewish people to Christ. Verdict: the third is more likely, since throughout this chapter “Israel” means the Jewish people, set against the Gentiles, and the “full inclusion” of v. 12 is more than a remnant. “In this way” means through the gospel and by faith.

What it does not mean. This does not support the dispensational scheme or make the modern state a fulfilment of prophecy. Paul promises the forgiveness of sins (v. 27), not territory, a temple or a thousand-year reign, and a future turning of the Jews fits the amillennial view. Nor is there a separate way for Israel without Christ: the Deliverer takes away sins (Isaiah 59:20).

On a Tuesday. This revelation was given to stop Christians thinking too well of themselves. Does your doctrine of the future make you humbler?
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God. Interpreters differ over whether “all Israel” means the Jewish people as a whole before the end, or the whole company of God’s people, Jew and Gentile. The more natural reading in context is the first: a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ.

parallels.desc: a Redeemer will come to Zion

verseByVerse.quote: "and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins." As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to take away Israel’s sins; and though now enemies of the gospel, they remain beloved because of God’s choice of their fathers.

The new covenant. The promise of forgiveness (Jeremiah 31:33–34; Isaiah 27:9).

Enemies and beloved. Both at once, from two angles: opposition to the gospel, and God’s covenant love for the fathers.

On a Tuesday. Hold firm convictions without ever withdrawing love.

parallels.desc: when he takes away his sin

verseByVerse.quote: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s gifts and calling cannot be revoked; Gentiles who were once disobedient have received mercy through Israel’s disobedience.

Irrevocable. God does not change his mind about those he calls. This is the ground of Israel’s hope, and of every believer’s assurance.

Calling. Here God’s calling of Israel as his people, the same faithful God who calls each believer (8:30).

For worship. Thank God that he never takes back his promises.

parallels.desc: God is not man, that he should lie

verseByVerse.quote: so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy. For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel has been disobedient so that, through the mercy shown to Gentiles, they too may receive mercy; for God has shut up all in disobedience so that he may have mercy on all.

Consigned all. Jew and Gentile alike are locked in disobedience (3:9, 23), so that no one is saved except by mercy.

Where Christians differ: mercy on all, so everyone saved? Universalists read this as the salvation of every person. Verdict: “all” here means Jew and Gentile, both groups, not every individual. The same chapter speaks of branches broken off, and Paul warns of wrath elsewhere (2:5–8). God has mercy on all without distinction, not on all without exception.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit the second “now”. Its presence suggests Israel’s mercy can come in the present age.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit the second “now.”

verseByVerse.quote: Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul bursts into praise at the depth of God’s riches, wisdom and knowledge, and the mystery of his ways.

Doctrine becomes doxology. Eleven chapters of hard thinking end not in a puzzle solved but in worship.

Unsearchable. We can know God truly, but never exhaustively.

For worship. When God’s ways are beyond you, let that move you to praise, not complaint.

parallels.desc: my thoughts are not your thoughts

verseByVerse.quote: "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has known the Lord’s mind or advised him.

Isaiah 40:13. God needed no counsellor when he made the world, nor when he planned salvation.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to understand everything God is doing in order to trust him.

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: "Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ever given God anything that obliges him to repay.

Job 41:11. God owes no one; all he gives is grace.

The end of merit. This verse sums up Romans 1–11. Salvation is never repayment.

parallels.desc: who has first given to me, that I should repay him?

verseByVerse.quote: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things are from God, through God, and for God; to him be the glory for ever.

From, through, to. God is the source, the means and the goal of everything.

Amen. The proper response to the gospel of Romans 1–11.

For worship. Make this verse your prayer: to him be glory for ever. Amen.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin.<sup>2</sup>God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel?<sup>3</sup>“Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have demolished your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.”<sup>4</sup>But what is God’s reply to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.”<sup>5</sup>So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace.<sup>6</sup>But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.<sup>7</sup>What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened,<sup>8</sup>as it is written, “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, down to this very day.”<sup>9</sup>And David says, “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them;<sup>10</sup>let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and bend their backs forever.”<sup>11</sup>So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous.<sup>12</sup>Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!<sup>13</sup>Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry<sup>14</sup>in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them.<sup>15</sup>For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?<sup>16</sup>If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches.<sup>17</sup>But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree,<sup>18</sup>do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.<sup>19</sup>Then you will say, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.”<sup>20</sup>That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but fear.<sup>21</sup>For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.<sup>22</sup>Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God’s kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.<sup>23</sup>And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again.<sup>24</sup>For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree, and grafted, contrary to nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted back into their own olive tree.<sup>25</sup>Lest you be wise in your own sight, I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in.<sup>26</sup>And in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written, “The Deliverer will come from Zion, he will banish ungodliness from Jacob”;<sup>27</sup>“and this will be my covenant with them when I take away their sins.”<sup>28</sup>As regards the gospel, they are enemies for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers.<sup>29</sup>For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.<sup>30</sup>For just as you were at one time disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,<sup>31</sup>so they too have now been disobedient in order that by the mercy shown to you they also may now receive mercy.<sup>32</sup>For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all.<sup>33</sup>Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!<sup>34</sup>“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”<sup>35</sup>“Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?”<sup>36</sup>For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen.

12.title: The Transformed Life
12.overview:
"Therefore" — with this word, chapters 12–16 are connected to everything that has gone before. The mercies of God described in chapters 1–11 are the foundation; the transformed life of chapters 12–16 is the superstructure. Paul does not move from theology to ethics because theology is the theoretical part and ethics is the practical part; he moves from theology to ethics because the ethics are the fruit of the theology.
