The mercies of God are not merely things to be believed; they are the motive force of a whole new way of living.

Chapter 12 opens with one of the most celebrated calls to consecration in the entire New Testament: "present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship" (v. 1). The language is deliberately sacrificial — the life of the justified Christian is offered to God in its entirety, not merely its "spiritual" dimension. And then the renewal of the mind (v. 2), which makes possible the discernment of God's will — the good, acceptable, and perfect. The rest of the chapter is the practical outworking of these two verses across the life of the Christian community.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Living Sacrifice and the Renewed Mind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God" — the ethical appeal is grounded entirely in the indicative of grace. Paul does not say "in view of your obligations" or "in view of the moral law." He says: in view of the mercies of God — the whole sweep of justification, adoption, the Spirit, the love that cannot be separated from, the glory that is coming. It is the mercies that create the motivation; the obligation flows from the gift, not from duty alone.

"Present your bodies" — not just your souls or your religious activities, but your bodies: the physical, concrete, embodied reality of your daily existence. The body that gets up in the morning and goes to work. The hands that type the email. The mouth that speaks in the meeting. The feet that walk into the neighbour's house. Paul insists on the bodily nature of Christian worship because God insists on it: the gospel is not a recipe for spiritual escapism but for the consecration of the whole life — body and soul, private and public, sacred and secular — to God.

"Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind" (v. 2) — the passive voice is significant: be transformed, not transform yourself. The transformation is something that happens to you, from the inside, through the renewal of your mind by the Spirit and the Word. The Christian does not achieve transformation by heroic effort; she submits to it by attending to the means through which God renews the mind — Scripture, prayer, worship, community, suffering. And the evidence of transformation is discernment: the ability to prove what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body as Instrument of Worship

Romans 12:1 demolishes the sacred-secular distinction that has plagued Christian thinking since the patristic era. The body — presented to God as a living sacrifice — is itself the site of worship. This means that the Christian's daily work, physical rest, sexual life, eating and drinking, financial decisions, and embodied relationships are all, in principle, acts of worship when offered to God in faith and obedience. The Reformers' insistence on the holiness of ordinary life is grounded here. John Calvin saw the entire creation as the theatre of God's glory; Paul grounds that vision in the consecrated body of the believer. Your body is not a vehicle for your soul; it is the instrument of your worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The language of sacrifice was immediately understood by both Jewish and Gentile readers. In the Jewish tradition, sacrifice was the central act of worship — the presentation of an offering to God. Paul is saying that the entire life of the Christian is now the sacrifice: not an animal brought to an altar, but a person brought to God in the totality of their daily existence. The temple has been interiorised; the altar is everywhere; the offering is ongoing. Now: The call to "not be conformed to this world" is perpetually urgent because the world perpetually presses in. Every culture — including Christian subculture — has its conforming pressures, its assumed values, its default ways of measuring worth, success, and meaning. The renewal of the mind is the counter-pressure: learning to see all of life through the lens of Scripture, of the gospel, of the mercies of God, until the world's categories no longer have automatic authority over us.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. — Romans 12:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
In view of God’s mercies, believers are to offer their whole selves to God as a living sacrifice and be transformed by a renewed mind, not squeezed into the world’s pattern.

Therefore. Chapters 1–11 come first. Grace is the root; obedience is the fruit, never the other way round.

Your bodies. Not just your soul or feelings. Faith is lived in hands, eyes, tongue, time and money.

A living sacrifice. The animals on the altar died once. Christ’s sacrifice is complete (Hebrews 10:14); ours is a lifelong offering of thanks, not atonement.

Spiritual worship. The word can mean “rational” or “reasonable”: the fitting response of a mind that has grasped the gospel. Worship is the whole of life, not only Sunday.

Conformed or transformed. The world presses from outside; the Spirit renews from inside, through the mind. Transformation happens as we think God’s thoughts after him in Scripture.

The will of God. Here God’s revealed will for how to live, which a renewed mind learns to recognise and approve. It is not chiefly about guessing hidden plans.

On a Tuesday. Before the day starts, offer it to God: your body, your schedule, your phone. Ask where the world’s pattern has been shaping your mind.

For worship. Present yourself to God, not to earn mercy, but because you have received it.
verseByVerse.note: “Therefore” builds on chapters 1–11: the mercies of God come first, then the response. The ESV notes that “spiritual worship” can also be rendered “rational service.”

parallels.desc: the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–8 — Gifts of Grace: Sober Self-Assessment in the Body
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The renewed mind produces, first, a sober assessment of oneself — neither inflated pride nor false modesty, but honest recognition of the measure of faith God has given and the gifts he has distributed. The image Paul uses is the body: one body, many members, each with a different function. No member of the body of Christ is the whole body; no gift given to one member is given to all; the diversity is not a deficiency but the design.

Paul's list of gifts in vv. 6–8 — prophecy, service, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading, showing mercy — is not exhaustive but representative. Each gift comes with a manner: prophesy in proportion to your faith, serve in your serving, teach in your teaching, exhort in your exhorting, give with generosity, lead with zeal, show mercy with cheerfulness. The gifts are not to be displayed but exercised — put to work in the service of the body for the benefit of all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Charismata: Gifts of the Spirit for the Common Good

The gifts listed in Romans 12 are what Paul elsewhere calls charismata — graces, gifts of the Spirit. The Reformed tradition has emphasised that every gift is given for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7), not for the personal spiritual enhancement of the recipient. The gift of teaching is not given so that the teacher can be admired; it is given so that the body can be built up. The gift of mercy is not given as an ornament of personal piety; it is given to be exercised toward those in need. Gift and function are inseparable; the gift that is not exercised in service is a lamp hidden under a bowl.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The early church was a remarkable mixture of social classes, ethnic backgrounds, and educational levels. The gifts distributed by the Spirit crossed every human boundary: the slave might have the gift of teaching; the educated Greek might have the gift of service. The body-of-Christ framework was the theological revolution that made sense of this diversity. Now: The contemporary church regularly struggles with two opposite errors in the theology of gifts: the inflation of spectacular gifts (leading to unhealthy spiritual hierarchy and competition) and the dismissal of ordinary gifts (leading to the impression that only the "up-front" gifts matter). Romans 12:6–8 keeps the balance: every gift, faithfully exercised in its proper sphere, is a grace from God and a service to the body.

verseByVerse.quote: For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned. — Romans 12:3
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul calls each believer to think of themselves with sober judgment, according to the measure of faith God has given.

By the grace given to me. Paul speaks with apostolic authority, which is itself grace.

Not too highly. The first effect of a renewed mind is humility.

Sober judgment. Not low self-esteem, but accurate self-assessment. False modesty is also a kind of pride.

The measure of faith. Probably the different gifts and capacities God assigns, received by faith. No one has reason to boast (1 Corinthians 4:7).

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly: what has God given me, and what has he not?
verseByVerse.note: A play on the verb “think” (phroneō): not to think too highly (hyperphronein) but to think with sober judgment (sōphronein).

verseByVerse.quote: For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church is one body with many members, each with a different function, and all belonging to one another.

One body in Christ. Unity is given, not manufactured.

Not the same function. Difference is God’s design, not a problem to be ironed out.

Members one of another. You do not just belong to Christ; you belong to his people. Isolated Christianity is a contradiction.

On a Tuesday. Who in your church needs what you have, and whose gifts do you need?

verseByVerse.quote: Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers have different gifts by grace, to be used faithfully; prophecy, for instance, according to the proportion of faith.

Gifts by grace. Charismata come from charis. A gift is never earned or a badge of rank.

In proportion to our faith. Either the measure of the prophet’s own faith, or agreement with “the faith”, the truth revealed. The phrase gave rise to the Reformed principle of the analogy of faith: Scripture interprets Scripture.

Where Christians differ: prophecy today. Continuationists hold that prophecy continues as a gift of the church. Cessationists hold that revelatory prophecy belonged to the foundation-laying apostolic era (Ephesians 2:20), and that the canon is now closed. Verdict: the cessationist view is to be preferred: no new revelation is given today. Yet preaching that applies Scripture with power to the present still does much of what prophecy did. Hold the view charitably.

On a Tuesday. Use the gift you have today rather than wishing for someone else’s.

verseByVerse.quote: ...if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching; the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness. — Romans 12:7–8
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul lists further gifts, each to be exercised wholeheartedly and in the right spirit: service, teaching, encouragement, giving, leading and mercy.

A mixed list. Public gifts like teaching sit beside quiet ones like mercy. None is more spiritual than the others.

The manner matters. Giving with generosity, not a hidden agenda; leading with zeal, not coasting; mercy with cheerfulness, not grudging duty.

Exhortation. Encouraging, urging and comforting: the gift of coming alongside.

On a Tuesday. If your role today is giving, leading or showing mercy, do it with all your heart, as service to Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–21 — Love in Action: The Ethics of the Transformed Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Verses 9–21 form a rapid-fire sequence of practical exhortations that read almost like headings from a sermon on the Christian life — compressed, vivid, and comprehensive. Love without hypocrisy. Abhorring evil, holding fast to what is good. Outdoing one another in showing honour. Fervent in spirit. Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, constant in prayer. Contributing to the needs of the saints. Blessing those who persecute. Weeping with those who weep. Not being haughty. Repaying no one evil for evil. Living at peace with everyone. Not taking revenge. Overcoming evil with good.

The section begins and ends with love: "Let love be genuine" (v. 9) and "overcome evil with good" (v. 21). Everything between is the anatomy of genuine love in practice. Paul is not describing an achievable moral programme; he is describing the shape of a Spirit-renewed life — what grace looks like when it has taken hold of a person and begun the long work of conforming her to Christ.

The command to bless persecutors (v. 14) and to overcome evil with good (v. 21) are among the most demanding in the entire New Testament. They presuppose a radical reorientation of the instinct for self-protection and retaliation — an instinct that the Spirit does not suppress but redirects. The Christian who blesses her persecutor is not pretending the persecution is acceptable; she is entrusting the righting of wrongs to the God who says "vengeance is mine" (v. 19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35) and acting from the love that wishes even the enemy's good.

Two things in the section deserve naming. The first is a piece of wordplay in v. 13. The command is not merely to show hospitality but to pursue it — and the verb is the one Paul uses in the very next line of those who persecute you. The same word, one sentence apart, running in opposite directions: some people are chasing you, and you are to go chasing after strangers.

The second is v. 20, which is the sharpest instruction here and the most misread: if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink. Paul takes it from Proverbs 25:21–22, and the burning coals are not a promise that your kindness will make him suffer in some superior way. The image is most naturally read as the burning of shame that leads to repentance. The aim of the exercise is not a defeated enemy. It is an enemy who has stopped being one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ethic of the Cross in Daily Life

The ethics of Romans 12:9–21 are the daily practical form of the theology of the cross. The crucified Christ did not retaliate; he blessed those who cursed him; he overcame evil with the supreme good of his self-offering. The Christian who lives by this ethic is not simply following rules but is embodying the pattern of the One who died for his enemies. This is why Paul can ground the command to bless persecutors in the experience of God's mercy (v. 1): the person who knows she was God's enemy and has been loved into sonship has the deepest possible motivation for loving her enemies. She is doing to them what was done to her.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman church included people from across the social spectrum — slaves, freedmen, members of Caesar's household (Philippians 4:22), wealthy patrons, poor migrants. The potential for social friction, hierarchy, and mutual contempt was enormous. Paul's commands — "outdo one another in showing honour" (v. 10), "do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly" (v. 16) — were written for a community in which these things were concrete daily challenges, not abstract ethical principles. Now: The contemporary church is no less stratified by income, education, race, and social status. Romans 12:9–21 is still the practical charter of a community that crosses every human division by the power of a love that is genuinely without hypocrisy. The test is not whether the church affirms diversity in principle but whether its members weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice — across every line that the world uses to divide.

verseByVerse.quote: Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good. Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor. — Romans 12:9–10
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love must be sincere, hating evil and clinging to good, warm with family affection and eager to honour others.

Genuine. Literally “without hypocrisy”: no acting.

Abhor and hold fast. Love is not soft on evil. Real love hates what destroys the beloved.

Brotherly affection. Philadelphia: the church is a family.

Outdo one another. The only competition allowed among Christians: who can honour the other more.

On a Tuesday. Find a way to honour someone today who will not expect it.

parallels.desc: hate evil, and love good

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are to be zealous, fervent and serving the Lord, joyful in hope, patient in trouble and faithful in prayer.

Not slothful. Spiritual laziness is a real danger. Zeal is eager, energetic commitment.

Patient in tribulation. Holding on under pressure without bitterness or giving up.

Fervent in spirit. Literally “boiling”. Possibly the Holy Spirit, as the ESV notes.

Three pairs. Hope gives joy, affliction calls for patience, and prayer keeps both going.

Textual note. A few manuscripts read “serving the time” (kairō) for “serving the Lord” (kyriō), a slip easily made between two similar abbreviations. “The Lord” is well attested and fits Paul’s style.

On a Tuesday. In a hard week: rejoice in what is coming, endure what is here, and pray without giving up.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “fervent in spirit” can also be read “fervent in the Spirit.”

verseByVerse.quote: Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers are to share with needy Christians, practise hospitality, and bless those who persecute them.

Contribute. The word is koinōneō: fellowship that reaches the wallet.

Seek to show hospitality. Literally “pursue” it. It is not waiting for the right moment but going after it.

Bless your persecutors. An echo of Jesus (Luke 6:28). To bless is to speak well of them and ask God’s good for them; to curse is to call down harm.

What it does not mean. Not approving what they do or pretending it does not hurt. You can name the wrong and still pray for the wrongdoer.

On a Tuesday. Open your home or table this week, and pray for good for someone who treats you badly.
verseByVerse.note: Hospitality to travelling believers was vital in a world of poor, unsafe inns.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians share each other’s joys and sorrows, live in harmony, associate with the humble, and do not think themselves wise.

Rejoice and weep. It is often harder to rejoice sincerely at another’s success than to weep at their loss.

Associate with the lowly. The Greek may mean lowly people or lowly tasks. Both apply: no job or person is beneath you.

Not wise in your own sight. Proverbs 3:7. Pride wrecks harmony.

On a Tuesday. Sit with someone others overlook.

parallels.desc: be not wise in your own eyes

verseByVerse.quote: Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Never repay evil with evil, do what all can see is honourable, and live at peace with everyone as far as it depends on you.

No revenge. Retaliation feels like justice but multiplies evil.

In the sight of all. Proverbs 3:4. Christians should be known even by outsiders for integrity.

If possible. Peace is not always possible. You cannot control another person’s response, only your own part, and you must not buy peace by giving up truth.

On a Tuesday. Is there a broken relationship where you have not yet done your part?

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord." To the contrary, "if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not take revenge but leave room for God’s wrath, and instead do good to your enemy, which will heap burning coals on his head.

Leave it to God. Deuteronomy 32:35. Justice is not abandoned but entrusted to the only one who judges perfectly. This is not passivity.

Proverbs 25:21–22. Feed your enemy; give him a drink.

Where Christians differ: burning coals. Some read it as increasing the enemy’s guilt and judgment. Others see it as shame and remorse that may lead to repentance; some scholars link it to an ancient Egyptian rite of penitence. Verdict: the second fits the context of overcoming evil with good (v. 21). Kindness aims to win the enemy.

What it does not mean. This is personal ethics. It does not forbid the state from punishing wrongdoers (13:4), nor victims from seeking justice through proper channels.

On a Tuesday. Do a specific act of kindness for someone who has hurt you.
verseByVerse.note: Heaping burning coals probably means bringing the enemy to shame and a change of heart through kindness.

parallels.desc: vengeance is mine
if your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let evil defeat you, but defeat evil by doing good.

Two battles. Evil wins not only when it hurts you, but when it makes you like it.

The way of the cross. Christ overcame evil by enduring it and returning good (1 Peter 2:23).

For worship. Thank Christ, who overcame your evil with his good.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.<sup>2</sup>Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.<sup>3</sup>For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned.<sup>4</sup>For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function,<sup>5</sup>so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.<sup>6</sup>Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, let us use them: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;<sup>7</sup>if service, in our serving; the one who teaches, in his teaching;<sup>8</sup>the one who exhorts, in his exhortation; the one who contributes, in generosity; the one who leads, with zeal; the one who does acts of mercy, with cheerfulness.<sup>9</sup>Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good.<sup>10</sup>Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor.<sup>11</sup>Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord.<sup>12</sup>Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer.<sup>13</sup>Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality.<sup>14</sup>Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse them.<sup>15</sup>Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep.<sup>16</sup>Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.<sup>17</sup>Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all.<sup>18</sup>If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.<sup>19</sup>Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.”<sup>20</sup>To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head.”<sup>21</sup>Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

13.title: Citizens of Two Kingdoms
13.overview:
Romans 13 addresses two dimensions of the Christian's life in the world that might seem unrelated but are theologically connected: the relationship to governing authorities (vv. 1–7) and the debt of love that fulfils the whole law (vv. 8–14). Both passages apply the gospel-transformed mind of 12:2 to concrete social realities. The Christian is not a free agent owing nothing to anyone; she is embedded in a created order (civil government) and a moral order (the law of love) that place real obligations on her life.

The passage on governing authorities is one of the most important and most abused in the New Testament — used to justify passive submission to every form of political power, and also to justify every form of political resistance. Paul's point is neither absolutist submission nor automatic resistance; it is the theological grounding of civil authority in God's own ordering of human society, combined with the practical obligation to honour, obey, and pay taxes to those who wield legitimate authority.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Governing Authorities: God's Servant for Good
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God" (v. 1). The theological foundation is clear: civil government is not a human invention that God tolerates; it is an ordering of human society that God has established for the good of human beings. The magistrate, the soldier, the tax official — in their legitimate exercise of authority, they are God's servants (diakonos — the same word used for church deacons) for the maintenance of order, the punishment of evil, and the commendation of good.

The context matters: Paul is writing to Rome under the early Nero, before the persecutions of the 60s. The Roman state, for all its paganism, provided the remarkable infrastructure of law, roads, and relative peace (the Pax Romana) that enabled the gospel to spread across the empire. Paul is not asking the Roman Christians to endorse every policy of the emperor; he is asking them not to be revolutionaries — not to treat their citizenship in the kingdom of God as a license to ignore or undermine the civil order that God has established.

The limits of this submission are implied by the rest of Scripture (Acts 5:29 — "We must obey God rather than men") and by Paul's own record of civil disobedience. When the governing authority commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, the Christian must obey God. But the default posture is submission, because the default function of civil government — even imperfect civil government — is the ordering of human life in a fallen world for the common good.

Three things in the passage should not be passed over. The first is v. 2, which supplies the sanction: whoever resists the authority resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment. Paul is not merely recommending civic good manners. He is saying that the ordering itself has God behind it, so that contempt for it is not a neutral act.

The second is the second half of v. 4, and it is the hinge on which the previous chapter turns. The magistrate does not bear the sword in vain; he is an avenger who carries out God’s wrath on the wrongdoer. A few verses earlier Paul forbade the Christian to avenge himself and told him to give place to the wrath (12:19). He now names the office through which some of that wrath is administered in the present. Vengeance was not abolished when it was taken out of your hands. It was relocated.

The third is v. 5, which gives the motive: submission is owed not only to avoid God’s wrath but also for the sake of conscience. That distinguishes the Christian citizen from the merely prudent one. Fear of penalty produces compliance wherever penalties are likely; conscience produces the same behaviour where no one is watching and nothing would follow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kingdoms and Civil Authority

The Reformation developed the doctrine of the two kingdoms — the kingdom of God's left hand (civil government) and the kingdom of his right hand (the church) — as the theological framework for understanding passages like Romans 13. God governs the civil sphere through natural law and common grace, using even unbelieving rulers to maintain order and restrain evil. God governs the church through Word and Spirit. The two kingdoms are distinct but not separate; the Christian citizen participates in both, with different modes of loyalty appropriate to each. Luther and Calvin both insisted on the legitimacy and dignity of civil authority while limiting its scope: Caesar has his domain; Christ has his; and the two must never be confused.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Roman Christians were tempted, for obvious reasons, to view the imperial state with suspicion or hostility — an institution that had crucified their Lord and would eventually persecute them. Paul's command to submit was not politically naive; it was theologically grounded. God uses even imperfect and eventually hostile governments to structure human life. The Christian who refuses all civil order in the name of heavenly citizenship has not understood the two-kingdom distinction. Now: In democracies, Romans 13 applies to the obligation of citizens to participate in civil society — paying taxes, respecting legitimate authority, working through legal channels to promote justice. It does not require silent compliance with injustice; the Christian who uses the legitimate tools of civil society to oppose evil is not violating v. 1 but fulfilling v. 4's vision of government as a servant of good.

verseByVerse.quote: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians are to submit to governing authorities, because all authority is appointed by God, and resisting it is resisting God’s ordinance.

Every person. No one is exempt, including Christians who know their true citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20).

Instituted by God. Government is God’s gift for ordering a fallen world, not merely a human contract.

Under Nero. Paul wrote this under a pagan emperor. Submission does not depend on the ruler being Christian or good.

Where Christians differ: are there limits? Some read the command as near-absolute. Most of the Christian tradition sees limits: when rulers command sin, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29; Daniel 3, 6). Calvin allowed that lower officials appointed to restrain kings might lawfully resist a tyrant. Verdict: submission is the rule, not unlimited obedience. Disobedience is right only where obedience would mean sinning, and then it should be open, non-violent where possible, and willing to bear the penalty.

What it does not mean. It does not make every government’s actions right, nor sanctify any particular party or nation.

On a Tuesday. Respect for authority shows in small things: speed limits, tax forms, how you speak of leaders.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote under the emperor Nero, in the early, better years of his rule. Jesus had said, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s.”

parallels.desc: by me kings reign

verseByVerse.quote: For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rulers exist to restrain evil and reward good; the one in authority is God’s servant, bearing the sword to punish wrongdoers.

God’s servant. The word is diakonos. Even a pagan magistrate serves God’s purposes, knowingly or not.

For your good. Order, justice and protection are real blessings.

The sword. The state may use force to punish. The vengeance believers must not take personally (12:19), God exercises in part through the state.

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some see the sword as authorising the death penalty (Genesis 9:6); others see it as only the general power to punish, and argue that mercy or the risk of error should rule it out today. Verdict: Scripture permits the state to use capital punishment for the gravest crimes; whether and how a nation uses it is a matter of wisdom and justice, with great care to avoid error.

What it does not mean. Paul describes what rulers are for, not that they always do it. A government that rewards evil and punishes good betrays its calling.
verseByVerse.note: The sword stood for the government’s power to punish, including capital punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience. — Romans 13:5
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers submit not only to avoid punishment but also because conscience tells them it is right.

Two motives. Fear of consequences, and a conscience shaped by God.

For conscience. A Christian obeys good laws even when no one is watching.

On a Tuesday. Would you keep the rules if you knew you would never be caught?

verseByVerse.quote: For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed. — Romans 13:6–7
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why Christians pay taxes; give to everyone what you owe: taxes, revenue, respect and honour.

Ministers of God. A third word for officials. Their work is a public service.

Taxes and revenue. Taxes were direct tribute paid by subject peoples; revenue was indirect tax such as customs and tolls. Nero’s Rome faced protests over tolls in AD 58, about when Paul wrote.

Render to all. An echo of Jesus: give to Caesar what is Caesar’s (Mark 12:17).

Respect and honour. Not only money. Christians must not speak with contempt of those in office, even when opposing their policies (1 Peter 2:17).

On a Tuesday. Pay what you owe honestly, and pray for those who govern (1 Timothy 2:1–2).
verseByVerse.note: “Taxes” were direct taxes; “revenue” meant customs and tolls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Love Fulfils the Law: Put on Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law" (v. 8). The transition from taxes and respect to love is sudden but logical: both are obligations owed to those among whom we live. But the debt of love is unique — it is a debt that is perpetually owed and perpetually paid but never fully discharged. You can pay a tax and be done with it; you can never be done with the obligation to love, because the opportunities to love are inexhaustible and the command is perpetual.

Paul's claim is audacious: love fulfils the entire law. The specific commandments — do not commit adultery, do not murder, do not steal, do not covet — are all "summed up" in this word: love your neighbour as yourself (quoting Leviticus 19:18). This does not make the specific commandments irrelevant; it establishes their theological root. Love is the soil from which all the particular expressions of right conduct grow. The person who truly loves her neighbour will not steal from him, will not lie to him, will not commit adultery against him. Love is not a substitute for the law's specific demands; it is the power that fulfils them from within.

The passage closes with the urgency of eschatological time: "the night is far gone; the day is at hand" (v. 12). The Christian lives in the interim between the first coming of Christ (which inaugurated the day of salvation) and his return (which will complete it). This is not time to sleep; it is time to wake, to lay aside the works of darkness, to put on the armour of light — and supremely to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ" (v. 14). The Christian life is not moral self-improvement; it is the clothing of oneself in Christ, day by day, until the transformation is complete.

Between the dawn and the clothing stands v. 13, which supplies the specifics: let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. Three pairs, and the order of them is the sting. The list begins where anyone would expect a vice list to begin and ends somewhere entirely respectable — with arguing and envy, which are set down in the same sentence, under the same heading, as the drunken procession through the streets.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Fulfilment of the Law

Romans 13:8–10 gives the summary of the second table of the law: love your neighbour as yourself. This is not a replacement of the law with an undefined sentiment; it is the identification of the animating principle from which all the law's specific demands flow. The Reformed tradition has insisted that love and law are not opposites — love is the motive; the law is the guide. The renewed person who loves God supremely and her neighbour genuinely will want to know concretely what that love requires in specific situations, and the law provides exactly that: the concrete shape of love in action.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's command to "put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh" (v. 14) was the verse that Augustine read in the garden in Milan in 386 AD, at the moment of his conversion. He had been struggling with the inability to break free from sexual sin; these words fell on him with the weight of divine command and divine grace simultaneously. The verse is still doing what it did to Augustine: convicting, commanding, and empowering. Now: The urgency of vv. 11–14 is the urgency of the gospel in every age: the window of this life is short; the return of Christ is certain; the works of darkness are not appropriate wear for people who are children of light. Every day lived in unrepentant sin is a wasted day; every day lived in Christ is a day that will outlast the sun.

verseByVerse.quote: Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. For the commandments, "You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet," and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leave no debt outstanding except the continuing debt to love one another, for love fulfils the law.

Owe no one anything. Pay what you owe when due.

Where Christians differ: is all borrowing forbidden? Some have taken this to forbid all debt, including mortgages. Verdict: Scripture allows lending and borrowing (Exodus 22:25; Matthew 5:42). The command is to pay debts when due and not live beyond your means. Wisdom urges caution with debt.

The debt of love. The one debt you can never pay off.

You shall not covet. The command that reaches the heart: not merely desiring, but craving what belongs to another (7:7). Love wants the neighbour’s good, not the neighbour’s goods.

Summed up. Love does not replace the commandments; it is what they look like when kept from the heart (Leviticus 19:18).

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add “You shall not bear false witness” to the list. The earliest lack it.

parallels.desc: love your neighbour as yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love never harms a neighbour, so love fulfils the law.

Love does no wrong. The commandments listed are all about not harming another.

What it does not mean. Love is not a vague feeling that lets us set aside God’s commands. It is their fulfilment, not their replacement.

On a Tuesday. Ask of each decision: will this harm my neighbour?

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed. The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. — Romans 13:11–12
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing the time, believers must wake from sleep, because their final salvation is nearer than when they first believed; the night is nearly over, so put off darkness and put on light.

The time. Kairos: the critical moment between Christ’s first and second comings.

Salvation nearer. Here salvation is its completion at Christ’s return (8:23).

Where Christians differ: did Paul expect Christ within his lifetime? Some critics say Paul expected an immediate return and was wrong. Verdict: Paul taught that the return is near in God’s timetable and could come at any time, without setting a date (1 Thessalonians 5:1–2). Every generation lives in the last hour (1 John 2:18).

Armour of light. The Christian life is a fight (Ephesians 6:11).

On a Tuesday. Live as if this were the morning Christ returns.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires. — Romans 13:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Live decently as in daylight, not in drunkenness, sexual sin or quarrelling, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ and give no opportunity to the flesh.

Three pairs. Orgies and drunkenness: wild, drunken parties. Sexual immorality and sensuality: sex outside marriage and shameless indulgence. Quarrelling and jealousy: strife and resentment. The last pair is as serious as the first two.

Properly as in the daytime. Decently, as people do things they would not mind being seen.

What it does not mean. Not a ban on feasting or celebration (Luke 15:23), but on excess that leaves God out.

Put on Christ. At conversion believers are clothed with Christ (Galatians 3:27); daily they put him on again, in character and conduct.

Make no provision. Do not plan ahead for sin. Remove what feeds it.

Augustine. These words were God’s means of his conversion in AD 386.

On a Tuesday. What “provision for the flesh” have you made that needs removing?

For worship. Ask Christ to clothe you with himself today.
verseByVerse.note: Augustine was converted on reading these verses in a garden in Milan in AD 386.

For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God.<sup>2</sup>Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment.<sup>3</sup>For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval,<sup>4</sup>for he is God’s servant for your good. 14.title: The Weak and the Strong: Liberty and Love
14.overview:
Romans 14–15 address a specific pastoral conflict in the Roman church: tension between Jewish Christians who maintained food laws and Sabbath observances ("the weak in faith") and Gentile Christians who felt free from such regulations ("the strong"). But Paul's treatment of this specific conflict generates principles that apply to every generation's version of the same tension: the conflict between Christian liberty and Christian love, between what I am free to do and what love requires me to do for the sake of my brother.

The governing principle is not the extension of legal restriction to those who are free, nor the dismissal of sensitive consciences as mere scrupulosity. It is love — the willingness to limit one's own legitimate freedom for the sake of the weaker brother's conscience and the unity of the body. Paul himself is clearly among "the strong" (15:1 — "we who are strong"), but his pastoral concern is to protect the weak while educating them toward greater freedom, without allowing either group to destroy the other with contempt or judgment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Welcome the Weak: Do Not Judge or Despise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions" (v. 1). The command is striking in both its positive and its negative dimensions. Positively: welcome him — bring him into the full fellowship of the community, do not treat his scruples as a reason for exclusion. Negatively: not to quarrel over opinions — do not make his welcome the occasion for pressuring him to adopt your view or defend your freedom. The welcome is genuine; the agenda of the welcome is his good, not your point-scoring.

The specific examples Paul uses — one person eats only vegetables, another observes certain days as special — are illustrations of a broader principle. The particulars may be first-century Jewish food laws and Sabbath observances; the principle is the obligation of both the strong and the weak to refrain from the two characteristic sins their positions generate: the strong's temptation to despise the scrupulous (treating their sensitivity as weakness or intellectual failure), and the weak's temptation to judge the free (condemning as sinful what God has declared clean).

"Each of us will give an account of himself to God" (v. 12) — the eschatological horizon is the great leveller. Neither the strong nor the weak will stand before God and be assessed on the basis of whether they were free in matters of food and days. They will give an account of themselves — whether they served Christ, whether they loved their brother, whether they built up the body. The things that divide them now will be irrelevant then; what will matter then should be what governs them now.

Four things in the section are worth adding, because the ground between the opening command and v. 12 is where the argument is actually made. The first is v. 4, which supplies the reason judging is out of order: Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? The picture is a domestic household. You do not discipline another man’s staff, however sure you are that they are doing it wrong, because they were not hired by you and do not answer to you.

And that verse ends in a promise rather than a rebuke — he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand. Paul’s confidence is not that the disputed practice does not matter but that the disputed brother is being personally held up by someone competent. God is already at work on the person you were about to correct.

The second is v. 6, and it is the criterion the whole section turns on. Both parties — the one who observes the day and the one who does not, the one who eats and the one who abstains — are described as acting in honour of the Lord, and both are said to give thanks to God. Paul is not calling the difference trivial. He is pointing out that the same thanksgiving is going up from both sides of the table.

The third is v. 9, which grounds the whole thing in the gospel rather than in tolerance: to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living. The purpose of the cross and resurrection is stated here as lordship — which settles who is entitled to rule another believer’s conscience, and the answer is the one who paid for it. And the fourth is vv. 10–11, where the argument is sealed with Isaiah 45:23: every knee bowing, every tongue confessing, the strong and the weak side by side at the same tribunal, neither of them presiding.
verseByVerse.theology:
Adiaphora and the Conscience

The Reformed tradition uses the term adiaphora (things indifferent) for matters that Scripture neither commands nor prohibits — the territory of Romans 14. In these matters, Christian liberty is real: what God has declared clean is clean; what the gospel has freed the conscience from need not be re-enslaved. But liberty is not the highest value; love is. Calvin insisted that in matters of adiaphora, the strong must exercise their freedom with sensitivity to the weaker conscience — not capitulating to every scruple indefinitely, but never using freedom as a weapon against the brother Christ died for.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific tensions in Rome were between Jewish and Gentile believers over Torah food laws and calendar observances — real, living issues that threatened the unity of a church in which both groups worshipped together. Paul does not resolve the tension by declaring one group right and the other wrong; he transcends it by pointing both groups to a standard higher than their own position: the lordship of Christ (v. 8) and the coming judgment (v. 12). Now: Every generation of the church has its equivalent of the Romans 14 debate: alcohol, entertainment, dress, worship style, political engagement. The principles are the same: welcome the brother with differing scruples; do not quarrel over opinions; do not despise; do not judge; remember that each will give account to God and not to you.

verseByVerse.quote: As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions. One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church must welcome believers with tender consciences, without turning disputed matters into quarrels.

Weak in faith. Not weak in trusting Christ, but not yet fully persuaded of the freedom the gospel gives in matters like food.

Only vegetables. Meat in Rome’s markets might not be killed by Jewish law, or might have been offered to idols. A believer unsure of it could avoid meat altogether, as Daniel did (Daniel 1:8–12).

Welcome him. The same word as 15:7: as Christ welcomed you.

Opinions. Paul is dealing with disputable matters, not the gospel itself. On the gospel he does not compromise (Galatians 1:8).

On a Tuesday. Welcome the Christian whose scruples you find tiresome, without trying to win the argument.
verseByVerse.note: The “weak” probably include Jewish believers who kept the food laws, and others who avoided meat that might have been offered to idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Neither the free nor the scrupulous may look down on or judge the other, for God has accepted both, and each answers to his own Master.

Two sins. The strong are tempted to despise; the weak are tempted to judge.

Another’s servant. You are not your fellow believer’s master. Christ is.

He will be upheld. The Lord is able to make his servant stand. A gentle word of perseverance.

On a Tuesday. Notice whether your reaction to a different Christian is contempt or condemnation, and drop both.

verseByVerse.quote: One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day, observes it in honor of the Lord. The one who eats, eats in honor of the Lord, since he gives thanks to God, while the one who abstains, abstains in honor of the Lord and gives thanks to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some esteem certain days as special and others treat all days alike; each should be fully convinced and act in honour of the Lord.

The days. Most likely the Jewish Sabbath, feasts and fasts.

Fully convinced. Act from conviction, not imitation or pressure.

Where Christians differ: does this include the Lord’s Day? Sabbatarians (the Westminster tradition) argue that Paul is speaking of Jewish ceremonial days only, and that the fourth commandment continues in the Christian Sunday. Others read it more widely: no day is binding on the Christian conscience. Verdict: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), so its rules do not bind the Christian conscience. Yet the Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is a privilege to be received gladly: a day for gathered worship and rest. Hold the view charitably.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add, “the one who does not observe the day, does not observe it in honor of the Lord.” It is a natural expansion; the earliest manuscripts lack it.

On a Tuesday. Whatever you do with your days, do it for the Lord with thanks.
verseByVerse.note: The days in question were probably the Sabbath and Jewish festivals.

verseByVerse.quote: For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself. For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord. So then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No believer lives or dies for himself; in life and in death, we belong to the Lord.

Not to himself. Not a statement about our social nature, but about whose we are.

We are the Lord’s. Compare the first answer of the Heidelberg Catechism: our only comfort is that we belong, body and soul, in life and in death, to our faithful Saviour.

For worship. Rest in this: whatever happens today, you are his.

verseByVerse.quote: For to this end Christ died and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ died and rose to be Lord of both the dead and the living.

Died and lived again. The cross and the resurrection won his lordship (Philippians 2:8–11).

Lord of the dead. Believers who have died are not beyond his care.

On a Tuesday. If Christ is Lord of your brother, leave the judging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you pass judgment on your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God; for it is written, "As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why judge or despise your brother, when all will stand before God’s judgment seat, where every knee will bow?

Your brother. The word Paul repeats. You are speaking of family.

The judgment seat. Believers are not condemned (8:1), yet they will give an account of their lives (2 Corinthians 5:10).

Isaiah 45:23. Every knee will bow to God. Philippians 2:10–11 applies the same text to Jesus.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “the judgment seat of Christ”, probably from 2 Corinthians 5:10. The earliest read “of God”.

parallels.desc: to me every knee shall bow

verseByVerse.quote: So then each of us will give an account of himself to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each of us will give an account of himself to God.

Of himself. Not of your brother. You answer for your own life.

On a Tuesday. Spend more energy on your own account than on other people’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — Do Not Cause a Brother to Stumble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother" (v. 13). The second half of chapter 14 moves from the mutual prohibition of judging and despising to the positive obligation of the strong: limit your freedom in cases where exercising it would damage your brother's conscience and lead him into sin. The governing concern is his welfare, not your rights.

Paul's theological grounding of this obligation is striking: "By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died" (v. 15). Christ died for the weak brother. The price paid for his soul is the blood of the Son of God. The strong believer who uses her freedom to demolish someone Christ purchased at infinite cost has committed something far more serious than poor table manners. She has treated as worthless what God treated as worth his Son.

The kingdom of God principle of v. 17 is the positive vision behind the self-limitation: "For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit." The things that matter most — right standing before God, harmony in the body, Spirit-given joy — are not determined by what we eat. The strong person who surrenders her food freedom for the sake of a brother's peace and joy has not lost anything that matters; she has demonstrated something that matters supremely: she cares more about his joy in the Holy Spirit than about her right to eat what she pleases.

Verses 13, 15 and 17 carry the section, and the rest of it carries the argument. Verse 14 is the pivot, and it is the boldest sentence in the chapter: I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. Both halves are asserted. The thing really is clean, and it really is defiling for the man whose conscience says otherwise — which is why the answer to his scruple is teaching rather than pressure.

Verses 16 and 19–21 then supply the working rules. Do not let the good thing you possess — your liberty — get itself a bad name (v. 16). Pursue what makes for peace and for building up (v. 19). And the counterpart: do not, for the sake of food, demolish the work of God (v. 20). Paul is running a construction metaphor across these verses, and the choice he puts to the strong is whether their freedom is putting walls up or taking them down.

Verse 22 turns to the free man personally: the faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Not conceal your convictions, but stop parading a liberty — and then a beatitude for the man who can act without a backward glance at himself.

And v. 23 closes the chapter with the sentence that has travelled furthest from it: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. In context it is about a specific man doing a specific thing while divided in his own mind. It has been made to carry a great deal more than that.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christian Liberty and the Law of Love

Romans 14:13–23 establishes the fundamental principle of Christian ethics in matters of liberty: freedom is real, but love is higher. The freedom the gospel gives is not a license to do everything the law permits without regard to others; it is the freedom to serve. The one who is free in Christ is freed from the bondage of sin and law — freed for the service of God and neighbour. To use freedom as a weapon against a brother's conscience is a misuse of freedom as fundamental as legalism; it is just as self-centred, only differently oriented.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific issue of meat offered to idols (closely related to the Romans 14 situation, developed more fully in 1 Corinthians 8–10) was a genuine and daily challenge in the first-century city. Much of the meat available in the marketplace had passed through a pagan temple. The strong knew the idol was nothing; the weak felt defiled. Paul's principle: your knowledge does not give you the right to wound your brother's conscience. Now: The strong Christian in every age is tempted to treat her freedom as a badge of theological maturity to be displayed rather than a gift to be managed with care. The test of genuine maturity is not the willingness to exercise freedom but the willingness to limit it out of love — to choose the brother's conscience over personal preference, his joy over your rights.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us not pass judgment on one another any longer, but rather decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean for anyone who thinks it unclean. — Romans 14:13–14
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stop judging one another and resolve never to put a stumbling block before a brother; nothing is unclean in itself, but it is unclean to the one who thinks it so.

A wordplay. Stop judging others; judge (decide) this instead: never trip a brother up.

Stumbling block, hindrance. An obstacle that trips someone, or the trigger of a trap: anything that leads another believer to act against conscience and so fall into sin or away from Christ. Not merely something that annoys them.

Nothing unclean in itself. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19). Paul is persuaded in the Lord.

Unclean for him. Conscience matters. To act against it, even when it is mistaken, is to sin (v. 23).

What it does not mean. This is about things indifferent. Sin does not become acceptable because someone thinks it fine.

verseByVerse.quote: For if your brother is grieved by what you eat, you are no longer walking in love. By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If what you eat grieves your brother, you are not walking in love; do not destroy for the sake of food one for whom Christ died.

Grieved. Not merely annoyed, but wounded, drawn to act against his conscience.

For whom Christ died. If Christ gave his life for him, can you not give up a meal?

Where Christians differ: can a believer be destroyed? Some argue that this proves a person Christ died for can finally perish. Verdict: Paul is warning about the real damage our conduct can do, and judging by what we can see: he is a brother. God keeps his elect (8:30–39), and he does so in part through warnings like this. The verse does not undo definite atonement or perseverance, but it leaves no room for carelessness.

On a Tuesday. Is there a freedom you enjoy that you should lay aside for someone’s sake?

verseByVerse.quote: So do not let what you regard as good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not let your freedom be slandered, for God’s kingdom is not about food and drink but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.

Your good. Christian liberty is good. Do not use it in a way that brings it into disrepute.

The kingdom. Food is not what matters: what matters is right standing and living, peace with God and each other, and Spirit-given joy.

On a Tuesday. Measure your church’s quarrels by this verse. Most turn out to be about eating and drinking.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever thus serves Christ is acceptable to God and approved by men. So then let us pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever serves Christ in this way pleases God and is respected by people; so pursue what makes for peace and builds each other up.

Pursue. Peace is not passive. It must be chased.

Mutual upbuilding. Ask of every freedom: does it build the other up?

verseByVerse.quote: Do not, for the sake of food, destroy the work of God. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for anyone to make another stumble by what he eats. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes your brother to stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not tear down God’s work over food; all food is clean, but it is wrong to cause another to stumble, and good to give up meat or wine or anything that does.

The work of God. Your brother is God’s workmanship (Ephesians 2:10).

Where Christians differ: total abstinence. Some have used this verse to require all Christians to abstain from alcohol. Verdict: Scripture treats wine as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15; John 2) and condemns drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18). Paul calls for willing, loving restraint in specific situations, not a universal rule. Abstinence is a good choice for some, and a loving one where it protects a brother, but it is not a test of faith.

On a Tuesday. Order your drink with the weakest person at the table in mind.

verseByVerse.quote: The faith that you have, keep between yourself and God. Blessed is the one who has no reason to pass judgment on himself for what he approves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep your convictions about these matters between yourself and God; blessed is the one whose conscience does not condemn what he approves.

Keep it to yourself. Not concealing the truth, but not parading your freedom to unsettle others.

A clear conscience. A real blessing, worth more than any freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: But whoever has doubts is condemned if he eats, because the eating is not from faith. For whatever does not proceed from faith is sin. — Romans 14:23
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever eats while doubting is condemned, because the eating is not from faith, and whatever does not come from faith is sin.

Doubts. Being divided in mind, not settled before God that the act is right.

Not from faith. Here faith means a confident conviction before God that an action is right.

Whatever does not proceed from faith. To act against conscience is sin, even if the act is harmless in itself.

What it does not mean. Not that conscience is infallible. A weak conscience should be taught by Scripture, but not bullied into acting before it is persuaded.

Textual note. Some manuscripts place the doxology of 16:25–27 here; others after 15:33; a few omit it. The letter may have circulated in more than one form, but the doxology is in almost all manuscripts, and its natural place is at the end.

On a Tuesday. Do not press another believer to do what their conscience forbids.

For worship. Thank God for a gospel that frees the conscience, and for the patience to wait for one another.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert 16:25–27 here, at the end of chapter 14. Others place it after 15:33, and a few omit it. The variation probably shows that the letter circulated in more than one form in the early church; but the doxology is found in almost all manuscripts, and its natural place is at the close of the letter, where the ESV prints it.
