15.title: Unity, Hope, and the Mission of Paul
15.overview:
Romans 15 brings together three threads: the conclusion of the weak/strong argument (vv. 1–13), the personal explanation of Paul's apostolic mission (vv. 14–21), and his travel plans and prayer requests (vv. 22–33). The chapter is held together by the theme of the worldwide scope of the gospel — Christ's own example of self-giving (vv. 1–3), the Gentile mission as the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecy (vv. 9–12), and Paul's ambition to preach where Christ has not yet been named (vv. 20–21).

The opening section (vv. 1–13) concludes the argument of chapter 14 by pointing to Christ as the model of the strong bearing with the failings of the weak. Christ did not please himself (v. 3) — He endured the reproaches of others for their sake. The strong who follow his example are not making a heroic sacrifice; they are imitating their Lord. And the doxological prayer of vv. 5–6 and 13 frames the whole argument in worship: the God of endurance, encouragement, hope, and peace is the one who enables the unity for which Paul prays.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Example of Christ and the God of Hope
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
"We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves" (v. 1). Paul has waited until now to identify himself with the strong — and he identifies himself only to place the obligation of the strong front and centre. The strong do not have the right to demand that the weak keep up with them; they have the obligation to bear with the weak, to build them up, to serve their good. "Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up" (v. 2).

The model is Christ: "For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, 'The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me'" (v. 3, quoting Psalm 69:9). The Son of God did not come to be served but to serve — to bear not only the sins of the weak but their reproaches, their insults, the consequences of their failure. The one who is most perfectly strong became the servant of all. The Christian who follows this pattern — bearing the burdens of others rather than asserting the rights of the free — is walking in the footsteps of the one who bore our ultimate burden at Calvary.

The doxological climax of the section (vv. 5–6, 13) frames the whole practical argument in prayer and worship. Paul's wish is not merely that the Roman Christians be nice to each other; it is that they glorify God together with one voice (v. 6) — the strong and the weak, Jew and Gentile, all singing the same praise to the same God. And the God of hope fills with all joy and peace in believing (v. 13) — not the meagre joy of people who have resolved their differences, but the overflowing joy of people who have been given hope by the Spirit.

Between the example of Christ and that benediction stand four more things, and they carry the argument to its conclusion. The first is v. 4, which explains why Paul has just settled a first-century dispute about food by quoting a psalm: whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. The Old Testament was written for the benefit of readers who did not yet exist, and its stated product is not information but hope.

The second is v. 7, and it is the summit of everything since 14:1: welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God. The same verb Paul used in 14:1 for receiving the weak, and in 14:3 of God receiving him, now appears a third time with Christ himself as the measure. The strong were told to welcome; here everyone is told to welcome everyone, on the pattern of a welcome none of them deserved.

The third is vv. 8–9, where Paul states how one Christ serves two peoples. He became a servant to the circumcised to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs — that is, to demonstrate God’s truthfulness — and he did it so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. The two halves are not symmetrical, and the asymmetry is the point: Israel receives a kept promise, the nations receive sheer mercy, and neither group has grounds to look down on the other.

The fourth is the chain of quotations in vv. 9–12, drawn deliberately from every part of the Hebrew Bible — the Law (Deuteronomy 32:43), the Writings (Psalm 18:49; Psalm 117:1) and the Prophets (Isaiah 11:10). Paul is not producing a proof text. He is showing that the inclusion of the nations was the settled expectation of the whole canon, and the chain ends on the word the benediction will pick up: in him will the Gentiles hope.
verseByVerse.theology:
Christ as the Model of Solidarity with the Weak

The Christological grounding of the strong's obligation in Romans 15:3 is one of Paul's most important ethical moves. Ethics derived from the example of Christ is not mere imitation-of-a-good-man moralism; it is participation in the pattern of the one who is Lord, whose servanthood was the shape of his sovereignty, whose self-giving is the source of the Christian's capacity for self-giving. When Paul says "bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2), the law of Christ is precisely this: the pattern of the one who bore what he did not owe so that we might be released from what we could not pay.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The unity Paul prays for in vv. 5–6 — "that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ" — was not an abstract aspiration. The Roman church had real divisions: Jewish and Gentile believers, strong and weak, people from different social classes and national backgrounds. The one voice of praise was the visible, social miracle that would demonstrate to the watching city of Rome that something genuinely new had entered the world. Now: The unity of diverse believers in genuine, cross-cultural, cross-social worship is still the most powerful apologetic the church has available. A community of people who have every reason to be divided — by race, class, culture, education, politics — worshipping together with one voice glorifies the God whose gospel is the only power that creates such unity.

verseByVerse.quote: We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for his good, to build him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The strong must bear with the weaknesses of the weak, seeking their neighbour’s good rather than their own pleasure.

We who are strong. Paul counts himself among them (14:14), and so takes on the greater obligation.

Bear with. Carry, not merely tolerate. Strength exists to lift others.

Please his neighbour. Not flattery or people-pleasing (Galatians 1:10), but seeking his real good: building him up.

On a Tuesday. Where can you use your strength to carry someone weaker rather than to get your way?

parallels.desc: bear one another’s burdens

verseByVerse.quote: For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, "The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ did not please himself, but took on himself the insults aimed at God.

Psalm 69:9. David’s psalm of suffering for God’s sake, fulfilled in Christ’s passion.

The pattern. Paul’s ethics always return to the cross. If Christ bore reproach for us, we can bear inconvenience for one another.

For worship. Thank Christ who bore the reproach that was yours.

parallels.desc: the reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen on me

verseByVerse.quote: For whatever was written in former days was written for our instruction, that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope. May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to live in such harmony with one another, in accord with Christ Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Old Testament was written to teach us, so that through endurance and the encouragement of Scripture we might have hope; and Paul prays that God would give them harmony.

For our instruction. The Old Testament is Christian Scripture (1 Corinthians 10:11; 2 Timothy 3:16).

Endurance, encouragement, hope. Scripture produces endurance and encouragement, and these produce hope.

The God of endurance. What Scripture gives, God gives: Scripture is his voice.

In accord with Christ. Harmony is not uniformity of opinion, but shared allegiance to Christ.

On a Tuesday. When hope runs low, go back to the Old Testament stories of God’s faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: that together you may with one voice glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you, for the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goal of harmony is united praise to God; therefore welcome one another as Christ welcomed you, to God’s glory.

One voice. Strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, singing together. Unity is for worship.

As Christ welcomed you. The measure and motive: Christ welcomed you while you were weak, ungodly and an enemy (5:6–10).

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “welcomed us” instead of “welcomed you”. Both are well attested; the sense is the same.

On a Tuesday. Whom in your church are you slow to welcome?

verseByVerse.quote: For I tell you that Christ became a servant to the circumcised to show God's truthfulness, in order to confirm the promises given to the patriarchs, and in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written, "Therefore I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ became a servant to the Jews to confirm God’s promises to the patriarchs, and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy.

A servant to the circumcised. Jesus was born a Jew and ministered chiefly to Israel (Matthew 15:24).

Truthfulness and mercy. To Israel, God proved faithful to his word. To the Gentiles, who had no promise, he showed sheer mercy.

Psalm 18:49. David praises God among the nations.

parallels.desc: I will praise you, O LORD, among the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again it says, "Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people." And again, "Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scripture repeatedly calls the Gentiles to rejoice with God’s people and praise the Lord.

Deuteronomy 32:43 and Psalm 117:1. From the Law and the Psalms. God always meant the nations to praise him.

With his people. Gentiles join Israel’s worship; they do not replace it.

For worship. Join the praise of all the nations.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites the Law, the Psalms and the Prophets to show God always intended Gentiles to praise him.

parallels.desc: rejoice with him, O heavens
praise the LORD, all nations

verseByVerse.quote: And again Isaiah says, "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah foretold that the root of Jesse would rise to rule the nations, and the Gentiles would hope in him.

Isaiah 11:10. The promised son of David, ruling over more than Israel.

Law, Psalms and Prophets. Paul has quoted all three parts of the Old Testament. The Gentile mission was not an afterthought.

In him will the Gentiles hope. This prepares for v. 13.
verseByVerse.note: Jesse was David’s father; the “root of Jesse” is the promised king from David’s line.

parallels.desc: the root of Jesse, of him shall the nations inquire

verseByVerse.quote: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope. — Romans 15:13
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that the God of hope will fill them with joy and peace as they trust him, so that they overflow with hope by the Spirit’s power.

The God of hope. Hope is his gift and comes from his character.

In believing. Joy and peace come through ongoing trust, not through circumstances.

Abound. Not just enough hope to get by, but overflowing.

By the power of the Holy Spirit. Hope is not optimism by effort but the Spirit’s work.

For worship. Pray this verse for yourself and for a friend who is losing heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–33 — Paul's Priestly Ministry and His Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul now turns from theology and pastoral exhortation to autobiography and travel plans — and the transition is less abrupt than it appears. His account of his apostolic ministry is itself a miniature theology of mission. He describes himself as a minister (leitourgos — a cultic, priestly term) of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, performing the priestly service of the gospel of God, offering the Gentiles as an acceptable offering, sanctified by the Holy Spirit (v. 16). The mission to the Gentiles is not merely evangelistic strategy; it is priestly worship — the bringing of the nations as an offering to God.

The scope of Paul's completed mission (vv. 19–21) is staggering: from Jerusalem to Illyricum (modern-day Croatia), he has "fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ." Not because every person has heard it but because he has planted the gospel in strategic centres throughout the eastern Mediterranean, from which the word can spread into every surrounding region. His ambition going forward is equally characteristic: not to build on another man's foundation, but to preach where Christ has not yet been named. The pioneer missionary impulse is written into the logic of the commission.

The prayer request of vv. 30–33 is one of the most moving passages in Paul's letters. He asks the Roman church to "strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf" — the word for "strive together" (sunagōnizomai) is an athletic term, contending alongside someone in a contest. Prayer is work, and Paul wants co-labourers in it. He asks for three things: deliverance from unbelievers in Judea, acceptance of his offering by the Jerusalem church, and the joy of reaching Rome. All three will be granted, none in the form he pictured; the Rome visit will happen, but in chains.

Two stretches of the section deserve adding. The first is how it opens (vv. 14–15). Having written the most demanding letter in the New Testament, Paul tells its recipients that he is satisfied about them — full of goodness, filled with knowledge, able to instruct one another — and that what he has written is offered by way of reminder. He does not present a word of it as news.

The second is vv. 22–29, which contains the two most concrete things in the chapter. One is Spain (v. 24): Paul is not looking for another province but for the western edge of the known world, and he is asking Rome to become the base that sends him there. This is why the letter exists in the form it does.

The other is the Jerusalem collection (vv. 25–28), a relief fund gathered from the Gentile churches of Macedonia and Achaia for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Paul is in Corinth, he intends to go west, and he is about to travel east instead — at real personal risk — to deliver money. And he does not call it charity. He says the Gentiles owe it to them (v. 27): having shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, they owe material ones back. The collection is the argument of chapters 9–11 converted into currency and carried some eight hundred miles in the wrong direction.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mission as Priestly Worship

Romans 15:16 is one of the most theologically rich descriptions of apostolic mission in the New Testament. Paul images his Gentile mission as priestly service — the offering of the nations to God as a sacrifice acceptable and sanctified by the Holy Spirit. This means that evangelism is not merely a strategy for church growth or a duty to be discharged; it is an act of worship, the gathering of the nations to lay them as a living offering before the God who created and redeemed them. This priestly vision of mission has sustained every great missionary movement in the Reformed tradition, from Calvin's Geneva sending missionaries to France, to William Carey going to India, to the countless sent ones who have carried the gospel to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul's completed mission from Jerusalem to Illyricum represents perhaps fifteen years of gruelling apostolic labour — multiple missionary journeys, imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, cold and hunger. The nonchalance with which he refers to having "fulfilled the ministry of the gospel" in this vast region is the confidence of a man who has done what he was sent to do and is already looking at the next frontier. Now: The pioneer missionary impulse of v. 20 — to preach where Christ has not been named — remains the highest calling in the church's mission. There are still places, peoples, and communities where the name of Christ has not been proclaimed. The obligation Paul felt is the obligation the church still carries, until all nations have heard.

verseByVerse.quote: I myself am satisfied about you, my brothers, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge and able to instruct one another. But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is confident in the Roman Christians’ goodness and knowledge, yet has written boldly to remind them, because of the grace God gave him.

Able to instruct one another. Mutual teaching is the normal life of a healthy church.

By way of reminder. Christians need to hear again what they already know.

Boldly. Paul’s authority is not his own; it is grace given to him.

On a Tuesday. Do not despise reminders of familiar truth. They are how faith stays alive.

verseByVerse.quote: to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to be proud of my work for God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul describes his work as a priestly ministry, offering the Gentiles to God as an acceptable offering made holy by the Spirit, and this is his only ground for pride.

Minister. Greek leitourgos, a public servant, used in the Greek Old Testament of priests serving at the altar.

Priestly service. A picture: the gospel is preached, and believing Gentiles are presented to God as a living offering (12:1).

Where Christians differ: a ministerial priesthood? Roman Catholic theology has sometimes used such language to support an ordained priesthood offering sacrifice. Verdict: Paul’s priestly language is a metaphor for gospel preaching. The only atoning sacrifice is Christ’s (Hebrews 10:10–14), and all believers are priests (1 Peter 2:9).

Sanctified by the Spirit. It is the Spirit, not ritual, that makes the offering holy.

Proud in Christ. Not self-congratulation, but joy in what Christ has done.
verseByVerse.note: Paul pictures his mission as priestly work, offering the believing Gentiles to God.

parallels.desc: they shall bring your brothers as an offering

verseByVerse.quote: For I will not venture to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience — by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God — so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fulfilled the ministry of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul will speak only of what Christ has done through him to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word, deed, signs and the Spirit’s power, from Jerusalem to Illyricum.

What Christ has accomplished. Paul takes no credit; Christ is the worker.

Obedience. The obedience of faith (1:5).

Signs and wonders. Marks of an apostle (2 Corinthians 12:12).

Where Christians differ: signs and wonders today. Continuationists expect the same signs to accompany evangelism today. Verdict: these signs confirmed the apostolic message in the foundation-laying era (Hebrews 2:3–4). God still heals in answer to prayer, but the gospel’s power today lies in the Spirit working through the word. Hold the view charitably.

Illyricum. The Roman province on the east coast of the Adriatic, roughly modern Albania and the former Yugoslavia: some 1,400 miles (2,250 km) from Jerusalem.

Fulfilled. Not that every person had heard, but that the foundation was laid in key centres across the region.

Textual note. Manuscripts vary: “the Spirit of God”, “the Holy Spirit”, or simply “the Spirit”. The meaning is the same.
verseByVerse.note: Illyricum lay along the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, north-west of Macedonia.

verseByVerse.quote: ...and thus I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else's foundation, but as it is written, 'Those who have never been told of him will see, and those who have never heard will understand.' — Romans 15:20–21
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s ambition was to preach Christ where he had not been named, not building on another’s foundation, as Isaiah foresaw.

Pioneer. Paul’s calling was to go where no church existed.

Isaiah 52:15. From the passage about the Suffering Servant: those who had never been told will see.

What it does not mean. Not that building on others’ foundations is wrong; Apollos watered what Paul planted (1 Corinthians 3:6). It was Paul’s particular calling.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the places and peoples where Christ is still not named.

parallels.desc: that which has not been told them they see

verseByVerse.quote: This is the reason why I have so often been hindered from coming to you. But now, since I no longer have any room for work in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
His work in the east had kept him from visiting Rome, but now that it is complete, he hopes at last to come.

Hindered. Paul’s plans were subject to God’s timing (1:13).

No more room. The pioneer work is done; others can build.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope to see you in passing as I go to Spain, and to be helped on my journey there by you, once I have enjoyed your company for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul hopes to visit Rome on his way to Spain, and to be helped by them on that journey.

Spain. The western end of the known world, with few Jewish communities. A bold vision.

Helped on my journey. The phrase means support with supplies and people. Part of Paul’s purpose in writing Romans was to win a base for mission.

Did he reach Spain? Uncertain. Clement of Rome, writing around AD 96, says Paul reached “the limit of the west”, which may mean Spain.

On a Tuesday. Support those going where you cannot go.
verseByVerse.note: Spain was the western edge of the known world. Whether Paul ever reached it is uncertain; early tradition says he did.

verseByVerse.quote: At present, however, I am going to Jerusalem bringing aid to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First, Paul must go to Jerusalem with a gift the churches of Macedonia and Achaia have collected for the poor believers there.

The collection. Years of Paul’s work went into it (1 Corinthians 16:1–4; 2 Corinthians 8–9).

Pleased. The giving was glad, not grudging.

Contribution. Koinōnia: fellowship in practical form.
verseByVerse.note: The collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem was a major project of Paul’s later ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them. For if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gentiles gave gladly and also owed it, because having shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings they should share their material ones.

Pleased and owed. Free and glad, yet fitting and right.

Spiritual and material. The gospel came from Jerusalem. Gratitude takes practical form (1 Corinthians 9:11).

On a Tuesday. Whom do you owe spiritually? How might you show thanks in practical ways?

verseByVerse.quote: When therefore I have completed this and have delivered to them what has been collected, I will leave for Spain by way of you. I know that when I come to you I will come in the fullness of the blessing of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Once the gift is delivered, Paul will come to Rome on the way to Spain, confident he will come in the fullness of Christ’s blessing.

Completed. Literally “sealed”: delivered safely and properly.

The fullness of the blessing. Paul came to Rome in chains (Acts 28), yet still in the fullness of blessing.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add “of the gospel” (“the blessing of the gospel of Christ”). The shorter reading is earlier.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul urges them to strive with him in prayer for his safety from unbelievers in Judea, and for his gift to be accepted by the Jerusalem believers.

Strive together. Prayer is a struggle, a shared wrestling (Colossians 4:12).

The love of the Spirit. The love the Spirit pours into hearts (5:5).

Two fears. Danger from opponents, and rejection by fellow believers. Unity between Jewish and Gentile believers was at stake.

Answered prayer. Paul was rescued, but by arrest. God answers in ways we do not expect.

On a Tuesday. Ask someone to pray for you specifically, and pray specifically for them.
verseByVerse.note: These prayers were answered in unexpected ways: Paul was arrested in Jerusalem and reached Rome as a prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: so that by God's will I may come to you with joy and be refreshed in your company. May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul hopes to come to them with joy by God’s will and be refreshed among them, and he prays the God of peace will be with them.

By God’s will. Paul plans, but leaves the outcome with God (James 4:15).

Refreshed. Even the apostle needed the encouragement of fellowship.

The God of peace. After chapters on division and unity, a fitting title.

For worship. Pray the God of peace to be with your church this week.

16.title: Greetings, Warnings, and the Final Doxology
16.overview:
Romans 16 is sometimes treated as an appendix — a list of greetings to be skimmed before putting the letter down. It is far more than that. The twenty-six people Paul greets in vv. 3–15 (twenty-four of them by name), with several households besides, constitute a remarkable social portrait of the early Roman church: women who worked hard in the Lord, co-workers who risked their necks for Paul, households that may have belonged to powerful men, and many names common among slaves and freedmen. The community Paul is writing to and for is not an abstraction; it is these people, in this city, with these names and these stories.

The chapter also contains a sharp warning against those who create division and cause obstacles contrary to the doctrine (vv. 17–20) — a reminder that the unity and the gospel Paul has laboured to establish require vigilance as well as love. And then the letter ends where it began: with the gospel. The doxology of vv. 25–27 is one of the most comprehensive summaries of Paul's gospel in the New Testament — the mystery kept secret for long ages, now disclosed through the prophetic Scriptures, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith, to the only wise God, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — A Network of Saints: The Social World of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The list of greetings in Romans 16 is the most extensive in Paul's letters and has rightly been treated as a window into the earliest church. Twenty-six individuals are greeted, twenty-four of them by name, along with several households and groups. The social diversity is remarkable: Phoebe, a deacon and patron from Cenchreae; Priscilla and Aquila, tentmakers and theological teachers; Andronicus and Junia, "well known to the apostles" and Christians before Paul; Epaenetus, the first convert in Asia; Mary, who worked very hard. Slaves and free, women and men, Jews and Gentiles — all members of the same body.

Phoebe (vv. 1–2) deserves special notice: Paul commends her as a deacon (diakonos — the same word used of male church officers) of the church in Cenchreae, and as a patron (prostatis) who has been of help to many, including Paul himself. She was almost certainly the letter-carrier — the person who bore the manuscript of Romans from Corinth to Rome and, as was customary for letter-carriers in antiquity, would have read and explained the letter to its recipients. The greatest theological letter ever written was entrusted to a woman for its first public delivery.

The greeting "holy kiss" (v. 16) — appearing in four of Paul's letters — was the physical expression of the family bond that the gospel created. In the ancient world, the kiss of greeting belonged chiefly to family. The church that greeted one another with a holy kiss was declaring, physically and publicly, that these people — strangers by blood, foreigners by origin, divided by every social category — were family. The gospel had done what nothing else could do: created a new human community that crossed every boundary the ancient world had erected.

Between the famous names and the holy kiss lies the bulk of the list, and it is worth not skipping. Verses 8–15 greet Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, Herodion, Tryphaena and Tryphosa, Persis, Rufus and his mother, then Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas.

Several of those are ordinary slave names, and three of them — Ampliatus, Stachys and Persis — Paul calls beloved. Two are greeted not as individuals but as households — and in one of them only those in the Lord. Three of the workers named in this stretch are women, and one man is remembered chiefly through his mother, who Paul says has been a mother to him as well (v. 13).

And the last two clusters are given no description at all — nine names and an unnamed sister, with nothing attached, followed by the brothers who are with them and all the saints who are with them, who are not named at all. That proportion is the honest shape of the church in every century: a few remembered for something, most remembered only for being there, and the majority not written down.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Humanity

Romans 16:1–16 is the embodiment in flesh-and-blood names of Paul's theological argument in chapters 1–15. The "no distinction between Jew and Greek" of 10:12, the olive tree of Jew and Gentile grafted together of 11:17–24, the "welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you" of 15:7 — all of these are visible in the list of names. This is what the gospel looks like when it has done its work: Phoebe and Priscilla and Andronicus and Junia, the patron and the tentmaker, the first convert and the former persecutor's associates, all belonging to each other in Christ. The doctrine of justification by faith produces a sociology.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The social mixing of Romans 16 was, by the standards of the first-century world, radical to the point of scandalous. Social boundaries in Rome were enforced with rigour; meals with social inferiors were a form of self-humiliation. The church that gathered Phoebe the patron and the slaves of great households and the Jewish tentmakers for common worship and common greeting was an institution the Roman world had no category for. Now: The contemporary church's ability or inability to embody the social diversity of Romans 16 is one of the most important tests of its gospel fidelity. A church that is racially, socially, or economically homogeneous by design has stopped short of what the gospel creates. The greetings of Romans 16 are not an antiquarian curiosity; they are the template for the new humanity the gospel is building.

verseByVerse.quote: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae, that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well. — Romans 16:1–2
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae and a generous patron, and asks the Romans to welcome and help her.

Phoebe. She probably carried the letter to Rome and may have read it aloud there first.

Servant. Diakonos, linked to a particular church, which points to a recognised role.

Patron. A benefactor who provided money, hospitality and protection. Paul himself was one of those she supported.

Where Christians differ: was Phoebe a deacon? Some read “servant” in a general sense; some see a recognised order of deaconesses; others see her in the same office as the deacons of 1 Timothy 3:8–13. Verdict: she most likely held a recognised serving role, and churches that appoint women deacons have good warrant. The deacon’s office is one of service, not of teaching and ruling, so this does not touch the eldership (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7).

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the people whose generosity keeps gospel work going, and welcome them warmly.
verseByVerse.note: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. The ESV notes that “servant” can also be rendered “deaconess.” Phoebe probably carried this letter to Rome. A patron was a benefactor who supported others with her resources.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets Prisca and Aquila, his fellow workers who risked their lives for him and are thanked by all the Gentile churches.

Prisca first. Often named before her husband (Acts 18:18, 26), perhaps because she was the more prominent in ministry.

Tentmakers on the move. Rome, Corinth, Ephesus, Rome again (Acts 18:2). They used their trade and home for the gospel.

Risked their necks. Perhaps in the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19). We do not know.

On a Tuesday. Your work and your home can both serve the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Prisca is a form of Priscilla. She and Aquila had returned to Rome after Claudius’s expulsion of Jews ended.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets the church that meets in their house, and Epaenetus, the first convert in Asia.

House church. There were no church buildings. Rome probably had several such congregations.

The first convert. Literally “firstfruits”, the first of a harvest still to come.

On a Tuesday. Pray for the first believers in a new place, and for the harvest that follows.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes; there were no church buildings.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets Mary, who worked hard for them, and Andronicus and Junia, fellow Jews who shared his imprisonment, were well known to the apostles, and became Christians before him.

Worked hard. The verb Paul uses of his own apostolic labour. In this chapter he uses it only of women: Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa and Persis.

Junia. Almost certainly a woman, as the early church read it. The masculine “Junias” is not attested anywhere in the ancient world.

Where Christians differ: an apostle? The Greek can mean “well known to the apostles” or “outstanding among the apostles”. Verdict: the ESV’s reading is a little more likely, but the point does not depend on it. If Junia was an apostle, it was in the broader sense of a missionary sent out by a church, like Barnabas (Acts 14:14), not the foundational office of the Twelve and Paul. So the verse does not overturn Paul’s teaching on elders.

On a Tuesday. Honour faithful believers who have suffered for Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the name may be read Junias (a man’s name). Andronicus and Junia had become believers before Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets Ampliatus, Urbanus and Stachys with affection.

Slave names. Several of these were common among slaves and freedmen. In Christ, they are beloved and fellow workers.

For worship. Thank God that no one is a mere name in his church.
verseByVerse.note: Several of these names were common among slaves and freedmen in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus. Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets Apelles, tested and approved, the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, and his fellow Jew Herodion.

Approved. Apelles had come through testing with his faith proved genuine.

Households. Probably their slaves and freedmen. The gospel had reached the servants of great houses.

Herodion. The name suggests a link with Herod’s family.

On a Tuesday. The gospel works quietly among the overlooked. Look for it there.
verseByVerse.note: The households of Aristobulus and Narcissus probably included their slaves and freedmen.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord. Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets the hard-working women Tryphaena, Tryphosa and Persis, and Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who had been like a mother to Paul.

Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Names meaning “dainty” and “delicate”, now labouring hard for the Lord.

Rufus. Perhaps the son of Simon of Cyrene, who carried Jesus’ cross (Mark 15:21).

A mother to me. The church is a family. Paul, who had no wife or children, had a mother in Christ.

On a Tuesday. Who has been a spiritual mother or father to you? Thank them.
verseByVerse.note: Rufus may be the son of Simon of Cyrene, whom Mark mentions as if known to his readers.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul greets two more groups of believers and all the saints with them.

Groups. Probably different house churches across the city.

Names. Many are otherwise unknown, but God knows them (2 Timothy 2:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet one another with a holy kiss; all the churches of Christ send their greetings.

A holy kiss. A customary family greeting, made holy by its meaning: we are one family in Christ.

Where Christians differ: is the kiss commanded today? A few groups still practise it as a command. Verdict: the command is to greet one another with warm, pure affection; the form may follow culture, whether a handshake, an embrace or a kiss.

All the churches. The Roman Christians belong to a worldwide fellowship.

On a Tuesday. Greet fellow believers warmly, especially those who may feel overlooked.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — Final Warning and the Doxology of the Gospel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Before the closing doxology, Paul inserts a sharp warning (vv. 17–20) against those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine the Romans have been taught. The letter has been, among other things, a sustained argument for the unity of the body across the strong/weak divide; it would be a bitter irony if the letter itself became a tool of division. Paul's instruction is clear: watch them, avoid them. The divisive person — whatever their theological credentials — is not serving Christ but their own appetites, and they deceive the naive with smooth talk and flattery.

The closing doxology (vv. 25–27) returns to the letter's great themes for one final, comprehensive statement. God is able to strengthen — the power of the gospel is not an argument but a strengthening. According to Paul's gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ — these are identified: Paul's gospel is the gospel of Jesus Christ, not a human theological construct. According to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for long ages — the gospel is not a new invention; it is the disclosure of what God planned from before time began. Now made known to all the nations — the universality Paul has argued throughout. For the obedience of faith — the phrase that bracketed the letter in 1:5 now closes it. To the only wise God — the doxology of chapter 11 returns, now applied to the whole letter's argument. Through Jesus Christ — the mediator of all grace and all glory. To whom be glory forever. Amen.

The letter that began with Paul introducing himself as a slave of Christ and set apart for the gospel ends with everything returning to God — from him, through him, and to him. The argument is complete. The doxology is the only adequate conclusion. Amen.

Two stretches sit between the warning and the doxology and should not be passed over. The first is v. 19, where Paul softens nothing but changes his tone: their obedience is known everywhere and he is glad of them, and what he wants is that they be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. It is the counterpart to the warning — the way to be undeceived is not to become worldly-wise about corruption but to know goodness well.

The second is vv. 21–24, a second greeting list, this time from Paul’s end of the journey: Timothy and three Jewish co-workers; Gaius, in whose house both Paul and the whole Corinthian church are lodged; Erastus, the city treasurer, whose name has plausibly been found on a paving inscription at Corinth; and Quartus. Between them stands v. 22, where Tertius, who wrote this letter, adds a greeting of his own — the only place in the New Testament where the man holding the pen speaks in his own voice.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mystery Revealed: Gospel and Old Testament Unity

Romans 16:25–27 returns to the theme announced in 1:1–4: the gospel was promised beforehand through the prophets; the Old Testament is the gospel in anticipation; the New Testament is the gospel in fulfilment. The "mystery" kept secret for long ages is not something the Old Testament was ignorant of but something it was pregnant with — the inclusion of the Gentiles in the covenant people, the extension of the Abrahamic blessing to all nations, the righteousness of God given through faith in Jesus Christ. Calvin's canon of interpretation applies: the two testaments are one Bible, one gospel, one covenant of grace, administered differently but pointing to the same Saviour.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The warning of vv. 17–20 against divisive teachers was written into the most doctrinally comprehensive letter Paul ever wrote. The letter's very depth makes it susceptible to misuse: its teachings on election, freedom, and grace can all be distorted into weapons of division. Paul's warning is therefore structurally appropriate — the deeper the theology, the greater the need for vigilance against those who weaponise it. Now: Every generation produces its version of the smooth-talking divisive teacher who uses theological language to advance personal agendas and create factions. Paul's three-fold response is the standing instruction: watch them carefully; avoid them; trust the God of peace who will soon crush Satan under your feet (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them. For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive. — Romans 16:17–18
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watch out for those who cause divisions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching you received, and avoid them; they serve their own appetites and deceive the naive with smooth talk.

Contrary to the doctrine. The measure is apostolic teaching, not personal preference.

Avoid them. Not debate endlessly, but keep away.

Their own appetites. False teaching often serves the teacher: money, influence, pleasure (Philippians 3:19).

Smooth talk. Error rarely sounds dangerous.

What it does not mean. After chapter 14, Paul is not telling Christians to separate over disputable matters. The issue is teaching that opposes the gospel.

On a Tuesday. Test teaching by Scripture, not by how attractive the teacher is.

verseByVerse.quote: For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil. The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul rejoices in their reputation for obedience but wants them wise about good and innocent about evil, for God will soon crush Satan under their feet.

Wise and innocent. Compare Matthew 10:16. Be expert in what is good; be inexperienced in evil.

Crush Satan. An echo of Genesis 3:15. Christ, the woman’s offspring, has won the victory; his people share in it.

The God of peace. He crushes the enemy who divides.

Soon. In God’s timing; the decisive blow fell at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

For worship. Praise the God who has defeated Satan and will finish the work.
verseByVerse.note: The promise echoes God’s word to the serpent in Eden.

parallels.desc: he shall bruise your head

verseByVerse.quote: Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen. I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy and Paul’s companions send greetings, and so does Tertius, who wrote the letter down.

Timothy. Paul’s son in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2).

Tertius. Paul dictated; Tertius wrote. Inspiration worked through an amanuensis without loss.

On a Tuesday. Hidden help counts. Tertius’s pen carried Romans to the world.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters; Tertius was the scribe who wrote this one down.

verseByVerse.quote: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gaius, host to Paul and the whole church, Erastus the city treasurer, and Quartus also send greetings.

Gaius. Probably the Gaius Paul baptised at Corinth (1 Corinthians 1:14), large-hearted enough to host the whole church.

Erastus. A public official. An inscription at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense, perhaps the same man. The gospel reached the city hall.

Our brother Quartus. No title, just “brother”. That is enough.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription found at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense, perhaps the same man.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse, a repeated grace blessing, is found only in some manuscripts.

Textual note. The earliest manuscripts lack v. 24, so the ESV places it in a footnote. It is probably a copy of the blessing from v. 20, added by a scribe where the closing doxology was moved. No teaching depends on it.

For worship. The grace of the Lord Jesus is still the best farewell.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 24: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

verseByVerse.quote: Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith —
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul gives glory to God, who can strengthen believers by the gospel, now revealing the long-hidden mystery to all nations through the prophetic Scriptures, to bring about the obedience of faith.

Able to strengthen. Romans ends where it began (1:11): with God establishing his people.

My gospel. Not Paul’s invention, but the gospel entrusted to him (Galatians 1:11–12).

The mystery. God’s plan to bring Jew and Gentile together in Christ, hidden for ages and now revealed (Ephesians 3:4–6).

The obedience of faith. The same phrase as 1:5: the whole letter is bookended by it.

Textual note. This doxology appears in different places in different manuscripts (after 14:23, after 15:33, or here), and is missing from a few. It is in almost all manuscripts, and most scholars accept it as Paul’s, at the end of the letter.
verseByVerse.note: A “mystery” in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the only wise God be glory for ever through Jesus Christ. Amen.

The only wise God. After chapters 9–11, his wisdom is the fitting note (11:33).

Through Jesus Christ. All glory comes to the Father through the Son.

Amen. Romans ends, as it should, in worship.

For worship. Read Romans 16:25–27 aloud as your own praise to God.

16.text: <sup>1</sup>I commend to you our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church at Cenchreae,<sup>2</sup>that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the saints, and help her in whatever she may need from you, for she has been a patron of many and of myself as well.<sup>3</sup>Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus,<sup>4</sup>who risked their necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks but all the churches of the Gentiles give thanks as well.<sup>5</sup>Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.<sup>6</sup>Greet Mary, who has worked hard for you.<sup>7</sup>Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners. They are well known to the apostles, and they were in Christ before me.<sup>8</sup>Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.<sup>9</sup>Greet Urbanus, our fellow worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.<sup>10</sup>Greet Apelles, who is approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the family of Aristobulus.<sup>11</sup>Greet my kinsman Herodion. Greet those in the Lord who belong to the family of Narcissus.<sup>12</sup>Greet those workers in the Lord, Tryphaena and Tryphosa. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked hard in the Lord.<sup>13</sup>Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord; also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.<sup>14</sup>Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers who are with them.<sup>15</sup>Greet Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the saints who are with them.<sup>16</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the churches of Christ greet you.<sup>17</sup>I appeal to you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them.<sup>18</sup>For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive.<sup>19</sup>For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil.<sup>20</sup>The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.<sup>21</sup>Timothy, my fellow worker, greets you; so do Lucius and Jason and Sosipater, my kinsmen.<sup>22</sup>I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord.<sup>23</sup>Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole church, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, and our brother Quartus, greet you.<sup>25</sup>Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages<sup>26</sup>but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith—<sup>27</sup>to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.
